Java Advanced

The runtime — threads and the memory model, locks and concurrent collections, executors, CompletableFuture and virtual threads, garbage collection, class loading, reflection, modules and performance measurement — as the warehouse becomes a concurrent reservation service that must stay correct and responsive under load.

How to use this module

Work through it at your own pace. Your section checkmarks, quiz answers, flashcard marks and notes are saved in this browser under a key scoped to this file, so closing the tab loses nothing and the earlier modules cannot overwrite it. Nothing is sent anywhere — this page makes no network requests at all. Press ? at any time for the keyboard shortcuts, and use Reset progress in the sidebar to start over.

Every code sample in this module was compiled and executed against a real JDK 21 as part of the build. If an Expected output block appears under a program, that text is what the program actually printed. This module adds one twist: much of it is about threads, and two runs of a threaded program rarely interleave the same way. So the verified programs print facts established after every thread has finished — all joined: true, a sorted list, a count compared with what it should be — never a raw number that depends on which thread won. Where you need to see a race unfold, an animation does it step by step and carries the Simulated badge. Java cannot run in a browser, and this module does not pretend otherwise.

The warehouse under load

Fundamentals built an InventoryService; Intermediate turned it into a pricing and reporting pipeline. Both were single-threaded on purpose. This module takes the same service and asks it to survive what production actually looks like:

  • Many pickers at once. Dozens of threads reserve BOLT-7 and NUT-3 simultaneously, and stock must never go negative or be double-counted (§1–§4).
  • A background re-pricing job that rewrites prices while orders are being totalled, without a report ever seeing half-updated state (§2, §3, §6).
  • Thousands of waiting requests served by a small pool, then by virtual threads, and the difference measured rather than asserted (§5, §7, §13).
  • A JVM that stays responsive while it does all of that: how the collector reclaims the garbage those orders produce, how the heap is sized, and how to read what the runtime tells you when it does not (§8, §9).
  • The machinery underneath — class loading, reflection, modules and serialization — which every framework you will meet is built from (§10–§12, §14).

Before you begin

Prerequisites

This module assumes Java Fundamentals and Java Intermediate, or the equivalent: you write idiomatic modern Java without thinking about the syntax, and you are here to learn what the runtime does with it. Each item below is leaned on directly, with the section that taught it:

Prerequisite skills, where they were taught, and what depends on them here
You should already be able to…Taught inBecause this module…
Implement equals and hashCode as a matched pairFundamentals §10puts those objects into ConcurrentHashMap, where a broken contract becomes a lost reservation
Make a class immutable with final fields and defensive copiesIntermediate §10treats immutability as the first and cheapest answer to every visibility problem in §2
Write a lambda and name its functional interfaceIntermediate §4submits Runnables and Callables to executors and chains Functions through CompletableFuture
Trace a stream pipeline and say where it is lazyIntermediate §5contrasts it with a parallel stream and a work-stealing pool in §5 and §13
Declare a record and consume a sealed type with a pattern switchIntermediate §8, §9models reservation outcomes as a sealed result type and serializes records in §14

What you need installed

A JDK 21 or newer — virtual threads (§7) and the Thread.ofPlatform() builder are final only from 21. Every diagnostic tool this module uses ships inside the JDK: jcmd, jstack, jfr, jconsole and javap live next to javac in its bin directory. No IDE, no profiler licence, nothing to download.

java -version       # expect: openjdk version "21.x" or newer
jcmd -l             # lists the JVMs you can attach to; an empty list is fine for now
jfr --version       # the Flight Recorder command-line tool (§13)

A machine with at least two cores makes the races in §1 reproducible. On a single core they are rarer, not absent — which is the whole point of §2.

Three habits to unlearn

Everything you wrote in the first two modules ran on one thread, and one thread lets you get away with assumptions that are simply false once there are two. Each of these is a bug you will write unless you consciously stop:

  • "count++ is one operation." It is three — load, add, store — and another thread can run between any two of them. §1 shows the increment vanish; §4 shows the one-instruction replacement.
  • "If I wrote it, the other thread can read it." Not unless something orders the write before the read. Without that, the reader is allowed to see the old value forever. §2 names the rules that create the ordering, and there are only a handful.
  • "One thread per task." A platform thread costs a megabyte of stack and a kernel object; ten thousand of them do not fit. §5 pools them, §7 replaces them with something a thousand times cheaper, and both come with new failure modes.

The contract

Learning objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to do each of the following without reaching for a reference. The final quiz tests exactly these fourteen.

  1. Explain what a thread owns (its stack and program counter) and shares (the heap), why count++ is three operations, and how to read a thread dump.
  2. State the happens-before rules that make a write visible to another thread, and why volatile guarantees visibility but not atomicity.
  3. Choose between synchronized, ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock and StampedLock, and prevent deadlock by lock ordering or tryLock with a timeout.
  4. Use AtomicInteger/LongAdder, ConcurrentHashMap.compute*/merge, CopyOnWriteArrayList and BlockingQueue correctly, and explain compare-and-swap.
  5. Size a thread pool for CPU-bound versus I/O-bound work, handle rejected tasks, and shut a pool down so the JVM can exit.
  6. Compose CompletableFuture chains with thenCompose, thenCombine, exceptionally/handle, timeouts and allOf, and say which thread runs each stage.
  7. Explain what a virtual thread is, how it mounts on a carrier, what pinning is, and when virtual threads do not help.
  8. Describe generational collection, what G1 and ZGC each optimise for, the three categories of GC pause, and how to read a GC log line.
  9. Reason about heap sizing flags (-Xms, -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage), metaspace, and the symptoms of an undersized heap versus a leak.
  10. Trace class loading, linking and initialization order, and the parent-delegation model, and diagnose NoClassDefFoundError versus ClassNotFoundException.
  11. Use reflection and annotations safely (and say what they cost), and state when a MethodHandle or VarHandle is the better tool.
  12. Declare a module with requires, exports, opens and uses/provides, and explain strong encapsulation and --add-opens.
  13. Measure before optimising: name the JIT tiers, the JMH pitfalls (dead-code elimination, constant folding, warm-up), and what JFR records.
  14. Serialize safely: why Serializable is a liability, how records serialize, and the shape of an HttpClient call with a timeout.
Deliberately out of scope

Frameworks — Spring, Jakarta EE, Micronaut, Quarkus — and build tools such as Maven and Gradle are not covered: every one of them is built from the mechanisms this module teaches, and they make far more sense once you know what a class loader, a proxy and a thread pool actually do. The Foreign Function & Memory API (the successor to JNI) and GraalVM native image each get a single mention where they fit, not a treatment. Distributed systems, databases and networking beyond one HTTP call are other courses entirely.

Section 1

Threads, stacks and the shared heap

A thread is the unit the operating system schedules: a program counter that says which instruction runs next, a set of registers, and a stack holding the frames of the methods it is currently inside — their parameters and local variables. Each thread has its own. What threads do not have their own copy of is the heap: every object, every field, every array element lives in one shared space that all threads of the process see. That split is the whole subject of this module. Locals are private and therefore safe; fields are shared and therefore need rules.

Picture the warehouse. Three pickers walking the aisles each carry their own clipboard — that is a stack. The stock board on the wall is the heap. Two pickers can write on their own clipboards all day without conflict; the moment both update the same line on the board, the number can be wrong, and nobody is told.

What each thread owns versus what all threads share
Per thread (private)Per process (shared)
Program counter — where this thread is in the codeThe heap — every object and array, including Strings and boxed values
The stack — one frame per active method call, holding parameters and localsstatic fields, which are heap data attached to a class
Registers, and whatever the JIT cached in themLoaded classes, the constant pool, interned strings
ThreadLocal values, the interrupt flag, the thread's name and daemon statusOpen files, sockets, the process's memory limit

One consequence is worth stating plainly: a reference held in a local variable is private, but the object it points to is not. Two threads holding references to the same ArrayList are sharing it, however private the variables look.

Worked example

Three ways to create a thread, a daemon, an interruption, and a demonstration that recursion on one thread cannot disturb another. Note what the program prints: nothing until every thread has been joined, and then only facts whose value does not depend on which thread ran first.

javaThreadBasics.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
 
public class ThreadBasics {
    // shared heap: every thread sees the same list, so it must be a thread-safe one
    static final List<String> results = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
    static volatile boolean flagRestored;
 
    // each call lives in a frame on the CALLING thread's stack: three threads can
    // recurse through this at once and n never interferes between them
    static int depth(int n) {
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        return 1 + depth(n - 1);
    }
 
    static class Picker extends Thread {                               // 1. subclass Thread
        private final String sku;
        Picker(String sku) { super("picker-" + sku); this.sku = sku; }
        @Override public void run() { results.add(sku + " depth=" + depth(500)); }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        Thread a = new Picker("BOLT-7");
        Thread b = new Thread(() -> results.add("NUT-3 depth=" + depth(700)), "picker-NUT-3");   // 2. Runnable
        Thread c = Thread.ofPlatform().name("picker-CAM-9")                                       // 3. builder (Java 21)
                         .start(() -> results.add("CAM-9 depth=" + depth(900)));              //    already started
 
        Thread housekeeping = new Thread(() -> {
            while (true) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } }
        }, "housekeeping");
        housekeeping.setDaemon(true);          // a daemon does not keep the JVM alive
        housekeeping.start();
 
        Thread sleeper = new Thread(() -> {
            try { Thread.sleep(10_000); }
            catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();                    // restore the flag for whoever is above us
                flagRestored = Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted();
            }
        }, "sleeper");
        sleeper.start();
        sleeper.interrupt();                   // cooperative: sleep throws, the loop above decides what to do
 
        a.start(); b.start();
        a.join(); b.join(); c.join(); sleeper.join();                  // nothing below runs until all four have finished
 
        List<String> sorted = new ArrayList<>(results);
        Collections.sort(sorted);
        System.out.println("all joined           : " + (!a.isAlive() && !b.isAlive() && !c.isAlive()));
        System.out.println("results (sorted)     : " + sorted);
        System.out.println("states after join    : " + a.getState() + " " + b.getState() + " " + c.getState());
        System.out.println("interrupt restored   : " + flagRestored);
        System.out.println("daemon still running : " + housekeeping.isAlive() + " (the JVM exits regardless)");
        System.out.println("this thread          : " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}
Expected output
all joined           : true
results (sorted)     : [BOLT-7 depth=500, CAM-9 depth=900, NUT-3 depth=700]
states after join    : TERMINATED TERMINATED TERMINATED
interrupt restored   : true
daemon still running : true (the JVM exits regardless)
this thread          : main

Four things to take from it:

  • Subclassing Thread is the oldest form and the worst. It couples the work to the worker. Pass a Runnable (or, from §5 on, submit it to a pool) so the same task can run on any thread. The Java 21 builder Thread.ofPlatform() is the modern spelling and has a sibling, ofVirtual(), in §7.
  • start() creates the thread; run() does not. Calling a.run() directly would execute the picker's code on main, sequentially, with no second thread at all — a mistake that compiles and "works".
  • join() is how a thread waits for another to finish. It is also a memory barrier: after it returns you are guaranteed to see everything the joined thread wrote (§2). That is why the results are read only after the joins.
  • The daemon is still alive when main ends, and the JVM exits anyway. The JVM shuts down when the last non-daemon thread finishes. Forget setDaemon(true) on a background loop and your program never exits; set it on a thread doing real work and that work is cut off mid-write.

Thread states

A thread is always in exactly one of six states, and Thread.getState() reports it. The names matter because they are what a thread dump shows you when something is stuck.

The six thread states, how a thread enters each, and what a dump shows
StateMeaningHow you get there
NEWCreated, not yet startednew Thread(…) before start()
RUNNABLERunning, or ready and waiting for a corestart(); the OS decides when it actually runs
BLOCKEDWaiting to enter a synchronized block another thread holdsContended monitor (§3). The classic sign of lock contention in a dump
WAITINGWaiting indefinitely for another thread to actObject.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park() — most idle pool workers sit here
TIMED_WAITINGWaiting with a deadlineThread.sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms), tryLock(timeout)
TERMINATEDrun() returned or threwCannot be restarted: a second start() throws IllegalThreadStateException

count++ is three operations

The compiler turns count++ on a field into a load from the heap into a register, an add, and a store back. Between any two of those steps the scheduler can switch to another thread, which does the same three steps on the same field. Step through two threads incrementing once each and watch one increment disappear.

A lost update Simulated ← → to step
Source
static int count = 0;              // shared, on the heap
 
// Thread A                        // Thread B
int rA = count;      // load        int rB = count;      // load
rA = rA + 1;         // add         rB = rB + 1;         // add
count = rA;          // store       count = rB;          // store
 
// both threads ran count++ once
Heap and registers
Standard output

Seeing it happen for real

Four pickers each increment a plain int a million times, and in parallel an AtomicInteger the same number of times. A CountDownLatch holds all four at a start line so they genuinely run together. The program prints the comparison, not the number: the number is different on every run and every machine, which is itself the lesson.

javaLostUpdate.java
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
 
public class LostUpdate {
    static int plain;                                   // plain++ is load, add, store: three steps
    static final AtomicInteger atomic = new AtomicInteger();
    static final int PICKERS = 4, PER_PICKER = 1_000_000;
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);      // a start gate, so all four run at once
        Thread[] pickers = new Thread[PICKERS];
        for (int t = 0; t < PICKERS; t++) {
            pickers[t] = new Thread(() -> {
                try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; }
                for (int i = 0; i < PER_PICKER; i++) {
                    plain++;                            // RACE: another thread can store between our load and our store
                    atomic.incrementAndGet();           // one indivisible read-modify-write
                }
            }, "picker-" + t);
            pickers[t].start();
        }
        go.countDown();
        for (Thread p : pickers) p.join();
 
        int expected = PICKERS * PER_PICKER;
        System.out.println("expected               : " + expected);
        System.out.println("plain int lost updates : " + (plain < expected));
        System.out.println("AtomicInteger exact    : " + (atomic.get() == expected));
    }
}
Expected output
expected               : 4000000
plain int lost updates : true
AtomicInteger exact    : true

Run it yourself and print plain: you will typically see somewhere between one and three million, different every time. Nothing about the program is random. The variation is the scheduler, and a program whose answer depends on the scheduler has a race condition.

Explore the race

How many increments survive? Simulated

A seeded scheduler runs each thread for a random slice of load / add / store steps before switching. Every switch that lands between a load and its store costs an increment. This is a model of the race, not a JVM; press Run again for a different interleaving.

Stopping a thread: interruption is a request

There is no safe way to kill a thread from outside; Thread.stop() was removed in Java 20 because it left locks and data in whatever state they happened to be in. What exists instead is a flag. t.interrupt() sets it; the target thread checks it, or is woken from a blocking call by InterruptedException, and decides for itself how to stop cleanly. Three rules keep this cooperative scheme working:

// a loop that does not block must check the flag itself
while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
    pickNextOrder();                 // CPU work, no sleeping or waiting
}
// fall out of the loop: release resources, return normally

isInterrupted() reads the flag and leaves it set. The static Thread.interrupted() reads and clears it, which is almost never what you want in a loop condition.

// a blocking call throws InterruptedException AND CLEARS THE FLAG
try {
    queue.take();                    // or sleep(), join(), wait(), Future.get()
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // put the flag back for the code that called us
    return;                               // then stop what we were doing
}

If you cannot propagate the exception (because a Runnable cannot throw it), restoring the flag is how the next layer up — a pool worker, a loop — finds out it was asked to stop. This is exactly what the sleeper thread in the worked example does.

try {
    Thread.sleep(1_000);
} catch (InterruptedException e) { }    // the interruption is now lost forever

The empty catch is the single most common concurrency bug an IDE will write for you. The flag was cleared by sleep, you threw the exception away, and the thread that asked you to stop will wait for you indefinitely. At minimum, restore the flag.

Reading a thread dump

When a service hangs, the first diagnostic is a thread dump: jstack <pid>, or jcmd <pid> Thread.print, or Ctrl+Break on Windows and kill -3 elsewhere. It lists every thread, its state, and its stack. Here are two entries from a stuck warehouse, annotated:

"picker-BOLT-7" #23 prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=12.50ms elapsed=0.31s tid=0x... nid=0x1f2c waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at InventoryService.reserve(InventoryService.java:41)
        - waiting to lock <0x000000071a2b3c40> (a java.lang.Object)
        at Picker.run(Picker.java:18)
 
"picker-NUT-3" #24 prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=15.00ms elapsed=0.31s tid=0x... nid=0x1f2d runnable
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
        at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0(Native Method)     <- reading from a socket while HOLDING the lock
        - locked <0x000000071a2b3c40> (a java.lang.Object)
        at InventoryService.reserve(InventoryService.java:44)
        at Picker.run(Picker.java:18)

Read it bottom-up per thread, and look for the same monitor address in a waiting to lock line and a locked line. Here picker-NUT-3 holds monitor 0x…3c40 while doing network I/O, and picker-BOLT-7 is BLOCKED waiting for it. One slow socket has serialised every picker in the building. The fix is in §3: never hold a lock across I/O. A dump with many threads BLOCKED on one address is contention; two threads each waiting to lock what the other has locked is deadlock, and modern dumps print Found one Java-level deadlock at the bottom to save you the search.

Thread gotchas
  • An exception in a thread kills only that thread. run() throwing an unchecked exception prints a stack trace to stderr and the thread dies; main never hears about it and the JVM carries on. Install Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler to log and alert, and prefer executors (§5), whose Future captures the exception for you.
  • ThreadLocal leaks in pools. A value set on a pool thread stays on it after the task ends, and the next task — possibly a different user's request — inherits it. Always remove() in a finally. Java 21 adds ScopedValue (preview) for exactly this reason.
  • Priorities are hints the OS may ignore. setPriority does nothing on most Linux configurations. Code that relies on a high-priority thread running first is wrong on the machine it will be deployed to.
  • sleep and wait are not the same kind of thing. Thread.sleep pauses and holds any locks it owns. Object.wait releases the monitor it is called on and must be called inside synchronized — it is a signalling primitive (§3), not a delay.
  • Platform threads are expensive. Each reserves roughly a megabyte of stack and costs a kernel call to create and to switch. Creating one per request works until the first busy day; §5 and §7 are the answers.

Check yourself

1.A colleague replaces picker.start() with picker.run() "because it's clearer". The program still prints the right results. What actually changed?

B. run() is an ordinary method; calling it executes the body on whichever thread called it. Only start() asks the OS for a new thread and then invokes run() on it. The results are correct because the work still happened — just with no concurrency, which is why this mistake survives code review.

A is the misconception exactly. C: the thread object stays NEW because it never started; join() on a NEW thread simply returns immediately. D: that exception comes from calling start() twice, not from calling run().

2.In the worked example, the sleeper's catch block calls Thread.currentThread().interrupt() after catching InterruptedException. Why is that necessary?

C. Blocking methods clear the flag as they throw. If the catch block cannot propagate the exception — a Runnable cannot — re-setting the flag is the only way a pool worker or an outer loop can learn that the thread was asked to stop.

A: interrupt() is called on the current thread, not on the interrupter. B would be true of a loop that slept again, but the point is the opposite — to stop, not to keep throwing. D: a thread terminates when run() returns, flag or no flag.

3.main has returned. Which of these threads keep the JVM running? Select all that apply.

A and C. The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread ends, and a thread's state — sleeping, blocked, running — is irrelevant to that rule. Both A and C are ordinary platform threads, non-daemon by default, so each alone keeps the process alive, possibly forever.

B is a daemon: the JVM abandons it at exit, loop or no loop. D: virtual threads are always daemon threads (§7), so a program whose only remaining work is on virtual threads exits — a surprise the first time it happens.

Section 2

The Java memory model: visibility and happens-before

Section 1 showed two threads corrupting a counter because an increment is three steps. This section is about a stranger problem: a thread writes a field, and another thread never sees the write at all. Not late — never. The reason is that "memory" is not one place. Each core has its own caches and a store buffer that holds writes before they reach shared memory; the JIT compiler keeps fields in registers and hoists reads out of loops; the CPU executes instructions out of order when they do not depend on each other. Every one of those optimisations is invisible to a single thread, which is exactly why they are legal. A second thread can see all of them.

The Java Memory Model (JLS chapter 17) is the contract that says when a write by one thread is guaranteed to be visible to a read by another. It is stated in terms of one relation, happens-before: if action A happens-before action B, then B sees the effects of A. If two threads touch the same field, at least one of them writes, and there is no happens-before between them, the program has a data race, and the JMM promises almost nothing about what the reader sees.

Worked example

Three guaranteed-visible patterns, each printing a fact that the JMM promises. There is deliberately no fourth program showing the failure: a racy read may happen to see the write on your machine today, so a demonstration of it cannot be verified. The failure is shown as a step-through below instead.

javaVisibility.java
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
 
public class Visibility {
    static volatile boolean stop;      // volatile: a write is guaranteed to become visible, promptly
    static int reserved;               // plain: visible to another thread only across a happens-before edge
    static int payload;                // plain, but published under a volatile write below
    static volatile int ready;
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        // 1. a volatile flag stops a spinning reader
        CountDownLatch spinning = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Thread reader = new Thread(() -> {
            spinning.countDown();
            while (!stop) Thread.onSpinWait();         // without volatile the JIT may hoist this read out of the loop
        }, "reader");
        reader.start();
        spinning.await();
        stop = true;
        reader.join(5_000);
        System.out.println("reader stopped         : " + !reader.isAlive());
 
        // 2. Thread.join is a happens-before edge: the plain write is visible after it
        Thread writer = new Thread(() -> reserved = 42, "writer");
        writer.start();
        writer.join();
        System.out.println("seen after join        : " + reserved);
 
        // 3. piggybacking: a plain write BEFORE a volatile write is visible AFTER the volatile read
        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> { payload = 7; ready = 1; }, "producer");
        producer.start();
        while (ready == 0) Thread.onSpinWait();
        System.out.println("payload after volatile : " + payload);
        producer.join();
    }
}
Expected output
reader stopped         : true
seen after join        : 42
payload after volatile : 7

Take stop and delete the word volatile. The program is now allowed to hang: the JIT, seeing a loop that reads a field no one in this thread writes, may read it once into a register and spin on the register forever. On HotSpot it frequently does exactly that once the loop gets hot. The second block shows that you do not always need volatile: join() is itself an edge, so reserved is plain and still correctly seen. The third block is the pattern the JDK's own collections rely on — one volatile write "publishes" every plain write that preceded it in program order.

The happens-before edges

There are only a handful of ways to create the relation, and every concurrency utility in the JDK is built from them. Within one thread, program order is an edge; between threads, you need one of the rows below. The relation is transitive, which is what makes piggybacking work: plain write → volatile write → volatile read → plain read chains into one guarantee.

The happens-before rules of the Java memory model
This…happens-before thisWhat it gives you
Each action in a threadevery later action in the same threadProgram order. Single-threaded code just works
Unlocking a monitor (synchronized exit)every later lock of the same monitorEverything done inside one synchronized block is visible inside the next one on that lock
A write to a volatile fieldevery later read of that fieldVisibility without a lock, plus the piggybacked plain writes before it
Thread.start()every action in the started threadConfigure an object, then hand it to a new thread, safely
Every action in a threadjoin() returning, or isAlive() returning falseResults are safe to read after joining — the pattern every verified program here uses
t.interrupt()the target detecting itRarely relied on directly
The end of a constructor that writes final fieldsany read of those fields through a reference published after itCorrectly constructed immutable objects need no synchronisation at all
java.util.concurrent hand-offs: countDown→await, put→take, submit→task→get, Atomic* write→read(as documented on each class)The reason you rarely write volatile by hand

Which synchronisation makes the write visible?

A writer sets reserved = 42; a reader reads it. Is 42 guaranteed?

Watch a reordering

The question that convinces most people the JMM is real: two threads, two plain fields, and an outcome that seems impossible if you believe writes happen in the order you wrote them.

Can r1 be 1 while r2 is 0? Simulated ← → to step
Source
int x = 0, y = 0;                  // two plain fields
 
// Thread 1              // Thread 2
x = 1;                   int r1 = y;
y = 1;                   int r2 = x;
 
// is (r1, r2) == (1, 0) possible?
What each thread observes
Outcome

What volatile is, and is not

A volatile field gives you two things: every read sees the most recent write (visibility), and the compiler and CPU may not move memory operations across it in the forbidden directions (ordering). It gives you nothing about atomicity. volatile int hits; hits++ is still a load, an add and a store, and two threads still lose updates — the only difference from §1 is that each load is guaranteed fresh, which does not help. The rule of thumb:

  • A flag or a reference that one thread writes and others read: volatile is enough and cheaper than a lock.
  • A value that is read-modified-written: a lock (§3) or an atomic (§4). Never volatile alone.
  • Several fields that must change together: a lock. volatile on each of them individually does not make the combination consistent.

Safe publication and the cheapest correct answer

Most visibility bugs are publication bugs: one thread builds an object and another thread reaches it through a shared reference before, or in the middle of, construction. The final-field rule in the table removes the problem for immutable objects: once a constructor has finished writing final fields, any thread that obtains a reference to the object afterwards — through any path, locked or not — sees those fields correctly initialised. A record (Intermediate §8) is therefore safe to hand between threads with no synchronisation at all. The single most effective concurrency technique is to make shared data immutable and share it freely.

When you genuinely need a lazily created, shared mutable singleton, the two correct shapes are:

class PriceTable {
    private static volatile PriceTable instance;    // volatile is the whole point: without it a thread can see a non-null reference to a half-built object
    static PriceTable get() {
        PriceTable p = instance;                    // one volatile read on the fast path
        if (p == null) {
            synchronized (PriceTable.class) {
                p = instance;
                if (p == null) instance = p = new PriceTable();
            }
        }
        return p;
    }
}
 
// simpler, just as lazy, and no volatile: class initialization is done once, under a lock the JVM owns (§10)
class PriceTable2 {
    private static class Holder { static final PriceTable2 INSTANCE = new PriceTable2(); }
    static PriceTable2 get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}

Double-checked locking without the volatile was the canonical broken idiom of the early 2000s, and it is still broken. The holder idiom avoids the question entirely, which is why it should be your default.

Memory model gotchas
  • "It works on my machine" proves nothing. A racy program is allowed to behave as you hoped. It will stop doing so on a different CPU, after a JIT recompilation, or at 3 a.m. under load. The only evidence that matters is a happens-before edge you can point to.
  • Synchronising the writer alone is not enough. The edge is from an unlock to a later lock of the same monitor. A synchronized setter and an unsynchronised getter is still a data race.
  • volatile on an array or collection reference covers the reference only. volatile int[] counts makes the assignment of a new array visible; counts[3]++ is still a plain, racy read-modify-write of an element. The same holds for a volatile List.
  • 64-bit plain fields may tear. A non-volatile long or double write is permitted to happen as two 32-bit halves, so a reader can see a value that was never written. In practice 64-bit JVMs do not tear, but the specification allows it; volatile forbids it.
  • Leaking this from a constructor defeats the final guarantee. Registering the object as a listener, or starting a thread that captures it, inside the constructor publishes it before the freeze. Use a static factory that constructs, then registers.
  • VarHandle offers finer modes. setRelease/getAcquire give the ordering half of volatile without the full fence, and setOpaque gives only progress. They are for library authors; §11 shows the mechanism.

Check yourself

1.static volatile int hits; and two threads each run hits++ a million times. After both join, what can hits be?

B. volatile guarantees that each load sees the latest store and that stores are ordered; it does nothing to make the three steps of ++ one step. Two threads can still load the same value and both store value+1. The theoretical minimum is tiny because, pathologically, almost every increment could be overwritten.

A and C confuse visibility with atomicity; no architecture makes a three-instruction sequence atomic by itself. D: it compiles fine, which is precisely the trap. Use AtomicInteger (§4).

2.The writer sets reserved = 42 inside synchronized (lockA). The reader reads reserved inside synchronized (lockB), where lockB is a different object. Is the reader guaranteed to see 42?

C. The monitor rule is per object. Locking lockB says nothing about writes made under lockA, so this is a data race dressed up as synchronised code — slower than no locks and exactly as wrong.

A describes a mental model ("flush the caches") that HotSpot does not implement and the JMM does not promise. B: wall-clock order is not happens-before; "after" in real time guarantees nothing without an edge. D: a final field cannot be reassigned, so the scenario could not exist; the final rule is about construction, not later writes.

3.Which of these create a happens-before edge between two threads? Select all that apply.

A, B and C. Thread start, thread termination observed through join, and the documented hand-off of every java.util.concurrent synchroniser are all edges in the table above.

D is the one that looks like it works. Sleeping orders nothing: when the reader wakes it performs an ordinary load, and the JMM permits that load to return the stale value no matter how long it waited. Code that "fixes" a visibility bug with a sleep has hidden it.

Section 3

synchronized, ReentrantLock and deadlock

§1 showed that count++ is three operations and that two threads interleaving them lose updates. §2 showed that even a correctly ordered write may never become visible to another core. A lock solves both at once: while one thread holds it, no other thread can enter the guarded code (mutual exclusion), and releasing it publishes everything that thread wrote to whoever acquires it next (happens-before). That second guarantee is the one people forget. A lock is not only a turnstile; it is also a memory barrier.

Every Java object carries an intrinsic lock, also called its monitor. synchronized (obj) { … } acquires obj's monitor on entry and releases it on exit, by any path — a return, an exception, a break. A synchronized instance method locks this; a synchronized static method locks the Class object. The monitor is reentrant: a thread that already owns it can acquire it again, which is why a synchronized method may call another synchronized method on the same object without deadlocking against itself.

Worked example: one lock, one invariant

Eight picker threads leave a CountDownLatch gate together and hammer one InventoryService holding 500 units. The invariant — reserved + on hand = 500, and every attempt is either applied or refused — must survive 800 racing calls. Then a synchronized method re-enters another, and a bounded buffer hands 1,000 items between two threads using nothing but wait and notifyAll.

javaSynchronized.java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
 
public class Synchronized {
 
    /* One lock, one invariant: onHand never goes negative and every
       reservation is either fully applied or refused. */
    static final class InventoryService {
        private int onHand;
        private int reserved;
        private int refused;
 
        InventoryService(int onHand) { this.onHand = onHand; }
 
        synchronized boolean reserve(int qty) {
            if (qty > onHand) { refused++; return false; }
            onHand -= qty;
            reserved += qty;
            return true;
        }
 
        synchronized void release(int qty) { onHand += qty; }
 
        // a synchronized method calling another synchronized method on the
        // same object: the thread already owns the monitor, so it re-enters
        synchronized boolean reserveTwice(int qty) {
            return reserve(qty) && reserve(qty);
        }
 
        synchronized int onHand() { return onHand; }
        synchronized int reserved() { return reserved; }
        synchronized int refused() { return refused; }
    }
 
    /* A bounded buffer built on wait/notifyAll: the textbook shape every
       BlockingQueue implements for you. */
    static final class BoundedBuffer {
        private final Deque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private final int capacity;
        BoundedBuffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }
 
        synchronized void put(int item) throws InterruptedException {
            while (items.size() == capacity) wait();   // loop, never if: spurious wakeups
            items.addLast(item);
            notifyAll();
        }
 
        synchronized int take() throws InterruptedException {
            while (items.isEmpty()) wait();
            int item = items.removeFirst();
            notifyAll();
            return item;
        }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        // ── 8 pickers hammer one service ────────────────────────────────────
        InventoryService inv = new InventoryService(500);
        int threads = 8, perThread = 100, qty = 1;
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(threads);
        for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) {
            Thread picker = new Thread(() -> {
                try { start.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; }
                for (int i = 0; i < perThread; i++) inv.reserve(qty);
                done.countDown();
            }, "picker-" + t);
            picker.start();
        }
        start.countDown();                          // everyone leaves the gate together
        done.await();
 
        int attempts = threads * perThread;         // 800 attempts against 500 units
        System.out.println("attempts        = " + attempts);
        System.out.println("reserved        = " + inv.reserved());
        System.out.println("refused         = " + inv.refused());
        System.out.println("on hand         = " + inv.onHand());
        System.out.println("invariant holds = " + (inv.reserved() + inv.onHand() == 500
                                                   && inv.reserved() + inv.refused() == attempts));
 
        // ── reentrancy ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        InventoryService small = new InventoryService(10);
        System.out.println("reentered       = " + small.reserveTwice(3) + " (on hand " + small.onHand() + ")");
 
        // ── wait / notifyAll producer-consumer ──────────────────────────────
        BoundedBuffer buffer = new BoundedBuffer(4);
        int n = 1000;
        long[] consumedSum = new long[1];
        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) buffer.put(i); buffer.put(-1); }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        }, "producer");
        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (int v; (v = buffer.take()) != -1; ) consumedSum[0] += v; }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        }, "consumer");
        producer.start(); consumer.start();
        producer.join(10_000); consumer.join(10_000);
        System.out.println("consumed sum    = " + consumedSum[0] + " (expected " + ((long) n * (n + 1) / 2) + ")");
    }
}
Expected output
attempts        = 800
reserved        = 500
refused         = 300
on hand         = 0
invariant holds = true
reentered       = true (on hand 4)
consumed sum    = 500500 (expected 500500)

Three things to notice. The reserve check-then-act — is there enough? then subtract — is exactly the compound operation §1 broke, and the only reason it survives 800 racing calls is that both halves sit inside the same monitor. The accessors are synchronized too: without that, a reader could see a stale onHand even after every writer has finished (§2). And every wait() sits inside a while, because the JVM is permitted to wake a waiting thread for no reason at all — a spurious wakeup — and because notifyAll wakes every waiter, most of whom will find the condition still false.

Watch the monitor

A monitor is more than a flag. It has an owner, an entry set of threads blocked trying to acquire it, and a wait set of threads that owned it, called wait(), and gave it up until notified. Step through a producer and a consumer sharing the buffer above.

Owner, entry set, wait set Simulated ← → to step
Source
synchronized int take() throws InterruptedException {
    while (items.isEmpty()) wait();
    int item = items.removeFirst();
    notifyAll();
    return item;
}
 
synchronized void put(int item) throws InterruptedException {
    while (items.size() == capacity) wait();
    items.addLast(item);
    notifyAll();
}
Monitor state
Buffer

What to lock on

synchronized methods lock this, which means any code holding a reference to your object can lock it too — and can therefore block your methods or, worse, deadlock against them. A private lock object keeps the lock inside the class:

private final Object lock = new Object();          // nobody outside can synchronize on it
 
void reserve(int qty) {
    synchronized (lock) { /* … */ }
}

Lock on a final field, never on a value that can be reassigned, and never on a boxed primitive or a String — Integer.valueOf(7) and "lock" are shared instances, so two unrelated classes can end up contending for the same monitor without knowing it.

synchronized or a Lock object?

  • Cannot be forgotten. Release is structural: the block ends, the lock is released. There is no unlock() to miss on an exception path.
  • Cannot be interrupted, timed, or tried. A thread blocked on a monitor waits until it gets it. If the owner never releases, the waiter is stuck for the life of the process.
  • One condition per lock. wait/notifyAll is a single wait set, so "not full" and "not empty" waiters are woken together and most go straight back to sleep.
  • The default. Correct, well optimised by the JIT (lock elision, biased-then-lightweight locking), and readable. Reach for ReentrantLock only when you need something from the next tab.
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();          // new ReentrantLock(true) = fair
private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
 
void put(int item) throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lockInterruptibly();                                      // or lock(), or tryLock(2, SECONDS)
    try {
        while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await();
        items.addLast(item);
        notEmpty.signal();                                         // wake ONE consumer, not everyone
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();                                             // the one line you must never forget
    }
}
  • tryLock() returns immediately; tryLock(timeout) gives up after a while; lockInterruptibly() lets a blocked thread be cancelled. These are the deadlock escape hatches a monitor lacks.
  • Multiple Conditions let producers and consumers wait on different queues, so a signal() wakes the right kind of thread.
  • Fairness (new ReentrantLock(true)) hands the lock to the longest waiter. It prevents starvation at a real throughput cost; the default is unfair and usually right.
  • Always unlock() in finally, and acquire outside the try — if lock() itself throws, there is nothing to release.
private final ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
 
int onHand(String sku) {
    rw.readLock().lock();                      // many readers at once …
    try { return stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
}
void restock(String sku, int qty) {
    rw.writeLock().lock();                     // … but a writer waits for all of them, and excludes everyone
    try { stock.merge(sku, qty, Integer::sum); } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
}
 
// StampedLock: optimistic reads that pay nothing when no write intervened
private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
int onHandOptimistic(String sku) {
    long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();       // no lock taken at all
    int v = stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0);
    if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {                 // a write happened meanwhile: fall back to a real read lock
        stamp = sl.readLock();
        try { v = stock.getOrDefault(sku, 0); } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
    }
    return v;
}
  • A read-write lock pays off only when reads vastly outnumber writes and the critical sections are long enough to amortise its heavier bookkeeping. For a short map lookup, a plain lock or a ConcurrentHashMap (§4) is faster.
  • StampedLock is not reentrant and has no conditions. Its optimistic mode is the fastest read path in the JDK when writes are rare, and the easiest to misuse: read every field you need before validate, and never dereference something you read optimistically until it validates.

Deadlock

Two threads, two locks, opposite order. Thread A holds BOLT-7's lock and wants NUT-3's; thread B holds NUT-3's and wants BOLT-7's. Neither can proceed, neither will release, and because monitors cannot be interrupted or timed out, the JVM will sit there until someone kills it. Four conditions must all hold for this to happen — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a circular wait — and the cures each break one of them. This is what jstack prints when it finds the cycle:

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"mover-A":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x000001e7 (object 0x7b2c, a LockOrdering$Stock),
  which is held by "mover-B"
"mover-B":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x000001e9 (object 0x7b30, a LockOrdering$Stock),
  which is held by "mover-A"
 
Java stack information for the threads listed above:
"mover-A":
        at LockOrdering.transferNaive(LockOrdering.java:31)
        - waiting to lock <0x7b2c> (a LockOrdering$Stock)
        - locked <0x7b30> (a LockOrdering$Stock)

Worked example: two cures that cannot deadlock

Two mover threads shift one unit at a time between BOLT-7 and NUT-3, 5,000 times each, in opposite directions — exactly the shape above. The naive version is deliberately absent: it would hang this page's build. Both versions here complete, and the latch's timed await is the proof: a deadlock would return false.

javaLockOrdering.java
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
 
public class LockOrdering {
 
    static final class Stock {
        final String sku;
        final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
        int units;
        Stock(String sku, int units) { this.sku = sku; this.units = units; }
    }
 
    /* Cure 1: every thread acquires in the same global order, here by SKU.
       Two threads moving stock in opposite directions still lock BOLT-7
       first and NUT-3 second, so neither can hold what the other needs. */
    static void transferOrdered(Stock from, Stock to, int qty) {
        Stock first = from.sku.compareTo(to.sku) < 0 ? from : to;
        Stock second = first == from ? to : from;
        first.lock.lock();
        try {
            second.lock.lock();
            try {
                if (from.units >= qty) { from.units -= qty; to.units += qty; }
            } finally { second.lock.unlock(); }
        } finally { first.lock.unlock(); }
    }
 
    /* Cure 2: no fixed order, but never wait forever. A thread that cannot
       get the second lock within the timeout releases the first and retries,
       so a would-be deadlock resolves itself. */
    static boolean transferTimed(Stock from, Stock to, int qty) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 1000; attempt++) {
            if (from.lock.tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                try {
                    if (to.lock.tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                        try {
                            if (from.units >= qty) { from.units -= qty; to.units += qty; }
                            return true;
                        } finally { to.lock.unlock(); }
                    }
                } finally { from.lock.unlock(); }
            }
            Thread.onSpinWait();            // back off, then try again
        }
        return false;
    }
 
    interface Transfer { void run(Stock from, Stock to, int qty) throws InterruptedException; }
 
    static void race(String label, Transfer transfer) throws InterruptedException {
        Stock bolt = new Stock("BOLT-7", 10_000), nut = new Stock("NUT-3", 10_000);
        int moves = 5_000;
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(2);
        Runnable ab = () -> { try { start.await(); for (int i = 0; i < moves; i++) transfer.run(bolt, nut, 1); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } done.countDown(); };
        Runnable ba = () -> { try { start.await(); for (int i = 0; i < moves; i++) transfer.run(nut, bolt, 1); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } done.countDown(); };
        new Thread(ab, "mover-A").start();
        new Thread(ba, "mover-B").start();
        start.countDown();
        boolean finished = done.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);   // a real deadlock would time out here
        System.out.println(label);
        System.out.println("  transfers completed = " + finished);
        System.out.println("  total units         = " + (bolt.units + nut.units) + " (expected 20000)");
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        race("ordered locks", LockOrdering::transferOrdered);
        race("tryLock with timeout", (f, t, q) -> transferTimed(f, t, q));
    }
}
Expected output
ordered locks
  transfers completed = true
  total units         = 20000 (expected 20000)
tryLock with timeout
  transfers completed = true
  total units         = 20000 (expected 20000)

The ordering cure breaks circular wait: with one global order there can be no cycle. The order must be something stable and total — a SKU string, a database id, a sequence number assigned at construction. System.identityHashCode is a popular choice that is almost right: two objects can share an identity hash, and then you need a tie-breaker lock. The timeout cure breaks hold-and-wait: a thread that cannot get everything it needs gives back what it has. It costs a retry loop and the possibility of livelock — both threads backing off and retrying in lockstep forever — which a small random delay before retrying removes. The third cure is the simplest and often the best: use one lock for both accounts, and accept the lost parallelism.

Will it deadlock?

Two threads, two locks

Starvation, livelock and granularity

Starvation is a thread that is runnable but never scheduled onto the lock — unfair locks under heavy contention can do this to a slow waiter; a fair ReentrantLock is the fix, at a cost. Livelock is the opposite of deadlock in appearance and identical in effect: every thread is busy, nothing progresses, because each keeps responding to the others. Granularity is the trade-off you make in choosing what a lock covers. One lock for the whole inventory is simple and serialises every picker; one lock per SKU is parallel and invites deadlock the moment an operation touches two. Lock striping — N locks, each covering a slice of the keys chosen by hash — is the middle path, and it is how ConcurrentHashMap was built before it moved to per-bin locking (§4).

Lock gotchas
  • if (cond) wait(); is a bug. Spurious wakeups are permitted by the specification, and notifyAll wakes threads whose condition is still false. Always while.
  • notify() can lose a wakeup. With two kinds of waiter on one monitor, waking "one thread" may wake the wrong kind, which goes back to sleep, and the right one never hears. Use notifyAll, or a ReentrantLock with two Conditions.
  • Calling out while holding a lock. Invoking a listener, a callback or an unknown object's method inside synchronized means its code runs under your lock. If it takes another lock, you have just created a lock-order dependency you cannot see. Copy what you need, release, then call.
  • Locking on this in a public class publishes your lock. Any caller can synchronized (yourObject) and block you. Prefer a private lock object.
  • synchronized on a static method and on an instance method are different locks. One guards the Class, the other the instance. Code that assumes they exclude each other is wrong.
  • A ReentrantLock without finally is a lock that leaks on the first exception. Every thread that arrives afterwards blocks forever, and the dump shows them all waiting on a lock whose owner has long since died.

Check yourself

1.A thread calls wait() inside a synchronized method. What happens to the monitor?

C. wait() atomically releases the monitor and parks the thread in the wait set. After a notify, the thread moves to the entry set and competes for the monitor like any other; wait() returns only once it owns it again — which is why the code after wait() may safely touch shared state, and why it must re-check its condition.

A would make producer-consumer impossible: the producer could never enter. B describes a thread running shared-state code without the lock, which Java never permits here. D is backwards — that exception is thrown when you call wait() without owning the monitor.

2.Which of these remove the possibility of deadlock between two threads that each need locks L1 and L2? Select all that apply.

B and D. A global acquisition order makes a circular wait impossible; a timed acquisition that gives back what it holds removes hold-and-wait. Each breaks one of the four necessary conditions.

A changes who gets a lock first, not whether two threads can each hold one and want the other. C is a different API with the same blocking semantics: lock() waits forever exactly as a monitor does. The escape hatches are tryLock and lockInterruptibly, and only if you use them.

3.Integer stock = 500; … synchronized (stock) { stock--; } — eight threads run this. What is wrong?

A. Integer is immutable: stock-- unboxes, decrements and boxes a new object into the variable. The next thread to arrive synchronizes on that new object, not the one the current holder owns, so there is no mutual exclusion at all. Lock on a final field that is never reassigned, and keep the counter separate from the lock.

B is wishful: boxing adds allocation, not atomicity. C — it compiles; any object reference is a legal monitor. D — cached Integers in −128…127 are shared instances, which is a different hazard (unrelated code contending on the same lock), but sharing a monitor causes contention, not deadlock.

Section 4

Atomics and concurrent collections

A lock is a pessimist: it assumes a conflict and makes everyone else wait. For a single-word update — a counter, a reference, a stock level — there is a cheaper optimist: do the computation without any lock, then ask the CPU to install the result only if nobody else changed the value meanwhile, and retry if someone did. That instruction is compare-and-swap (CAS), every modern processor has it, and java.util.concurrent is built on it from the atomics up to ConcurrentHashMap.

// what AtomicInteger.compareAndSet(expected, update) does, as one indivisible hardware step:
if (memory[address] == expected) { memory[address] = update; return true; }
else                             { return false; }

Because the compare and the swap are one instruction, two threads that both read 500, both compute 499, and both try to CAS — one succeeds and one is told no. The loser re-reads (499), recomputes (498), tries again. Nobody blocked, no lock was held, and no update was lost. Under light contention this beats a lock comfortably; under heavy contention the retries pile up, which is where LongAdder comes in.

Worked example: counting and reserving without a lock

javaAtomics.java
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;
 
public class Atomics {
 
    /* A bounded decrement with compare-and-swap: read, compute, try to swap,
       and retry if another thread moved the value first. No lock, and the
       invariant (never below zero) still holds. */
    static final class Stock {
        private final AtomicInteger units;
        Stock(int units) { this.units = new AtomicInteger(units); }
 
        boolean reserve(int qty) {
            while (true) {
                int current = units.get();
                if (current < qty) return false;            // refuse: nothing to swap
                if (units.compareAndSet(current, current - qty)) return true;
                // CAS failed: someone else changed units between get and CAS — loop
            }
        }
        int units() { return units.get(); }
    }
 
    record Price(String sku, int cents) { }
 
    static void runAll(int threads, Runnable body) throws InterruptedException {
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(threads);
        for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) {
            new Thread(() -> {
                try { start.await(); body.run(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { }
                done.countDown();
            }).start();
        }
        start.countDown();
        done.await();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        // ── incrementAndGet is one indivisible operation ────────────────────
        AtomicInteger picks = new AtomicInteger();
        runAll(8, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) picks.incrementAndGet(); });
        System.out.println("picks            = " + picks.get() + " (expected 800000)");
 
        // ── CAS loop: 8 threads fight over 600 units, 100 attempts each ─────
        Stock stock = new Stock(600);
        AtomicInteger reserved = new AtomicInteger(), refused = new AtomicInteger();
        runAll(8, () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
                if (stock.reserve(1)) reserved.incrementAndGet(); else refused.incrementAndGet();
            }
        });
        System.out.println("reserved         = " + reserved.get());
        System.out.println("refused          = " + refused.get());
        System.out.println("units left       = " + stock.units());
        System.out.println("never negative   = " + (stock.units() >= 0 && reserved.get() + stock.units() == 600));
 
        // ── LongAdder: the counter for write-heavy contention ────────────────
        LongAdder cents = new LongAdder();
        runAll(8, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) cents.add(25); });
        System.out.println("revenue (cents)  = " + cents.sum());
 
        // ── AtomicReference: swap an immutable record atomically ────────────
        AtomicReference<Price> price = new AtomicReference<>(new Price("BOLT-7", 80));
        runAll(4, () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                Price old, updated;
                do {
                    old = price.get();
                    updated = new Price(old.sku(), old.cents() + 1);
                } while (!price.compareAndSet(old, updated));
            }
        });
        System.out.println("price after 4000 = " + price.get());
    }
}
Expected output
picks            = 800000 (expected 800000)
reserved         = 600
refused          = 200
units left       = 0
never negative   = true
revenue (cents)  = 2000000
price after 4000 = Price[sku=BOLT-7, cents=4080]

The reserve loop is the pattern to memorise: read, decide, CAS, retry. The refusal happens before the CAS, on the value you just read, and the CAS guarantees that the value you decided on is the value you are decrementing. Note that the result is deterministic even though the interleaving is not: 800 attempts against 600 units must produce exactly 600 reservations, because the invariant is enforced on every path. The AtomicReference variant shows the same loop on an object: because Price is an immutable record, "update" means "build a new one and swap the reference", and a torn read is impossible.

Watch a CAS loop

Contending threads retrying compareAndSet Simulated
 

Every round, all the threads that are still running read the same current value and compute the same candidate, exactly one CAS wins, and the rest discover their expected is stale and go round again. With n contenders, finishing the whole batch costs about n(n+1)/2 CAS attempts for n successful updates — quadratic wasted work. That is the contention cost of optimism, and the reason the next two tools exist.

LongAdder, and the ABA problem

LongAdder is a counter that notices contention and splits itself into per-thread cells; sum() adds them up on read. Writes stop colliding, so eight threads incrementing see almost no retries, at the cost of a sum() that is a snapshot rather than an atomic value and cannot be used for a CAS. Use it for statistics and metrics — things you increment constantly and read occasionally. Use AtomicLong when you need compareAndSet or an exact read-modify-write result.

ABA is the one blind spot of CAS. Thread 1 reads value A and gets descheduled. Thread 2 changes A to B and back to A. Thread 1 wakes, its CAS sees A, and succeeds — even though the world changed underneath it. For a plain counter that is harmless. For a reference to the head of a lock-free list it is a corruption, because the node that looks the same may now have a different next. AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with a version counter so that an A that went away and came back no longer compares equal. In practice you will rarely write such a structure; you need to recognise the hazard when reading one.

Worked example: the concurrent collections

Each collection in java.util.concurrent makes a specific promise, and the shape of the API tells you what it is. ConcurrentHashMap.merge is atomic for that key, which is what makes it safe to count from eight threads without a lock. computeIfAbsent is atomic too, which is what makes "create the list if missing, then add" safe. A CopyOnWriteArrayList lets you iterate while others write, by copying the array on every write. An ArrayBlockingQueue blocks a producer when full and a consumer when empty. And a ConcurrentSkipListMap is the sorted map you reach for when a TreeMap would need a lock.

javaConcurrentMaps.java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentSkipListMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
 
public class ConcurrentMaps {
 
    enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MOTION }
    record Product(String sku, Category category) { }
 
    static final List<Product> CATALOGUE = List.of(
        new Product("BOLT-7", Category.FASTENER), new Product("NUT-3", Category.FASTENER),
        new Product("PIN-2", Category.FASTENER),  new Product("GIRD-1", Category.STRUCTURAL),
        new Product("ROD-4", Category.STRUCTURAL), new Product("CAM-9", Category.MOTION));
 
    static void runAll(int threads, Runnable body) throws InterruptedException {
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(threads);
        for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) {
            new Thread(() -> { try { start.await(); body.run(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } done.countDown(); }).start();
        }
        start.countDown();
        done.await();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        // ── merge: an atomic read-modify-write per key ──────────────────────
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> picks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        runAll(8, () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                Product p = CATALOGUE.get(i % CATALOGUE.size());
                picks.merge(p.sku(), 1, Integer::sum);           // never lost, never double-counted
            }
        });
        System.out.println("picks by sku       = " + new TreeMap<>(picks));
        int total = picks.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
        System.out.println("total picks        = " + total + " (expected 8000)");
 
        // ── computeIfAbsent: build a multimap without a race on the list ────
        ConcurrentHashMap<Category, CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>> byCategory = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        runAll(4, () -> {
            for (Product p : CATALOGUE) {
                byCategory.computeIfAbsent(p.category(), k -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()).addIfAbsent(p.sku());
            }
        });
        System.out.println("by category        = " + new TreeMap<>(byCategory));
 
        // ── compute: a conditional decrement that cannot go negative ────────
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> onHand = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of("BOLT-7", 500));
        runAll(8, () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
                onHand.compute("BOLT-7", (k, v) -> v != null && v > 0 ? v - 1 : v);   // 800 attempts, floor at 0
            }
        });
        System.out.println("BOLT-7 on hand     = " + onHand.get("BOLT-7") + " (800 attempts against 500)");
 
        // ── CopyOnWriteArrayList: iterate a snapshot while others write ─────
        CopyOnWriteArrayList<String> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("audit", "metrics"));
        for (String l : listeners) {                       // the iterator holds the old array ...
            if (l.equals("audit")) listeners.add("alerts");  // ... so this write does not throw
        }
        System.out.println("listeners          = " + listeners);
 
        // ── ArrayBlockingQueue: hand-off with a poison pill ─────────────────
        BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(8);
        int n = 2_000;
        long[] consumed = new long[1];
        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) queue.put(i); queue.put(-1); }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            try { for (int v; (v = queue.take()) != -1; ) consumed[0] += v; }
            catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        producer.start(); consumer.start();
        producer.join(10_000); consumer.join(10_000);
        System.out.println("consumed sum       = " + consumed[0] + " (expected " + ((long) n * (n + 1) / 2) + ")");
        System.out.println("queue drained      = " + queue.isEmpty());
 
        // ── ConcurrentSkipListMap: concurrent AND sorted ────────────────────
        ConcurrentSkipListMap<String, Integer> sorted = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>();
        runAll(4, () -> { for (Product p : CATALOGUE) sorted.merge(p.sku(), 1, Integer::sum); });
        System.out.println("skip list          = " + sorted);
        System.out.println("first / last key   = " + sorted.firstKey() + " / " + sorted.lastKey());
 
        // ── nulls are rejected at runtime, not by the compiler ──────────────
        try { picks.put("HUB-8", null); }
        catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("null value         = NullPointerException"); }
    }
}
Expected output
picks by sku       = {BOLT-7=1336, CAM-9=1328, GIRD-1=1336, NUT-3=1336, PIN-2=1336, ROD-4=1328}
total picks        = 8000 (expected 8000)
by category        = {FASTENER=[BOLT-7, NUT-3, PIN-2], STRUCTURAL=[GIRD-1, ROD-4], MOTION=[CAM-9]}
BOLT-7 on hand     = 0 (800 attempts against 500)
listeners          = [audit, metrics, alerts]
consumed sum       = 2001000 (expected 2001000)
queue drained      = true
skip list          = {BOLT-7=4, CAM-9=4, GIRD-1=4, NUT-3=4, PIN-2=4, ROD-4=4}
first / last key   = BOLT-7 / ROD-4
null value         = NullPointerException

Every printed line is a fact that holds on any machine — totals after every thread has joined, maps copied into a TreeMap for a stable order. The CopyOnWriteArrayList loop is the one that would have thrown ConcurrentModificationException on an ArrayList (Fundamentals §12); here the iterator walks the array that existed when it was created, and the write builds a new one. And the last line is a trap that compiles cleanly: ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values at runtime, because in a concurrent map "get returned null" must mean absent unambiguously — there is no safe moment to call containsKey afterwards.

Inside ConcurrentHashMap

The table is the same array of bins as HashMap (Intermediate §11). A write to an empty bin is a single CAS on the array slot — no lock at all. A write to an occupied bin synchronizes on that bin's first node, so two writers collide only if their keys hash to the same bin. With 16 bins that is frequent; with 65,536 it almost never happens. Resizing is cooperative: threads that arrive during a resize help move bins instead of waiting.

The older design, lock striping (Java 5–7's 16 "segments"), is where the mental model "a concurrent map is N small synchronized maps" comes from. It is still a useful picture, and still the right technique when you build your own.

  • Atomic per key: put, putIfAbsent, remove(k, v), replace, compute, computeIfAbsent, computeIfPresent, merge. The remapping function runs while the bin is locked, so it must be short and must not touch the same map — doing so throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update, or deadlocks on older versions.
  • Not atomic across keys: moving stock from BOLT-7 to NUT-3 is two operations, and a reader in between sees the units in neither place. For a cross-key invariant you are back to a lock (§3) or a transaction.
  • Not atomic at all: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) — a check-then-act that another thread can interleave. The fix is the single-call putIfAbsent. The same bug on Collections.synchronizedMap is the classic one: every method is synchronized, and every pair of methods is a race.
  • Reads never block. get takes no lock; it relies on volatile node fields (§2) to see a completed write. A read that races with a write sees either the old value or the new one, never a torn mixture.
  • size() is an estimate. It is computed from counter cells (the LongAdder trick) and may be stale by the time you read it. Use mappingCount(), which returns a long, and never write if (map.size() == 0) as a synchronisation device.
  • Iterators are weakly consistent. They never throw ConcurrentModificationException, they reflect the state at some point since creation, and they may or may not show a write made during iteration. That is the right contract for a map being modified under you; it is also why you cannot count on an iteration seeing a concurrent insert.

Which collection?

Concurrent collections and when to use each
You needUseThe trade-off
A shared map, mostly reads, some writesConcurrentHashMapno nulls; per-key atomicity only; size() approximate
A shared sorted map or setConcurrentSkipListMap / SetO(log n) like TreeMap, more memory per entry
A list of listeners: read on every event, changed rarelyCopyOnWriteArrayListevery write copies the whole array — O(n) per add
Producer–consumer hand-off, boundedArrayBlockingQueuefixed capacity; one lock for both ends
Producer–consumer, optionally bounded, higher throughputLinkedBlockingQueueseparate locks per end; unbounded by default — a memory risk (§5)
Tasks ordered by priority or due timePriorityBlockingQueue / DelayQueueunbounded; head is the smallest, not the oldest
Direct hand-off with no bufferingSynchronousQueueput blocks until a take arrives — the queue behind cached thread pools
A non-blocking FIFO with no capacity boundConcurrentLinkedQueuelock-free CAS; size() is O(n) and approximate
Concurrent-collection gotchas
  • A thread-safe collection does not make your code thread-safe. Every compound action — check-then-put, read-then-update, "get the list then add to it" — is still a race unless you use the single atomic method that does both.
  • A mutable value inside a concurrent map is unprotected. map.get(k).add(x) on an ArrayList value races just as it would anywhere. Either the value is itself concurrent (as the CopyOnWriteArrayList above), or you update it inside compute.
  • computeIfAbsent with an expensive function runs it while the bin is locked, blocking other writers to that bin. Compute outside, then putIfAbsent, if the work is slow.
  • CopyOnWriteArrayList as a work queue is a classic performance bug: every add copies the array, so N adds cost O(N²). It is for rarely-changing lists only.
  • Blocking queues and interruption. put/take throw InterruptedException; swallowing it and looping makes the thread uncancellable. Restore the flag or propagate.

Check yourself

1.Eight threads each run if (!stock.containsKey(sku)) stock.put(sku, 100); on a ConcurrentHashMap. What can go wrong?

B. containsKey and put are each atomic; the pair is not. Here the overwrite is harmless (same value), but with put(sku, new Stock()) one thread's object is lost and any reference it handed out points at an orphan. putIfAbsent and computeIfAbsent make the check and the write one atomic step.

A is the misconception this section exists to remove. C — concurrent maps never throw it. D — the map's own invariant (one entry per key) is always maintained; the race is in your logic, not its structure.

2.A metrics counter is incremented by 64 threads thousands of times per second and read once a minute. Which type fits best?

C. Write-heavy, read-rare, no need for an exact atomic read-modify-write: that is the LongAdder profile exactly. Sixty-four threads hitting one AtomicLong would spend most of their time retrying a failed CAS on the same cache line.

A is correct but slow under this contention. B is wrong, not merely slow: volatile makes the read and the write each visible, but ++ is still read-add-write and loses updates (§2). D works and serialises 64 threads through one monitor.

3.Which statements about ConcurrentHashMap are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. Weakly consistent iteration is the contract; and the remapping function executing under the bin lock is why it must be fast and must not re-enter the map.

B is false — null is rejected with NullPointerException, because get returning null must unambiguously mean absent. C is false — atomicity is per key; two merge calls are two independent operations with a visible gap between them.

Section 5

Executors, thread pools and Future

Creating a platform thread costs a system call, a megabyte or so of reserved stack, and a scheduler entry; and a server that creates one per request will, under load, create ten thousand of them and fall over. A thread pool separates the two decisions that new Thread(task).start() fuses together: what work to run, and how many threads should run it. You submit tasks; a fixed set of worker threads pulls them from a queue. The number of threads is a resource budget you set once, and the queue is where the overflow waits.

The abstraction is ExecutorService: submit a Runnable (no result) or a Callable<T> (a result, and it may throw), and get back a Future<T> — a handle to a result that does not exist yet. get() blocks until it does; get(timeout) gives up; cancel interrupts; and an exception thrown by the task is stored and re-thrown from get, wrapped in ExecutionException.

Worked example: a pool's whole life

One program, five lessons: a fixed pool running twenty Callables through invokeAll; a task that throws; an orderly shutdown; a scheduled task; and then a deliberately tiny pool that is handed more work than it can hold, twice — once with the default abort policy and once with caller-runs.

javaPoolExecutors.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture;
