import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
 
public class PoolExecutors {
 
    record Reservation(String sku, int qty) { }
 
    static final String[] SKUS = { "BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "CAM-9", "GIRD-1", "ROD-4" };
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // ── a fixed pool runs 20 Callables; invokeAll waits for every one ───
        ExecutorService pool = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named("picker"));
        List<Callable<Reservation>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
            final int n = i;
            tasks.add(() -> new Reservation(SKUS[n % SKUS.length], n + 1));
        }
        List<Future<Reservation>> futures = pool.invokeAll(tasks);
 
        int totalQty = 0;
        List<String> skus = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Future<Reservation> f : futures) {
            Reservation r = f.get();                       // already complete after invokeAll
            totalQty += r.qty();
            if (!skus.contains(r.sku())) skus.add(r.sku());
        }
        System.out.println("tasks completed    = " + futures.stream().allMatch(Future::isDone));
        System.out.println("total qty          = " + totalQty + " (1+2+...+20)");
        System.out.println("skus (sorted)      = " + skus.stream().sorted().toList());
 
        // ── a task that throws: the exception travels inside the Future ─────
        Future<Integer> bad = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("BOLT-7 out of stock"); });
        try {
            bad.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            System.out.println("wrapped cause      = " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        }
 
        // ── orderly shutdown: no new tasks, finish queued ones, then wait ───
        pool.shutdown();
        System.out.println("terminated         = " + pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
 
        // ── scheduling: run once after a delay ──────────────────────────────
        ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(named("repricer"));
        ScheduledFuture<String> reprice = scheduler.schedule(() -> "reprice done", 20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        System.out.println("scheduled result   = " + reprice.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
        scheduler.shutdown();
 
        // ── rejection: 1 thread, a queue of 1, 3 tasks that block ───────────
        CountDownLatch gate = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ThreadPoolExecutor tiny = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
            1, 1, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1), named("tiny"),
            new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());                    // the default handler
        Runnable blocker = () -> { try { gate.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } };
        tiny.execute(blocker);                                          // taken by the one thread
        tiny.execute(blocker);                                          // sits in the queue
        try {
            tiny.execute(blocker);                                      // nowhere to go
            System.out.println("third task         = accepted");
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
            System.out.println("third task         = rejected (RejectedExecutionException)");
        }
        gate.countDown();
        tiny.shutdown();
        System.out.println("tiny terminated    = " + tiny.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
 
        // ── CallerRunsPolicy: the submitting thread does the work itself ────
        CountDownLatch gate2 = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ThreadPoolExecutor polite = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
            1, 1, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1), named("polite"),
            new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
        AtomicInteger ranOnMain = new AtomicInteger();
        Runnable blocker2 = () -> { try { gate2.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } };
        polite.execute(blocker2);
        polite.execute(blocker2);
        polite.execute(() -> { if (Thread.currentThread().getName().equals("main")) ranOnMain.incrementAndGet(); });
        System.out.println("overflow ran on    = " + (ranOnMain.get() == 1 ? "the caller (main)" : "a pool thread"));
        gate2.countDown();
        polite.shutdown();
        System.out.println("polite terminated  = " + polite.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
    }
 
    // name your threads: a dump full of "pool-3-thread-7" is useless at 3 a.m.
    static ThreadFactory named(String prefix) {
        AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger();
        return r -> new Thread(r, prefix + "-" + n.incrementAndGet());
    }
}
Expected output
tasks completed    = true
total qty          = 210 (1+2+...+20)
skus (sorted)      = [BOLT-7, CAM-9, GIRD-1, NUT-3, ROD-4]
wrapped cause      = IllegalStateException: BOLT-7 out of stock
terminated         = true
scheduled result   = reprice done
third task         = rejected (RejectedExecutionException)
tiny terminated    = true
overflow ran on    = the caller (main)
polite terminated  = true

Two details carry most of the weight. First, shutdown() is polite: it stops accepting work and lets queued tasks finish, and the pool is only terminated once the last one has — which is what awaitTermination waits for. shutdownNow() instead interrupts every worker and returns the tasks that never started; it is the emergency stop, and it only works on tasks that honour interruption. Forget to shut a pool down and its non-daemon workers keep the JVM alive after main returns — the classic "my program never exits". Second, the tiny pool: one worker takes the first task directly, the second sits in the one-slot queue, and the third has nowhere to go. What happens next is the rejection policy — the default throws, and CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitting thread do the work itself, which is a crude but effective form of back-pressure: a producer that is busy running a task is not producing more.

Watch a pool fill up

A ThreadPoolExecutor has a core size, a maximum size and a queue, and the order in which it uses them surprises almost everyone. It does not grow to the maximum when the core threads are busy. It queues. Only when the queue is full does it add threads beyond the core, and only when both the queue and the maximum are exhausted does it reject.

core 2, max 4, queue capacity 2 Simulated ← → to step
Source
var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    2, 4, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS,          // core, max, keep-alive
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2));        // bounded queue
 
pool.execute(t1);
pool.execute(t2);
pool.execute(t3);
pool.execute(t4);
pool.execute(t5);
pool.execute(t6);
pool.execute(t7);   // all seven tasks are long-running

The factory methods, and what each one hides

Executors factory methods and their configuration
Factorycore / maxQueueThe risk
newFixedThreadPool(n)n / nLinkedBlockingQueue, unboundedthe queue grows without limit — a slow consumer means an OutOfMemoryError hours later
newCachedThreadPool()0 / Integer.MAX_VALUESynchronousQueue (no buffering)one thread per concurrent task, unbounded — a burst creates thousands of threads
newSingleThreadExecutor()1 / 1unboundedserial execution guaranteed; same unbounded queue
newScheduledThreadPool(n)n / MAX_VALUEDelayedWorkQueuea task that throws is silently cancelled from its schedule
newWorkStealingPool()parallelism = coresper-worker dequesa ForkJoinPool; daemon threads, so it does not keep the JVM alive
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()one virtual thread per tasknoneno pooling, no bound — see §7 for when that is right

The factories are convenient and every one of them hides an unbounded something. For a service that must survive a burst, construct ThreadPoolExecutor yourself with a bounded queue and a rejection policy you chose on purpose. The work-stealing pool is the ForkJoinPool, and the one you get from ForkJoinPool.commonPool() is shared with every parallel stream in the JVM: a blocking task submitted there starves every parallelStream() in the process.

How many threads?

Size a pool from what the tasks do

Scheduling, and the exception that kills it

var scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1, named("repricer"));
 
// fixed RATE: starts every 60 s regardless of how long the last run took (runs may pile up)
scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(repricer::run, 0, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
 
// fixed DELAY: waits 60 s after the previous run FINISHES — the safer default for most jobs
scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(repricer::run, 0, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

If a scheduled task throws, the scheduler does not log it, does not retry it, and does not run it again: the exception is captured in the ScheduledFuture nobody is reading, and the job silently stops forever. Every periodic task should catch Throwable at its top level, log, and return — or be wrapped by a utility that does.

Executor gotchas
  • A task that throws into execute() kills its worker thread and the exception goes to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler — usually stderr, usually unnoticed. A task submitted with submit() stores the exception in its Future instead, and if nobody calls get(), it is lost entirely. Either way: catch inside the task.
  • Blocking inside a pool on a result from the same pool — task A submits task B and calls get() — deadlocks the moment all workers are doing the same thing. Nobody is free to run B. The fix is CompletableFuture (§6), or two pools.
  • No shutdown, no exit. Pool threads are non-daemon by default; a forgotten shutdown() keeps the JVM running after main. Java 19+ ExecutorService is AutoCloseable: try (var pool = …) shuts down and waits.
  • Default thread names make a thread dump unreadable. Pass a ThreadFactory that names threads after the pool's purpose.
  • Future.cancel(true) only interrupts. A task that never checks isInterrupted() or calls a blocking method keeps running to completion, holding its thread.
  • ThreadLocal values survive between tasks on a pooled thread. Clear them in finally, or the next task inherits the previous request's user.

Check yourself

1.A ThreadPoolExecutor has core 4, max 16, and an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Under sustained load, how many threads will it run?

C. Growth beyond core happens only when the queue rejects an offer. An unbounded queue never rejects, so maximumPoolSize is dead configuration: the pool runs 4 threads and the queue grows until memory runs out. This is the single most common thread-pool misconfiguration.

A is what everyone assumes and what the executor does not do. B would require the executor to watch queue length, which it does not; it only reacts to an offer failing. D — rejection needs a full queue and a full pool; this queue is never full.

2.A task submitted with submit() throws a NullPointerException, and the caller never calls get() on the returned Future. Where does the exception go?

B. submit wraps the task in a FutureTask, which catches everything and stores it for get() to re-throw as ExecutionException. No get(), no report — the worker thread quietly moves on to the next task.

A is what happens with execute(), which does not wrap the task; the exception then kills the worker and the pool replaces it. C — the task has not even run when submit returns. D — nothing an individual task does shuts a pool down.

3.Your program finishes main but the process never exits. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

A and C. Both create non-daemon threads, and the JVM exits only when every non-daemon thread has ended. The fixed pool's idle core threads live forever; the scheduler's thread is waiting for the next run.

B — ForkJoinPool workers are daemon threads, so they never hold the JVM open (which is also why work left in the common pool at exit is simply abandoned). D — an unread Future is an object, not a thread; it holds nothing open.

Section 6

CompletableFuture: composing asynchronous work

§5 ended with a Future, and a Future can do exactly two things: block until the value arrives, or tell you whether it has arrived yet. There is no way to say "and when it does, do this with it". A quote that needs a price and a stock level and then a supplier lookup becomes a thread that blocks three times in a row, which is the thread-per-wait design that pools were meant to avoid.

CompletableFuture is a Future that is also a completion stage: a cell that will hold either a value or a failure, to which you attach the next step before the value exists. When the cell completes, the attached steps run, each producing a new cell. A pipeline of lookups becomes a description of what to do, written once on the calling thread, and executed by whichever threads happen to finish the work. The two questions that explain everything in this section are which thread runs a stage and what happens to a failure.

Worked example

Every lookup here is a stand-in for a remote call. The pool is explicit, every future is joined before anything is printed, and the fan-out results are sorted, so the output is the same on every machine even though the work is genuinely parallel.

javaComposing.java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
 
public class Composing {
 
    record Quote(String sku, int priceInCents, int onHand) {
        String line() { return sku + " @ " + priceInCents + "c, " + onHand + " on hand"; }
    }
 
    static final Map<String, Integer> PRICES = Map.of(
            "BOLT-7", 80, "NUT-3", 25, "CAM-9", 2300, "GIRD-1", 120_000, "ROD-4", 4500);
    static final Map<String, Integer> STOCK = Map.of(
            "BOLT-7", 400, "NUT-3", 1200, "CAM-9", 2, "GIRD-1", 3, "ROD-4", 40);
    static final Map<String, String> SUPPLIER = Map.of("BOLT-7", "ACME", "NUT-3", "ACME", "CAM-9", "KINETIC");
 
    // Each "lookup" stands in for a remote call: slow, independent, may fail.
    static int price(String sku) {
        Integer p = PRICES.get(sku);
        if (p == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown sku " + sku);
        return p;
    }
    static int stock(String sku) { return STOCK.getOrDefault(sku, 0); }
    static String supplier(String sku) { return SUPPLIER.getOrDefault(sku, "none"); }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
 
        // 1. Two independent lookups, combined when BOTH are done.
        CompletableFuture<Integer> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> price("BOLT-7"), pool);
        CompletableFuture<Integer> stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> stock("BOLT-7"), pool);
        CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = price.thenCombine(stock, (p, s) -> new Quote("BOLT-7", p, s));
        System.out.println("thenCombine  = " + quote.join().line());
 
        // 2. A dependent lookup: thenCompose flattens a stage that itself returns a future.
        CompletableFuture<String> supplier = quote.thenCompose(q ->
                CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> supplier(q.sku()), pool));
        System.out.println("thenCompose  = " + supplier.thenApply(s -> "supplied by " + s).join());
 
        // 3. A failing lookup. Nothing is thrown here: the failure is stored in the future.
        CompletableFuture<Integer> bad = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> price("NOPE"), pool);
        System.out.println("recovered    = " + bad.exceptionally(ex -> -1).join());
        System.out.println("handle       = " + bad.handle((v, ex) ->
                ex == null ? "value " + v : "failed: " + ex.getCause().getMessage()).join());
        String wrapping = bad.handle((v, ex) ->
                ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + " wrapping " + ex.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()).join();
        System.out.println("stage saw    = " + wrapping);
        try { bad.join(); }
        catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.println("join threw   = CompletionException -> " + e.getCause().getMessage()); }
        try { bad.get(); }
        catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get threw    = ExecutionException -> " + e.getCause().getMessage()); }
 
        // 4. Fan out five quotes, wait for all, read them back in a stable order.
        List<String> skus = List.of("ROD-4", "BOLT-7", "GIRD-1", "NUT-3", "CAM-9");
        List<CompletableFuture<Quote>> quotes = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String sku : skus) {
            quotes.add(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> price(sku), pool)
                    .thenCombine(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> stock(sku), pool),
                                 (p, s) -> new Quote(sku, p, s)));
        }
        CompletableFuture<Void> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(quotes.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0]));
        all.join();                                              // Void: it only says "every one is done"
        List<String> lines = quotes.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).map(Quote::line).sorted().toList();
        System.out.println("allOf        = done " + all.isDone() + ", " + lines.size() + " quotes");
        lines.forEach(l -> System.out.println("    " + l));
 
        // 5. A stage that never completes, bounded by a timeout (Java 9+).
        CompletableFuture<String> never = new CompletableFuture<>();
        System.out.println("onTimeout    = " + never.completeOnTimeout("cached quote", 50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join());
        CompletableFuture<String> never2 = new CompletableFuture<>();
        try { never2.orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); }
        catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.println("orTimeout    = " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()); }
 
        // 6. A value already in hand enters the same pipeline without touching a thread.
        System.out.println("completed    = " + CompletableFuture.completedFuture(21).thenApply(x -> x * 2).join());
 
        pool.shutdown();
        System.out.println("pool stopped = " + pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
    }
}
Expected output
thenCombine  = BOLT-7 @ 80c, 400 on hand
thenCompose  = supplied by ACME
recovered    = -1
handle       = failed: unknown sku NOPE
stage saw    = CompletionException wrapping IllegalArgumentException
join threw   = CompletionException -> unknown sku NOPE
get threw    = ExecutionException -> unknown sku NOPE
allOf        = done true, 5 quotes
    BOLT-7 @ 80c, 400 on hand
    CAM-9 @ 2300c, 2 on hand
    GIRD-1 @ 120000c, 3 on hand
    NUT-3 @ 25c, 1200 on hand
    ROD-4 @ 4500c, 40 on hand
onTimeout    = cached quote
orTimeout    = TimeoutException
completed    = 42
pool stopped = true

Six things to take from it, in order:

  • thenCombine joins two independent stages. Price and stock were submitted together and ran in parallel; the combining function ran once, after the later of the two finished, on whichever thread finished it.
  • thenCompose is for a step that returns a future. With thenApply you would have got a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<String>>. thenCompose unwraps it, exactly as flatMap does for Optional and streams (Intermediate §5, §7).
  • A failure is a value in the cell, not a thrown exception. price("NOPE") threw on a pool thread and nobody saw a stack trace. The future completed exceptionally, and every dependent stage sees that state wrapped in a CompletionException. exceptionally substitutes a value; handle sees both outcomes; join rethrows the wrapper and get rethrows an ExecutionException instead. Either way the real cause is one getCause() away.
  • allOf gives you Void. It signals that every input is done and nothing else; you read the values back from the inputs you kept. Sorting them is what makes the printed order stable.
  • Timeouts are a property of the stage. completeOnTimeout supplies a fallback, orTimeout fails the stage with a TimeoutException. Both exist since Java 9; before that, every timeout meant a blocking get(n, unit).
  • completedFuture is the unit. A value you already hold joins the pipeline without a thread, which is how caches and fast paths plug into the same code as the slow path.

Which thread runs what

A chain, two runs: one succeeds, one fails Simulated ← → to step
Source
CompletableFuture<Integer> stock =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> stock("CAM-9"), pool);   // stage A
 
CompletableFuture<Void> done = stock
    .thenApply(s -> new Quote("CAM-9", 2300, s))                 // stage B
    .thenCompose(q -> enrichAsync(q))                            // stage C: returns a future
    .exceptionally(ex -> Quote.unavailable("CAM-9"))             // stage D
    .thenAccept(q -> report(q));                                 // stage E
 
done.join();
Stages
Standard output

The rule the stepper shows: a non-async stage (thenApply, thenCompose, thenAccept…) runs on the thread that completes its input, or on the calling thread if the input was already complete when you attached it. An *Async stage is always handed to an executor: the one you pass, or ForkJoinPool.commonPool() if you pass none. Two consequences: a cheap stage should stay non-async to avoid a hand-off, and a stage that does real work after a fast input may run on your caller's thread unless you say Async.

The API by question

CompletableFuture methods grouped by the question they answer
You want to…UseNotes
start work on a threadsupplyAsync(supplier, executor) / runAsyncalways pass the executor; the common pool is sized for CPU work and shared with parallel streams
transform the valuethenApplythe map; function returns a plain value
chain a step that returns a futurethenComposethe flatMap; avoids a nested future
combine two independent futuresthenCombine(other, fn)runs when the later one completes
consume the value / just run afterthenAccept / thenRunresult type is Void
wait for manyallOf(cf…) / anyOf(cf…)allOf → Void; anyOf → Object, first to complete, including a failure
recover from failureexceptionally(fn)runs only on failure; return value replaces it
see both outcomes and produce a valuehandle((v, ex) -> …)exactly one of v, ex is non-null
observe both outcomes, change nothingwhenComplete((v, ex) -> …)logging/metrics; the result passes through, failure included
bound the waitorTimeout / completeOnTimeoutJava 9+; uses a shared scheduler thread
get the value on this threadjoin() / get()join is unchecked (CompletionException); get is checked (ExecutionException, InterruptedException)
wrap a value you already havecompletedFuture(v) / failedFuture(ex)no thread involved
Five ways this goes wrong in production
  • Blocking inside a stage. thenApply(x -> other.join()) ties up a pool thread doing nothing. With the common pool, which has cores − 1 threads, a handful of these deadlocks the whole JVM's async work. Compose instead of joining.
  • Forgetting the executor. supplyAsync(s) without an executor uses the common pool. Put I/O there and every parallel stream in the process slows down with you. Give I/O its own bounded pool (§5) or, in Java 21, a virtual-thread executor (§7).
  • A dropped failure. A future nobody joins or attaches a handler to fails silently. If you fire and forget, at least whenComplete a log line.
  • cancel() does not interrupt. It completes the cell with a CancellationException; the supplier keeps running to its end on the pool thread. If the work must stop, the task has to check a flag of its own.
  • Wrapping, twice. A failure inside exceptionally's own function, or a CompletionException rethrown from a stage, gets wrapped again. When unwrapping, loop on getCause() while the throwable is a CompletionException rather than calling it once.

One last thing. A pipeline of a dozen stages across three pools is powerful and very hard to read six months later: the structure of the computation is spread across callbacks, a failure in the middle produces a stack trace that names none of your methods, and cancelling a sub-task means nothing. §7 shows the other direction Java 21 is taking: give each concurrent task a cheap thread of its own and write the waiting as ordinary, sequential code.

Check yourself

1.CompletableFuture<Integer> a = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(1); a.thenApply(x -> heavyWork(x)); — which thread runs heavyWork?

C. thenApply is a non-async stage. Its input is already complete, so there is no completing thread to inherit; the stage runs immediately on the thread that attached it. If heavyWork takes a second, the caller is stuck for a second.

A is what thenApplyAsync would do. B: nothing in CompletableFuture creates threads; it only submits to executors. D: stages are eager, not lazy — a future is not a stream, and join only waits.

2.A stage's function is q -> fetchSupplierAsync(q), where fetchSupplierAsync returns CompletableFuture<Supplier>. You attach it with thenApply. What is the type of the result, and what should you have used?

B. thenApply wraps whatever the function returns, and the function returns a future, so you get a future of a future. thenCompose expects a function that returns a CompletionStage and flattens it: the outer stage completes when the inner one does.

A and C: it compiles, and the type is nested — the compiler is perfectly happy to infer CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Supplier>>, which is why this bug survives until someone tries to join() and gets a future back. D: thenCombine joins two independent futures with a two-argument function; here the second lookup depends on the first.

3.cf = supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("offline"); }, pool).thenApply(v -> v + 1); Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. The failure is stored in the first cell, skips the thenApply stage (which completes exceptionally with the same wrapped cause), and surfaces from join as a CompletionException. Attaching exceptionally anywhere downstream substitutes a value, and the chain continues normally from there.

B: a normal-path stage is never run on a failed input; it is bypassed. C: nothing is printed anywhere — the whole point, and the whole danger, of a stored failure is that it is silent until someone looks. An uncaught exception in a plain Thread would print; inside a CompletableFuture it is captured.

Section 7

Virtual threads and structured concurrency

Every thread you have met so far in this module is a platform thread: a thin wrapper over an operating-system thread, with a stack reserved up front (half a megabyte or more), created and scheduled by the kernel. That is why §5 taught you to pool them: you can afford a few hundred, not a few hundred thousand, and the thread-per-request server that is the simplest thing to write runs out of threads long before it runs out of CPU. §6 was one response to that — stop blocking, describe the work as a pipeline of callbacks, let a small pool execute it. It works, and it is hard to read, debug, and cancel.

Java 21's answer (JEP 444) is to make the thread itself cheap. A virtual thread is a thread whose stack lives on the heap as an ordinary object and which is scheduled not by the kernel but by the JVM, onto a small pool of platform threads called carriers. When a virtual thread blocks — on a socket, a sleep, a lock from java.util.concurrent — the JVM copies its frames off the carrier (unmounts it), and the carrier picks up another virtual thread. When the I/O completes, the virtual thread is mounted again on whichever carrier is free. The cost of a blocked virtual thread is a few hundred bytes of heap. You can have a million of them. And the code you write is the sequential, blocking code from Fundamentals, with no callbacks at all.

Worked example

Ten thousand pickers each wait ten milliseconds for a scanner. On platform threads that is either a 100-second sequential run or ten thousand OS threads. On virtual threads it is neither.

javaVirtualThreads.java
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
 
public class VirtualThreads {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        LongAdder done = new LongAdder();
        LongAdder virtualInside = new LongAdder();
 
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
                ex.submit(() -> {
                    Thread.sleep(10);                               // a blocking call: the thread unmounts
                    if (Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()) virtualInside.increment();
                    done.increment();
                    return null;
                });
            }
        }                                                           // close() waits for every task
        long seconds = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000_000L;
        System.out.println("tasks completed       = " + done.sum());
        System.out.println("all ran virtual       = " + (virtualInside.sum() == 10_000));
        System.out.println("100 s of sleeps took under 30 s = " + (seconds < 30));
 
        Thread picker = Thread.ofVirtual().name("picker-", 0).unstarted(() -> { });
        System.out.println("isVirtual             = " + picker.isVirtual());
        System.out.println("isDaemon              = " + picker.isDaemon());
        System.out.println("name                  = " + picker.getName());
        System.out.println("priority              = " + picker.getPriority() + " (always NORM_PRIORITY)");
        System.out.println("platform isVirtual    = " + Thread.ofPlatform().unstarted(() -> { }).isVirtual());
 
        // ThreadLocal is per thread, virtual or not. That is what makes it expensive at a million threads.
        ThreadLocal<String> tenant = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> "unset");
        Thread vt = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> tenant.set("warehouse-A"));
        vt.join();
        System.out.println("main sees ThreadLocal = " + tenant.get());
 
        // A j.u.c. lock parks the virtual thread and frees its carrier for someone else.
        ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
        LongAdder counter = new LongAdder();
        try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) {
                ex.submit(() -> { lock.lock(); try { counter.increment(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } });
            }
        }
        System.out.println("locked increments     = " + counter.sum());
    }
}
Expected output
tasks completed       = 10000
all ran virtual       = true
100 s of sleeps took under 30 s = true
isVirtual             = true
isDaemon              = true
name                  = picker-0
priority              = 5 (always NORM_PRIORITY)
platform isVirtual    = false
main sees ThreadLocal = unset
locked increments     = 1000

On the machine this page was built on, the ten thousand sleeps finished in well under a second; the output says "under 30 s" only because a verified output must be true on any machine. Read the rest of it:

  • newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor creates a thread per task and never reuses one. It is an ExecutorService, so the submit/shutdown API from §5 is unchanged, and it is AutoCloseable: the try-with-resources block ends only when every task has finished. That is the simplest form of structured concurrency — the tasks cannot outlive the block that started them.
  • Virtual threads are always daemon threads with normal priority, and setDaemon(false) or setPriority on one is ignored or rejected. The JVM does not wait for them at exit; your executor's close does.
  • ThreadLocal works exactly as before, which is the problem: a value cached per thread is now cached per task, a million times over. Prefer passing context as parameters, and watch for scoped values (ScopedValue, preview in 21, final in a later release) which were designed for this.
  • A ReentrantLock unmounts cleanly. A thousand virtual threads contended for one lock; each one that had to wait was parked off its carrier, so the carriers kept serving others. The same program with a synchronized block behaves differently in 21, as the next part shows.

Mounting, parking and pinning

The scheduler is a ForkJoinPool whose size defaults to the number of cores. Those are the carriers. Watch what happens to them under three kinds of task, with a handful of carriers and many virtual threads.

Virtual threads on carriers Simulated

The three cases are the whole story of when virtual threads help:

  • Blocking I/O is the design target. Each virtual thread needs a carrier only for its two ticks of CPU; while it waits, its carrier serves someone else. Throughput is bounded by the I/O, not by the thread count, and two carriers finish sixty-four tasks almost as fast as sixty-four would.
  • CPU-bound work gains nothing. A virtual thread that never blocks never unmounts, so at most carriers tasks progress at once — exactly the fixed pool of §5, with extra bookkeeping. Virtual threads do not create parallelism; they make waiting cheap.
  • Pinning is the trap in Java 21. A virtual thread that blocks while holding a monitor (synchronized) or inside a native frame cannot be unmounted, so its carrier sits idle for the whole wait. With a handful of carriers, a few pinned threads collapse throughput to that of a tiny platform pool. The fix in 21 is to use ReentrantLock on blocking paths; JEP 491 (Java 24) removes the synchronized limitation. -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full prints a stack whenever it happens.

What changes, and what does not

Platform versus virtual thread
Platform threadVirtual thread
Backed byone OS thread, for its whole lifea heap object; borrows a carrier only while running
Stackreserved up front, typically 512 kB–1 MBgrows and shrinks on the heap; frames copied on unmount
Scheduled bythe kernel, pre-emptivelythe JVM's ForkJoinPool, at blocking points only
Sensible counthundredsmillions
Blocking callthe OS thread waitsthe virtual thread unmounts; the carrier is reused
Daemon / priorityconfigurablealways daemon, always normal priority
Creationnew Thread, Thread.ofPlatform()Thread.ofVirtual(), Thread.startVirtualThread, newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor

Underneath is a continuation: the JVM can freeze a running frame stack into an object and thaw it later on any carrier. That mechanism is internal, but it explains why a virtual thread's identity, stack trace and ThreadLocals survive a move from one carrier to another.

A pool exists to amortise the cost of creating a thread. A virtual thread costs about as much as a small object, so pooling it saves nothing and loses the one-task-per-thread model that makes stack traces and cancellation make sense. The rule is: never pool virtual threads; create one per task, and if you need to limit concurrency on a scarce resource — a database that allows 50 connections — limit that with a Semaphore, not by capping the threads.

// WRONG: a fixed pool of virtual threads caps concurrency for no benefit
ExecutorService wrong = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(200, Thread.ofVirtual().factory());
 
// RIGHT: one virtual thread per task; bound the scarce resource instead
Semaphore dbSlots = new Semaphore(50);
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (Order o : orders) {
        ex.submit(() -> {
            dbSlots.acquire();
            try { return reserve(o); } finally { dbSlots.release(); }
        });
    }
}

Cheap is not free. Each virtual thread still allocates its stack chunks on the heap and still carries its ThreadLocal map, so a million threads each caching a 1 MB buffer in a ThreadLocal is a terabyte. Audit what libraries stash per thread before you turn the dial up.

Cheap threads make a new discipline affordable: a task that forks sub-tasks waits for all of them before it returns, so the sub-tasks are scoped to a block like local variables. If one fails, the others are cancelled; if the parent is cancelled, so are the children; a thread dump shows the tree. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in Java 21 (JEP 453; it needs --enable-preview, so this block is not compiled at build time) and the shape is:

// PREVIEW in Java 21 — requires --enable-preview; shape only
try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
    Subtask<Integer> price = scope.fork(() -> priceService.lookup(sku));
    Subtask<Integer> stock = scope.fork(() -> stockService.lookup(sku));
 
    scope.join()            // wait for both
         .throwIfFailed();  // rethrow the first failure, after cancelling the other
 
    return new Quote(sku, price.get(), stock.get());
}   // leaving the block guarantees no sub-task is still running

Compare this with the thenCombine of §6: same two lookups, but the code reads top to bottom, the failure propagates as a normal exception on the caller's thread, and cancelling the lost sibling is automatic. Until the API is final, newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor in a try-with-resources gives you the "cannot outlive the block" half of the guarantee today.

A classic jstack dump lists platform threads only, and a million virtual threads would not fit in it anyway. The JDK 21 tools:

# every thread, grouped by the executor / scope that owns it, as JSON
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json threads.json
 
# JFR records virtual-thread starts, ends and pinning events
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=rec.jfr ... MyApp
jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned rec.jfr
 
# print a stack trace whenever a virtual thread pins its carrier
java -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full MyApp

Two knobs you will meet: -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism sets the carrier count (default: cores), and -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize caps the extra carriers the scheduler may add temporarily to compensate for pinned ones.

Where teams get burnt in the first month
  • synchronized on a blocking path. A JDBC driver or an old HTTP client that synchronises around socket reads pins every carrier it touches. Check the libraries before you check your own code; the pinned-threads trace will tell you.
  • Unbounded fan-out. "One thread per task" with no limit on tasks means one virtual thread per row of a ten-million-row table, all of them opening a connection. Virtual threads remove the thread limit, not the limits of the things the threads talk to.
  • Expecting speed-ups on CPU work. A parallel sort does not get faster on virtual threads; it may get slower. Keep the §5 fixed pool for compute.
  • Relying on daemon semantics. The JVM exits while virtual threads are still running. Always own them in an executor you close, or join them.
  • Thread-identity assumptions. Code that keyed caches or locks by thread, or counted "active threads" to size itself, now sees a different thread for every request. That is usually a sign the design was leaning on the pool.

Check yourself

1.A service does CPU-heavy price optimisation, no I/O. It moves from a fixed pool of 8 platform threads to one virtual thread per request on an 8-core box. What happens to throughput?

B. A virtual thread that never blocks never unmounts, so only as many run as there are carriers — eight, the core count. The CPU was the bottleneck before and still is. Virtual threads make waiting cheap; they do not add cores.

A describes an I/O-bound service, where the old pool spent most of its time blocked. C: they run any code; they just cannot be descheduled mid-computation. D is invented; the scheduler is an ordinary ForkJoinPool of platform threads.

2.In Java 21 a virtual thread calls socket.read() inside a synchronized method. Which is true while the read waits?

C. In 21 the monitor's ownership is tied to the carrier's native frame, so the virtual thread cannot be unmounted while it holds one. The scheduler may compensate by adding a temporary carrier, up to maxPoolSize, but under load the effect is a tiny platform pool. ReentrantLock avoids it; JEP 491 in Java 24 fixes it for synchronized too.

A is true for java.util.concurrent locks and for blocking calls outside a monitor. B: monitors work; they just pin. D: nothing converts thread kinds; a virtual thread stays virtual.

3.Which statements about Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() are true? Select all that apply.

A and C. The name says it: a thread per task, unbounded, never reused. close() (which try-with-resources calls) shuts the executor down and waits for termination, which is what makes the worked example's counts reliable.

B is a fixed pool; there is no queue here because there is no reason to wait for a thread. D is backwards: virtual threads are daemon threads, so an un-closed executor's tasks die with the JVM — the opposite of a platform pool, which keeps the JVM alive until you shut it down.

Section 8

Garbage collection: generations, G1 and ZGC

Fundamentals §1 said the JVM frees memory for you and left it there. The mechanism matters the day a service that was fine for a month starts pausing for two seconds, or dies with OutOfMemoryError at 3 a.m. with plenty of RAM on the box. Both are garbage-collection stories, and both are diagnosable once you know what the collector is doing.

The collector's job has one definition: an object is reachable if some chain of references leads to it from a root — a local variable or operand on any thread's stack, a static field, a JNI handle, a few JVM-internal structures. Everything else is garbage, and the collector may reclaim it at any time. It does not count references (cycles would leak), it does not run when you call System.gc() (that is a hint), and it does not know what your object "means"; it only knows whether anything can still get to it. The entire section follows from that definition plus one empirical fact: most objects die young.

Worked example

The four reference strengths, a root that keeps an object alive no matter what, a map whose entries vanish with their keys, and the modern replacement for finalize(). Every System.gc() here is a request in a bounded loop, and the program prints facts, never sizes.

javaReachability.java
import java.lang.ref.Cleaner;
import java.lang.ref.Reference;
import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue;
import java.lang.ref.SoftReference;
import java.lang.ref.WeakReference;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.WeakHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.function.BooleanSupplier;
 
public class Reachability {
 
    static final class Pallet {
        final String sku;
        Pallet(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
    }
 
    static Pallet pinned;                                   // a static field is a GC root
 
    // System.gc() is a request, not a command. Ask repeatedly, with a bound, and report the fact.
    static boolean gcUntil(BooleanSupplier condition) throws InterruptedException {
        for (int i = 0; i < 50 && !condition.getAsBoolean(); i++) {
            System.gc();
            Thread.sleep(20);
        }
        return condition.getAsBoolean();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // 1. Weak: cleared as soon as nothing strong reaches the object.
        ReferenceQueue<Pallet> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>();
        Pallet p = new Pallet("BOLT-7");
        WeakReference<Pallet> weak = new WeakReference<>(p, queue);
        System.out.println("weak while a strong ref exists = " + (weak.get() != null));
        p = null;                                           // the last strong reference is gone
        System.out.println("weak cleared after gc          = " + gcUntil(() -> weak.get() == null));
        Reference<? extends Pallet> notified = queue.remove(5_000);
        System.out.println("reference enqueued             = " + (notified == weak));
 
        // 2. A root keeps it alive no matter how often you ask.
        pinned = new Pallet("GIRD-1");
        WeakReference<Pallet> weakPinned = new WeakReference<>(pinned);
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) System.gc();
        System.out.println("rooted object still reachable  = " + (weakPinned.get() != null));
 
        // 3. Soft: cleared only under memory pressure, so an idle gc leaves it alone.
        SoftReference<Pallet> soft = new SoftReference<>(new Pallet("CAM-9"));
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) System.gc();
        System.out.println("soft survives an idle gc       = " + (soft.get() != null));
 
        // 4. WeakHashMap: the entry goes when the key goes.
        Map<Pallet, Integer> onHand = new WeakHashMap<>();
        Pallet key = new Pallet("NUT-3");
        onHand.put(key, 1200);
        System.out.println("entries while key is held      = " + onHand.size());
        key = null;
        System.out.println("entries after key dropped + gc = " + (gcUntil(() -> onHand.isEmpty()) ? 0 : onHand.size()));
 
        // 5. Cleaner: the replacement for finalize(). The action must not capture the object.
        Cleaner cleaner = Cleaner.create();
        CountDownLatch ran = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Runnable release = ran::countDown;                  // captures the latch, not the Pallet
        Pallet handle = new Pallet("ROD-4");
        Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable = cleaner.register(handle, release);
        handle = null;
        gcUntil(() -> ran.getCount() == 0);
        System.out.println("cleaner ran after gc           = " + ran.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
 
        CountDownLatch ran2 = new CountDownLatch(1);
        Cleaner.Cleanable explicit = cleaner.register(new Pallet("PIN-2"), ran2::countDown);
        explicit.clean();                                   // deterministic release: call it yourself, from close()
        System.out.println("explicit clean() ran at once   = " + (ran2.getCount() == 0));
        explicit.clean();                                   // idempotent
        cleanable.clean();                                  // already run by the cleaner thread: also a no-op
        System.out.println("repeated clean() is a no-op    = " + (ran2.getCount() == 0));
    }
}
Expected output
weak while a strong ref exists = true
weak cleared after gc          = true
reference enqueued             = true
rooted object still reachable  = true
soft survives an idle gc       = true
entries while key is held      = 1
entries after key dropped + gc = 0
cleaner ran after gc           = true
explicit clean() ran at once   = true
repeated clean() is a no-op    = true
The four reference strengths
ReferenceCollector clears it when…Use it for
strong (Pallet p = …)never, while reachableeverything, by default
SoftReferencememory is short; recently used ones last longer (-XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB)a cache that may be dropped under pressure — but a real cache (Caffeine) with a size bound is almost always better
WeakReferenceat the next collection that finds no strong pathcanonicalising maps, listener lists, WeakHashMap keyed by objects you do not own
PhantomReferenceafter the object is finalizable; get() always returns nullpost-mortem cleanup — what Cleaner is built on

Why finalize() is gone. It ran on an unspecified thread at an unspecified time, could resurrect the object, delayed reclamation by at least one extra cycle, and a slow finalizer stalled every other one behind it. It has been deprecated for removal since Java 18 (JEP 421). Cleaner keeps the one legitimate use — releasing a native resource whose owner forgot to close() — and fixes the design: the cleanup action is a separate object that must not reference the thing being cleaned (or the thing is reachable and never cleaned), it runs at most once, and calling clean() yourself from close() makes release deterministic with the cleaner as a safety net.

Generations, and why copying is cheap

Mark-and-sweep over a whole heap costs time proportional to the heap. The generational hypothesis — most objects die almost immediately, and the ones that survive a while tend to survive a long while — turns that around. Allocate everything in a small young area (eden). When it fills, trace from the roots and copy only the live objects out into a survivor space; everything else is reclaimed by doing nothing at all. The cost is proportional to the survivors, which is a small fraction of what was allocated. Objects that survive enough young collections are promoted to the old generation, which is collected rarely and differently.

Ten seconds of young collections Simulated

Three readings to try. Keep the defaults and note that a collection copies a tenth of what was allocated. Push still alive to 40%: now each young collection is copying almost half of eden and the old generation fills within the run — the hypothesis is false for that workload and no amount of eden helps. Set alive to 20% with a tenuring threshold of 15: the survivor space (an eighth of eden, the JVM's default SurvivorRatio) overflows and objects are promoted early, where they will die in the old generation and cost a far more expensive collection to reclaim. The real flags are -Xmn (young size), -XX:SurvivorRatio and -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold, and the real signal is the GC log in §9.

Which collector, and what it is trading

A collector's two costs are pause time (the application stops while the collector moves things: "stop-the-world", STW) and throughput (CPU spent collecting rather than working). You cannot minimise both. Each collector in the JDK picks a point on that line:

HotSpot collectors compared
CollectorOptimises forPausesHeap sweet spotNotes
Serial (-XX:+UseSerialGC)footprint; one coreSTW, single-threaded, proportional to live data< 1 GB, containers with 1 CPUdefault when the JVM sees < 2 CPUs or < 2 GB (a "client-class" machine)
Parallel (-XX:+UseParallelGC)throughputSTW, all cores, can be long on big heapsbatch jobs, any sizedefault in Java 8; still the best choice when only total time matters
G1 (-XX:+UseG1GC)predictable pauses with good throughputSTW young and mixed collections, concurrent marking; targets -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=2002 GB – tens of GBdefault since Java 9 on server-class machines
ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC)sub-millisecond pauseseverything concurrent except tiny root scans; pauses do not grow with the heap8 GB – terabytesgenerational mode in Java 21 with -XX:+ZGenerational (default from Java 23)
Shenandoahlow pause, like ZGCconcurrent compaction via forwarding pointerssimilar to ZGCRed Hat's; not in every JDK build
Epsilonnothing — it never collectsnone; dies when the heap is fulltests, 100 ms batch toolsa measurement tool, not a production choice

A G1 cycle, region by region

G1 abandons the fixed young/old split of a contiguous heap. The heap is cut into a few thousand equal regions (1–32 MB each), and every region is, at any moment, eden, survivor, old, humongous (one object too large for half a region), or free. Collections pick a set of regions to evacuate, which is how G1 keeps a pause under its target: it evacuates as many as it predicts it can afford.

Young collections, marking, mixed collections Simulated ← → to step
What the application and the collector are doing
// 32 regions: E eden, S survivor, O old, H humongous, . free
allocate(orders);        // the application fills eden regions
youngCollect();          // STW: live eden+survivor objects copied, ages++
allocate(orders);
youngCollect();          // objects past the tenuring threshold -> old
allocateHuge(report);    // bigger than half a region: humongous, old at once
// old occupancy crosses the initiating threshold (IHOP)
concurrentMark();        // mostly concurrent: which old regions are mostly garbage?
mixedCollect();          // STW: young regions + the emptiest old regions
mixedCollect();
// back to young-only collections until IHOP is crossed again
Regions (of 32) and collector state
GC log

ZGC: moving objects without stopping

Even G1's pauses grow with the live set, because copying live objects happens while the world is stopped. ZGC copies them while the application runs. Two ideas make that possible. First, coloured pointers: a 64-bit reference has spare bits, and ZGC uses a few of them to record the object's GC state (marked, remapped, relocated). Second, a load barrier: every time the application reads a reference from the heap, a few instructions check those colour bits and, if the object has been moved, fix the reference up to the new address before the application sees it. The application therefore never observes a stale pointer, and the collector can relocate objects at its own pace. The pauses that remain only scan the thread roots, so they stay around a millisecond on a terabyte heap. The price is throughput — those barriers run on every load — and, before generational ZGC, no cheap young collections; -XX:+ZGenerational in Java 21 adds a young generation on top of the same machinery and is the default from Java 23.

Memory leaks in a garbage-collected language

A leak in Java is an object that is still reachable but will never be used. The collector is doing its job; the program is lying to it. The usual suspects:

  • A static or long-lived collection that only grows. A Map<OrderId, Order> "cache" with no eviction. Bound it (Caffeine, LinkedHashMap with removeEldestEntry from Intermediate §11) or key it weakly.
  • Listeners and callbacks never removed. The subject holds the listener, the listener holds its whole object graph. Unsubscribe in close(), or hold listeners through WeakReference.
  • ThreadLocal in a thread pool. The pool thread lives forever, so its thread-local map does too. Always remove() in a finally; §7 showed why this multiplies with virtual threads.
  • Unclosed resources. A stream, connection or socket holds buffers and native memory the heap collector cannot see. Try-with-resources, always (Fundamentals §11).
  • Inner-class and lambda captures. An anonymous listener inside an activity-sized object keeps the object alive (Intermediate §2). Static nested classes capture nothing by accident.

The four OutOfMemoryErrors

OutOfMemoryError messages and their meaning
MessageWhat ran outFirst thing to check
Java heap spacethe heap: live data exceeds -Xmxa heap dump (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError) opened in a tool that shows dominator trees; is it a leak or just a bigger working set?
GC overhead limit exceededtime: > 98% of it in GC recovering < 2% of heapthe same as above — the heap is effectively full; this error fires before the slow death
Metaspaceclass metadata, outside the heapclass loaders that are never unloaded (§10): redeploys in an app server, runtime code generation, a proxy per request
unable to create native threadOS threads or their stacksa thread leak, or a pool per request; ulimit -u, -Xss; virtual threads make this one rare
Direct buffer memoryoff-heap ByteBuffers-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize; buffers are freed by a Cleaner, so they wait for a GC the heap may not need

§9 picks up from here: how to size the heap so these do not happen, which flags matter in 2026 and which are folklore, and how to read the log lines the stepper showed.

Check yourself

1.A young collection in a copying collector is cheap mainly because…

B. The collector traces from the roots and copies what it reaches; everything it does not reach is reclaimed by simply reusing the region. Under the generational hypothesis most of eden is dead, so most of eden is free. The sandbox shows this breaking down when the survival fraction climbs.

A: the collector does not "scan" eden at all — it never visits dead objects, whatever eden's size. C: young collections in Serial, Parallel and G1 are stop-the-world; only ZGC and Shenandoah collect concurrently. D: they do have references, and those into the old generation are tracked by card tables or remembered sets so the whole old space need not be scanned.

2.You register a native handle with a Cleaner: cleaner.register(this, () -> nativeFree(this.ptr)). What is wrong?

C. The cleaner keeps the action strongly reachable until it runs; the action references this; so this is reachable from a root for as long as the cleaner lives. The object becomes immortal and the handle leaks. The fix is a static nested Runnable holding only the long ptr — exactly why the worked example captures a latch, not the Pallet.

A is the trap the Javadoc warns about in its first paragraph. B: freeing native memory is the main use case. D: there is no finalizer here, and Cleanable.clean() is guaranteed to run the action at most once.

3.A service on a 48 GB heap sees 1.5-second pauses logged as Pause Young (Mixed) under G1. Which responses are sound? Select all that apply.

A and D. A G1 pause is a copy of live objects, so the two levers are "copy them concurrently instead" (ZGC) and "have fewer of them" (a smaller live set, less premature promotion, fewer humongous allocations). Both address the cause.

B: an explicit System.gc() under G1 is a full, stop-the-world collection by default — the longest pause there is, now on a schedule. C: Parallel GC maximises throughput and its old-generation pauses are longer still, since it compacts the entire old space in one stop.

Section 9

Heap sizing, JVM flags and reading GC logs

Section 8 explained what the collector does. This section is about the knobs on the outside of it, and about the evidence the JVM leaves behind when something is wrong. Nothing here is a verified program: every number depends on the machine, the container and the workload, which is precisely why you have to learn to read the JVM's own output rather than trust a rule of thumb.

The mental model to hold: the JVM process is bigger than its heap. The heap is the part -Xmx bounds. Around it sit Metaspace (class metadata), the code cache (JIT output), thread stacks (one per thread), GC bookkeeping, direct byte buffers and whatever native libraries allocate. Most production incidents filed as "the JVM ran out of memory" are one of those other regions, or the container limit, not the heap.

The flags that matter

There are hundreds of -XX flags. These are the ones you will actually set, in roughly the order you will reach for them.

bashstart.sh
# Heap bounds. Set both to the same value in production so the heap never
# resizes under load; the JVM then skips the shrink/grow cycles.
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g ...
 
# In a container, size the heap as a share of the cgroup limit instead.
# The JVM reads the limit itself (it has since JDK 10). Default is 25%.
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 ...
 
# Pick the collector explicitly rather than relying on ergonomics.
java -XX:+UseG1GC ...                 # the default on server-class machines
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational ...   # sub-millisecond pauses, more CPU and memory
java -XX:+UseSerialGC ...             # one core, tiny heap: a sidecar or CLI tool
 
# A goal, not a guarantee: G1 sizes the young generation to try to meet it.
java -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 ...
 
# Metaspace starts small and grows; set the initial size to avoid early full GCs
# in apps that load many classes (anything with a framework).
java -XX:MetaspaceSize=256m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m ...
 
# Thread stack size. 1 MB is the 64-bit default; thousands of platform threads
# add up. Virtual threads (§7) do not use this.
java -Xss512k ...
 
# Always on in production: the one artefact you need after an OOM.
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps ...
 
# Unified logging. Cheap enough to leave on permanently.
java -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m ...
 
# What did ergonomics actually choose? Ask, do not guess.
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E 'MaxHeapSize|UseG1GC|UseZGC|MaxRAMPercentage'
Ergonomics, and why the defaults surprise people

With no flags at all, the JVM picks a collector and a heap size from what it can see: G1 if there are at least two CPUs and 2 GB, Serial otherwise; a maximum heap of one quarter of available memory. On a developer laptop that is 8 GB of heap and nobody notices. In a 1 GB container it is 256 MB, and the first real load test fails with an OutOfMemoryError that goes away when someone "adds memory" — by which they mean raises the container limit, which raises the 25%. The fix was always MaxRAMPercentage or an explicit -Xmx.

Worked example: reading a GC log

This is the output of -Xlog:gc from a G1 collector on JDK 21 — the default log level, one line per collection. It is the first thing to look at when a service is slow, and the format is stable enough to be worth memorising.

Sample GC log (-Xlog:gc, G1, JDK 21)
[0.012s][info][gc] Using G1
[0.351s][info][gc] GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 24M->4M(256M) 3.412ms
[1.204s][info][gc] GC(1) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 100M->12M(256M) 5.118ms
[2.980s][info][gc] GC(2) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 180M->60M(256M) 7.905ms
[2.981s][info][gc] GC(3) Concurrent Mark Cycle
[3.040s][info][gc] GC(3) Pause Remark 72M->70M(256M) 1.233ms
[3.071s][info][gc] GC(3) Pause Cleanup 74M->74M(256M) 0.182ms
[3.072s][info][gc] GC(3) Concurrent Mark Cycle 91.014ms
[3.500s][info][gc] GC(4) Pause Young (Prepare Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 150M->64M(256M) 6.200ms
[3.900s][info][gc] GC(5) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 140M->40M(256M) 9.871ms
[9.414s][info][gc] GC(6) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 250M->200M(256M) 212.556ms

Take line GC(1) field by field. [1.204s] is uptime when the event was logged. GC(1) is the collection's sequence number; every line about the same collection shares it, which is how the four GC(3) lines belong together. Pause Young is the kind of collection — the whole application was stopped and only the young generation was collected. (Normal) is G1's sub-type; (G1 Evacuation Pause) is the cause, here simply "the young generation filled up". Then the part you read first: 100M->12M(256M) — heap occupancy before, occupancy after, and the total committed heap in parentheses. Finally 5.118ms, the pause duration, which is what your latency percentiles feel.

Now read the shape rather than the lines. Young pauses drop occupancy from ~100 M to ~12 M each time: most objects die young, exactly as §8 predicted. GC(2) was triggered by a humongous allocation — an object bigger than half a G1 region, almost always a large array — and it also started a concurrent mark cycle, which ran for 91 ms alongside the application with only two short pauses (Remark, Cleanup). The mark found garbage in the old generation, so the next young collections became Mixed, reclaiming old regions too. And then GC(6): a Pause Full, 212 ms, from 250 M to only 200 M. That line is the problem. Full collections mean G1 could not keep up concurrently; a full collection that frees little means the live set is genuinely ~200 M in a 256 M heap, and the next one will come sooner. Either the heap is too small for the workload or something is being retained that should not be.

Symptoms, causes, and what to check first

Memory and GC symptoms with their likely cause and first diagnostic step
You seeMost likely causeCheck first
Young pauses growing from 5 ms to 50 ms+Large live set surviving each young collection — survivor spaces overflowing, premature promotion-Xlog:gc+age for the tenuring distribution; is the young generation too small for the allocation rate?
Old generation higher after every full GCA leak: something holds references forever (a static Map cache, a listener list, a ThreadLocal in a pool)Heap dump, then the dominator tree (below). Compare two dumps minutes apart.
OutOfMemoryError: MetaspaceClasses loaded and never unloaded: a classloader leak (§10), or a framework generating proxies per requestjcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats; count loaded classes over time with -Xlog:class+load
OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceededMore than 98% of time in GC recovering under 2% of heap — the heap is effectively full of live dataIt is a leak or an undersized heap; the dump taken at the OOM tells you which
OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native threadNot heap at all: the OS refused another thread — ulimit -u, container pid limit, or thread stacks exhausting the memory limitjcmd <pid> Thread.print | grep -c tid; who is creating threads without a pool?
Container restarts with exit code 137, no Java errorKernel OOM killer: the process exceeded the cgroup limit while the heap was still under -XmxHeap + non-heap + stacks must fit the limit — use the sandbox below; jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary
Periodic multi-second pauses, heap mostly emptySomething other than GC: safepoint stalls, a huge thread dump, swap, or the OS paging a file-backed region-Xlog:safepoint; check vmstat for swap activity

Will it fit in the container?

The question every deployment has to answer and few do explicitly. The JVM sizes its heap from the cgroup limit, but the heap is not the whole process, and the kernel counts the whole process.

Heap + non-heap + thread stacks against a memory limit

The percentage form and the explicit form give the same heap; the explicit form is better when something else shares the container's memory — a logging sidecar, a cache process — because then "75% of the limit" is 75% of a number that no longer describes what the JVM may use. State what you mean in megabytes.

Starting points by workload

# A request/response service in a 2 GB container, moderate allocation rate.
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 \
     -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime \
     -jar inventory.jar

G1 is the right default: it balances throughput and pause time and needs almost no tuning. Leave 30% for non-heap and the unexpected. Do not set -Xmn or survivor ratios — G1 sizes those itself, and fixing them removes its ability to meet the pause goal.

# A nightly re-pricing job: pauses are irrelevant, total runtime is everything.
java -Xms6g -Xmx6g -XX:+UseParallelGC -XX:ParallelGCThreads=8 \
     -Xlog:gc:file=gc.log -cp inventory.jar com.acme.Reprice

The Parallel collector has the highest throughput: it stops the world and uses every core to collect. A 200 ms pause in a job that runs for twenty minutes costs nothing. Fix -Xms to -Xmx so no time is spent growing the heap in the first minute.

# A reservation API with a 20 ms p99 target and a large live set.
java -Xms8g -Xmx8g -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational \
     -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime -jar reservations.jar

ZGC keeps pauses under a millisecond regardless of heap size, paying with more CPU for its concurrent work and more memory headroom (it needs room to allocate while collecting). AlwaysPreTouch commits and touches the whole heap at start-up so the first requests do not pay page faults. Budget 20–30% more memory than the live set.

When it is already broken: dumps and jcmd

A heap dump is a snapshot of every object and every reference. It is the only tool that answers "what is holding this memory" rather than "how much memory is held". The workflow:

jcmd 12345 GC.heap_dump /var/dumps/inv.hprof     # live objects only, after a full GC
jmap -histo:live 12345 | head -20                # quick look: instance counts by class
# Open inv.hprof in Eclipse MAT (or VisualVM) and go straight to the
# Dominator Tree: it ranks objects by the memory that would be freed if that
# one reference were cut. A leak is a single entry retaining far more than its
# own size — a HashMap whose "retained heap" is 1.4 GB.
Useful jcmd commands
jcmd <pid> …Tells you
VM.flagsEvery flag that differs from the default — what this JVM is actually running with
GC.heap_infoGeneration sizes and occupancy right now, without a dump
Thread.printA thread dump: every thread's state and stack. Three of these ten seconds apart find most deadlocks and stuck pools (§3, §5)
VM.native_memory summaryWhere non-heap memory went, by region — needs -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary at start-up
GC.class_histogramLive instance counts by class, cheaper than a dump
JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfrStart a flight recording on a running JVM (§13)
Tuning gotchas
  • A bigger heap is not faster. It delays collections and makes each full collection longer. If the live set is 300 MB, a 16 GB heap means a very rare but very long pause. Size for the live set plus allocation headroom, then let the collector work.
  • System.gc() in application code forces a full collection with G1 and Parallel. It is almost always a leftover from a benchmark. -XX:+DisableExplicitGC exists for exactly that reason.
  • Copying flags from a blog post written for JDK 8 (-XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC, PermSize) makes JDK 21 refuse to start or silently ignore them. Check PrintFlagsFinal after any change.
  • Metaspace is not bounded by default. A classloader leak grows it until the container dies. Set MaxMetaspaceSize so it fails as a Java error with a dump instead.
  • GC logs are cheap; the absence of them is expensive. There is no way to reconstruct what the collector did yesterday. Leave -Xlog:gc* on with rotation.

Check yourself

1.A service runs with no JVM flags in a 1 GB container and dies with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space under load. On a 16 GB laptop the same load runs fine. What is the most likely explanation?

C. The default maximum heap is one quarter of what the JVM can see. In the container that is 256 MB; on the laptop, 4 GB. Same code, same load, sixteen times the heap. Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage or -Xmx.

A would show as long pauses or GC overhead limit exceeded, not a plain heap-space OOM at a small size. B is backwards — the JVM has honoured cgroup limits since JDK 10, which is why the heap is small. D is invented; collectors are part of every JDK and JRE build.

2.In the log line GC(5) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 140M->40M(256M) 9.871ms, what does (256M) mean?

B. before->after(total): occupancy went from 140 M to 40 M in a heap that currently has 256 M committed. The parenthesised number can grow between lines as the JVM expands the heap towards -Xmx.

A is 140 − 40 = 100M, computed, not printed. C is not shown at this log level (-Xlog:gc+heap prints generation sizes). D is only equal to the committed size once the heap has grown to its maximum, or when -Xms equals -Xmx.

3.A container is restarted by the orchestrator every few hours with exit code 137. The JVM's own logs show no error and the heap never exceeded 70% of -Xmx. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

A and D. Exit 137 is SIGKILL from the OOM killer: the whole process — heap, metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct buffers — outgrew the limit while the heap itself was fine. Non-heap is where to look, so VM.native_memory and the thread count are the right next steps.

B makes it worse: a larger heap ceiling leaves less room for everything else under the same limit. C is wrong because no OutOfMemoryError was ever thrown — the JVM never got the chance; the kernel killed it mid-instruction.

Section 10

Class loading, linking and initialization

Fundamentals §1 said the JVM "loads" a class the first time it is needed. That one word hides three phases with different timing, different failure modes and different rules, and the gaps between them are where some of Java's most confusing errors live: a class that is found but not usable, a static field that reads as zero, a NoClassDefFoundError for a class that is plainly on the class path.

The three phases are loading (find the bytes, parse them, create a Class object), linking (verify the bytecode is well-formed and safe, prepare static fields with their default values, optionally resolve symbolic references), and initialization (run the static initializers, in order). Loading and linking happen when a class is first referenced; initialization is deferred until the class is first actively used — and the JLS lists exactly what counts as active use.

The triggers of class initialization
Initialization is triggered by (JLS §12.4.1)Not triggered by
Creating an instance with newReferencing the class literal Foo.class
Invoking a static methodLoading via ClassLoader.loadClass
Assigning or reading a static field that is not a compile-time constantReading a static final compile-time constant (javac inlined it)
Class.forName(name) (its default is initialize = true)Class.forName(name, false, loader)
Initializing a subclass (the superclass goes first)Initializing a class that implements an interface (the interface stays uninitialized unless it has default methods)
Being the class that holds mainDeclaring an array of the type: Foo[] a = new Foo[8]

Worked example: when static initializers run

Every static block here prints when it runs. Read the output against the triggers above; the ordering is specified, not accidental.

javaClassInit.java
public class ClassInit {
 
    static int trace(String what, int value) {
        System.out.println("  init: " + what);
        return value;
    }
 
    static class Base {
        static int counter = trace("Base.counter", 1);
        static { trace("Base static block", 0); }
    }
 
    static class Derived extends Base {
        static int level = trace("Derived.level", 2);
        static { trace("Derived static block", 0); }
    }
 
    static class Lazy {
        static { trace("Lazy static block", 0); }
        static final int SIZE = 8;                 // compile-time constant: inlined by javac
        static int size = 8;                       // a real static field
    }
 
    static class ViaName {
        static { trace("ViaName static block", 0); }
    }
 
    static class Holder {
        static { trace("Holder static block", 0); }
        static final Object INSTANCE = new Object();
    }
 
    interface Config {
        int LIMIT = trace("Config.LIMIT", 10);     // not a constant: initialised on first use
    }
 
    static class Trap {
        static int first = Trap.second + 1;        // qualified name: legal, reads the DEFAULT 0
        static int second = 5;
    }
 
    static class Broken {
        static int value = 1 / zero();
        static int zero() { return 0; }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("-- a compile-time constant does not initialise its class --");
        System.out.println("Lazy.SIZE = " + Lazy.SIZE);
        System.out.println("Lazy.size = " + Lazy.size);
 
        System.out.println("-- superclass first, then subclass, textual order within each --");
        System.out.println("Derived.level = " + Derived.level);
 
        System.out.println("-- loadClass loads but does not initialise; Class.forName does --");
        ClassLoader app = ClassInit.class.getClassLoader();
        Class<?> loaded = app.loadClass("ClassInit$ViaName");
        System.out.println("loaded " + loaded.getSimpleName() + ", nothing printed yet");
        Class.forName("ClassInit$ViaName", false, app);
        System.out.println("forName(init=false): still nothing");
        Class.forName("ClassInit$ViaName");
        System.out.println("forName(): initialised");
 
        System.out.println("-- the holder idiom: lazy, thread-safe, no locks --");
        System.out.println("about to touch Holder.INSTANCE");
        Object o = Holder.INSTANCE;
        System.out.println("got instance: " + (o != null));
 
        System.out.println("-- an interface initialises when a non-constant field is read --");
        System.out.println("Config.LIMIT = " + Config.LIMIT);
 
        System.out.println("-- forward reference: a static reads a later static's default --");
        System.out.println("Trap.first = " + Trap.first + ", Trap.second = " + Trap.second);
 
        System.out.println("-- a failing initialiser: two different errors --");
        try {
            System.out.println(Broken.value);
        } catch (ExceptionInInitializerError e) {
            System.out.println("first use : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                    + " caused by " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
        try {
            System.out.println(Broken.value);
        } catch (NoClassDefFoundError e) {
            System.out.println("second use: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
Expected output
-- a compile-time constant does not initialise its class --
Lazy.SIZE = 8
  init: Lazy static block
Lazy.size = 8
-- superclass first, then subclass, textual order within each --
  init: Base.counter
  init: Base static block
  init: Derived.level
  init: Derived static block
Derived.level = 2
-- loadClass loads but does not initialise; Class.forName does --
loaded ViaName, nothing printed yet
forName(init=false): still nothing
  init: ViaName static block
forName(): initialised
-- the holder idiom: lazy, thread-safe, no locks --
about to touch Holder.INSTANCE
  init: Holder static block
got instance: true
-- an interface initialises when a non-constant field is read --
  init: Config.LIMIT
Config.LIMIT = 10
-- forward reference: a static reads a later static's default --
Trap.first = 1, Trap.second = 5
-- a failing initialiser: two different errors --
first use : ExceptionInInitializerError caused by ArithmeticException
second use: NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ClassInit$Broken

Six facts, one per block of output:

  • Lazy.SIZE printed without initializing Lazy. static final int SIZE = 8 is a compile-time constant, so javac copied the literal 8 into main's bytecode; at runtime Lazy is never consulted. This is also why changing a constant in a library and not recompiling its users leaves them with the old value.
  • Superclass before subclass, and textual order within a class. Field initializers and static blocks are one sequence, executed top to bottom.
  • loadClass and forName(…, false, …) produce a Class object but run no code. Only the one-argument Class.forName initializes — which is why JDBC drivers historically registered themselves from a static block triggered by Class.forName("com.vendor.Driver").
  • The holder idiom is lazy initialization for free. Holder is not initialized until INSTANCE is read, the JVM guarantees initialization happens exactly once even under contention, and no lock is ever visible to you. It beats double-checked locking on every axis.
  • The forward-reference trap. first = second + 1 is a compile error, but first = Trap.second + 1 is legal — and reads the default value 0 that linking's prepare step gave second before any initializer ran. The result is 1, silently.
  • A static initializer that throws poisons the class. The first use gets ExceptionInInitializerError wrapping the real cause. Every later use gets a bare NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class with no cause attached — the class is marked erroneous forever in this JVM. When you see that message in a log, scroll up: the real exception was logged once, earlier, often at start-up.

Who loads what: the loader hierarchy

A class loader is an object that turns a name into a Class. Since JDK 9 there are three built-in ones, arranged parent-first, and each is responsible for a set of modules:

The built-in class loaders
LoadergetName()LoadsParent
Bootstrap— (appears as null)java.base and the core modules: String, Object, collectionsnone
PlatformplatformThe rest of the JDK: java.sql, java.net.http, java.xml…bootstrap
Application (system)appYour class path and module pathplatform
