The rule connecting them is parent delegation: a loader asked for a class first asks its parent, and only searches its own sources if every ancestor came back empty. The consequence is that java.lang.String is always the bootstrap loader's String, no matter what jar someone puts on the class path — you cannot replace core classes by shadowing them, which is a security property, not an inconvenience.

javaLoaders.java
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;
 
public class Loaders {
 
    /* Follows standard delegation and, once every parent has given up,
       refuses — so the fall-through is visible. */
    static class Strict extends ClassLoader {
        Strict(ClassLoader parent) { super(parent); }
        @Override protected Class<?> findClass(String name) throws ClassNotFoundException {
            System.out.println("  Strict.findClass(" + name + "): parents had no answer");
            throw new ClassNotFoundException(name);
        }
    }
 
    public static class Twin { public Twin() { } }   // public: the copy lives in a different runtime package
 
    /* Child-first for one class: defines its own copy from the bytes on the
       class path instead of asking its parent. */
    static class ChildFirst extends ClassLoader {
        ChildFirst(ClassLoader parent) { super(parent); }
        @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException {
            if (name.equals("Loaders$Twin")) {
                try (InputStream in = Loaders.class.getResourceAsStream("Loaders$Twin.class")) {
                    byte[] bytes = in.readAllBytes();
                    return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length);
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    throw new ClassNotFoundException(name, e);
                }
            }
            return super.loadClass(name, resolve);
        }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ClassLoader app = Loaders.class.getClassLoader();
        System.out.println("-- the built-in hierarchy --");
        System.out.println("String's loader is bootstrap (null) : " + (String.class.getClassLoader() == null));
        System.out.println("java.sql.Driver's loader           : " + java.sql.Driver.class.getClassLoader().getName());
        System.out.println("Loaders' loader                    : " + app.getName());
        System.out.println("its parent                         : " + app.getParent().getName());
        System.out.println("the platform loader's parent       : " + app.getParent().getParent());
 
        System.out.println("-- delegation: parents are asked first --");
        Strict strict = new Strict(app);
        Class<?> s = strict.loadClass("java.lang.String");
        System.out.println("String via Strict is the same Class : " + (s == String.class));
        Class<?> me = strict.loadClass("Loaders");
        System.out.println("Loaders via Strict is the same Class: " + (me == Loaders.class)
                + " (defined by " + me.getClassLoader().getName() + ")");
        try {
            strict.loadClass("com.acme.Missing");
        } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) {
            System.out.println("ClassNotFoundException: " + e.getMessage());
        }
 
        System.out.println("-- identity is (loader, name): the same bytes loaded twice --");
        Class<?> twin2 = new ChildFirst(app).loadClass("Loaders$Twin");
        System.out.println("same name      : " + twin2.getName().equals(Twin.class.getName()));
        System.out.println("same Class     : " + (twin2 == Twin.class));
        Object copy = twin2.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
        System.out.println("instanceof Twin: " + (copy instanceof Twin));
        System.out.println("named module   : " + Loaders.class.getModule().isNamed()
                + "; String lives in " + String.class.getModule().getName());
    }
}
Expected output
-- the built-in hierarchy --
String's loader is bootstrap (null) : true
java.sql.Driver's loader           : platform
Loaders' loader                    : app
its parent                         : platform
the platform loader's parent       : null
-- delegation: parents are asked first --
String via Strict is the same Class : true
Loaders via Strict is the same Class: true (defined by app)
  Strict.findClass(com.acme.Missing): parents had no answer
ClassNotFoundException: com.acme.Missing
-- identity is (loader, name): the same bytes loaded twice --
same name      : true
same Class     : false
instanceof Twin: false
named module   : false; String lives in java.base

The last block is the one to remember. ChildFirst read the same .class bytes the application loader had already used and defined them again. The result is a second, unrelated Class object with the same name: a Twin from one loader is not instanceof the Twin from the other, and a cast between them throws ClassCastException with the baffling message "Loaders$Twin cannot be cast to Loaders$Twin". A class's identity is the pair (defining loader, binary name), not the name alone. Application servers and plugin systems exploit this deliberately — a child-first loader per deployment lets two web apps ship different versions of the same library — and it is also why they leak: a loader stays alive as long as any of its classes is reachable, and with it every class it defined and all of their statics.

Watch delegation resolve a request

loadClass("com.acme.Picker") Simulated ← → to step
ClassLoader.loadClass, simplified
Class<?> c = appLoader.loadClass("com.acme.Picker");
 
// inside ClassLoader.loadClass(name):
Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name);          // already defined by me?
if (c == null) {
    if (parent != null) c = parent.loadClass(name);   // ask up the chain
    else                c = findBootstrapClassOrNull(name);
}
if (c == null) c = findClass(name);           // only now: search my own sources
Loaders currently asked (top = active)
State

Two errors that look alike

Both say a class could not be used. They mean opposite things about when it went wrong.

Two different failures
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: com.acme.Picker
        at java.base/jdk.internal.loader.BuiltinClassLoader.loadClass(BuiltinClassLoader.java:641)
        at java.base/java.lang.Class.forName0(Native Method)
        at java.base/java.lang.Class.forName(Class.java:534)
        at com.acme.Boot.main(Boot.java:12)

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: com/acme/Picker
        at com.acme.Boot.main(Boot.java:12)
Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: com.acme.Picker
        ... 1 more
  • ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception thrown by an explicit lookup by name — Class.forName, loadClass. The loader searched and found nothing. The fix is a class path or spelling fix.
  • NoClassDefFoundError is an error thrown by the JVM itself when bytecode that compiled against a class cannot resolve it at runtime. Two causes, told apart by the message: with a Caused by: ClassNotFoundException, the class existed at compile time and is missing now — a dependency not shipped, a jar with the wrong version. With "Could not initialize class" and no cause, the class was found but its static initializer failed earlier; look for the ExceptionInInitializerError that preceded it.
Class-loading gotchas
  • Classloader leaks eat Metaspace. A ThreadLocal set from a web app and never removed, a JDBC driver registered in the DriverManager (which lives in the platform loader), a shutdown hook, a static cache in a shared library keyed by an app's class — each pins the app's loader after undeployment. Redeploy ten times and the Metaspace OOM arrives. §9's table has the diagnostics.
  • Static state is per loader, not per JVM. A "singleton" in a library loaded by two child-first loaders is two singletons. Logging frameworks and DriverManager have had decades of bugs from this.
  • Initialization can deadlock. Two classes whose static initializers touch each other, initialized concurrently by two threads, each hold their own initialization lock while waiting for the other's. The JVM does not detect it; a thread dump shows both threads "in <clinit>". Keep static initializers free of cross-class calls.
  • The verifier is not optional. -Xverify:none and -noverify are deprecated for removal because skipping verification lets malformed bytecode corrupt the JVM; the start-up time they saved is now negligible.
  • Resolution is lazy too. A method call to a class that does not exist fails only when that line executes, not when the calling class loads — which is why a missing optional dependency can lurk until a rarely used feature is hit. javap -v shows the constant pool entries that will be resolved.

Check yourself

1.Class Prices has a static block that prints "loaded". Which of these lines prints it?

B. Reading a static field that is not a compile-time constant is active use, and the class is initialized first — even though count is zero and the read looks trivial.

A loads the class (the literal needs a Class object) but does not initialize it. C never touches Prices at runtime: javac inlined 100. D creates an array object whose element type is Prices; the array class is loaded, Prices is not initialized until an element is constructed.

2.A plugin system loads each plugin with its own child-first URLClassLoader. Plugin A returns an Order object to the host, and the host's (Order) result cast throws ClassCastException: com.acme.Order cannot be cast to com.acme.Order. Why?

C. Child-first means the plugin loader defined Order itself instead of delegating to the host's loader. Identity is (loader, name), so the plugin's Order and the host's are two types. The fix is the standard one: shared API classes must live only in the parent, and the child loader must delegate for them.

A is about serialization, which is not involved in a cast. B confuses initialization with type checking; casts never trigger or need initialization. D is false — delegation is the default for every package, and the problem here is that the plugin loader deliberately broke it.

3.A service logs NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.acme.RateTable on every request, with no "Caused by". Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. "Could not initialize class" is the second-and-later failure of a class whose <clinit> threw. The first failure carried the cause as ExceptionInInitializerError; later ones do not. Find the first one.

B would produce a NoClassDefFoundError with a Caused by: ClassNotFoundException. C is false within one JVM: an erroneous class stays erroneous; the only retry is a restart (or a fresh class loader).

Section 11

Reflection, annotations and method handles

Everything so far has been code that knows, at compile time, which class it is talking to. Reflection is the escape hatch: a program that inspects classes it has never heard of, reads their fields, calls their methods, and constructs them, all by name and all at runtime. Every framework you will use is built on it — dependency injection finds constructors, serializers find fields, test runners find methods, validators find annotations. You will rarely write reflective code in application logic, and you will constantly debug code that does.

The price is real: the compiler cannot check names or types, the JIT cannot inline through a Method.invoke, arguments are boxed, every call re-checks access, and since JDK 16 the JDK's own internals are closed to it. This section covers the API, its costs, the annotation system it usually serves, and the two modern alternatives — method handles and var handles — that recover most of the speed.

Worked example: inspecting and invoking at runtime

javaReflection.java
import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodType;
import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle;
import java.lang.reflect.Field;
import java.lang.reflect.InaccessibleObjectException;
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.lang.reflect.Modifier;
import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;
import java.lang.reflect.RecordComponent;
import java.util.Arrays;
 
public class Reflection {
 
    interface PriceSource {
        int priceInCents(String sku);
        String name();
    }
 
    record Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { }
 
    static class Vault {
        private final String secret = "rotate-me";
        private volatile int stock = 10;
 
        private static final VarHandle STOCK;
        static {
            try {
                STOCK = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Vault.class, "stock", int.class);
            } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) {
                throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e);
            }
        }
        boolean reserve(int expected, int remaining) { return STOCK.compareAndSet(this, expected, remaining); }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable {
        System.out.println("-- inspecting a record --");
        Class<Product> c = Product.class;
        System.out.println("isRecord         = " + c.isRecord() + ", final = " + Modifier.isFinal(c.getModifiers()));
        System.out.println("components       = " + Arrays.stream(c.getRecordComponents()).map(RecordComponent::getName).sorted().toList());
        System.out.println("declared methods = " + Arrays.stream(c.getDeclaredMethods()).filter(m -> !m.isSynthetic()).map(Method::getName).sorted().toList());
 
        System.out.println("-- constructing and invoking by name --");
        Product p = c.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class, int.class).newInstance("BOLT-7", 80);
        Method sku = c.getMethod("sku");
        System.out.println("sku()            = " + sku.invoke(p) + "  (public: " + Modifier.isPublic(sku.getModifiers()) + ")");
 
        System.out.println("-- private access: your own class yes, java.base no --");
        Field secret = Vault.class.getDeclaredField("secret");
        secret.setAccessible(true);
        System.out.println("Vault.secret     = " + secret.get(new Vault()));
        try {
            Field value = String.class.getDeclaredField("value");
            value.setAccessible(true);
            System.out.println("opened java.lang.String.value");
        } catch (InaccessibleObjectException e) {
            System.out.println("String.value     : blocked by strong encapsulation");
        }
 
        System.out.println("-- a dynamic proxy --");
        PriceSource source = (PriceSource) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
                Reflection.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] { PriceSource.class },
                (self, method, a) -> {
                    System.out.println("  intercepted " + method.getName() + (a == null ? "()" : Arrays.toString(a)));
                    return method.getName().equals("name") ? "proxy" : 80;
                });
        System.out.println("proxy price      = " + source.priceInCents("BOLT-7"));
        System.out.println("proxy name       = " + source.name());
 
        System.out.println("-- method handles and var handles --");
        MethodHandle price = MethodHandles.lookup()
                .findVirtual(Product.class, "priceInCents", MethodType.methodType(int.class));
        int cents = (int) price.invokeExact(p);
        System.out.println("invokeExact      = " + cents);
        Vault vault = new Vault();
        System.out.println("CAS 10 -> 7      = " + vault.reserve(10, 7));
        System.out.println("CAS 10 -> 3      = " + vault.reserve(10, 3) + "  (stock is now " + vault.stock + ")");
    }
}
Expected output
-- inspecting a record --
isRecord         = true, final = true
components       = [priceInCents, sku]
declared methods = [equals, hashCode, priceInCents, sku, toString]
-- constructing and invoking by name --
sku()            = BOLT-7  (public: true)
-- private access: your own class yes, java.base no --
Vault.secret     = rotate-me
String.value     : blocked by strong encapsulation
-- a dynamic proxy --
  intercepted priceInCents[BOLT-7]
proxy price      = 80
  intercepted name()
proxy name       = proxy
-- method handles and var handles --
invokeExact      = 80
CAS 10 -> 7      = true
CAS 10 -> 3      = false  (stock is now 7)

Five things happened, and each is a different tool:

  • Class is the entry point. getRecordComponents, getDeclaredMethods, getDeclaredConstructor and Modifier describe the type. The declared variants return what the class itself declares, private included; the plain variants (getMethod) return public members including inherited ones. Note the program sorts every listing — the JDK documents the order as unspecified, and it really does vary between JVM builds.
  • setAccessible(true) is the switch that bypasses access control, and it works on Vault because Vault is in your own module (the unnamed module, here). It fails on String.value with InaccessibleObjectException: java.base does not open java.lang to you. That is strong encapsulation (§12), the JDK 17 change that broke a generation of libraries which had been poking at JDK internals. The escape is --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED on the command line, and it should feel like what it is: a deliberate hole.
  • Proxy fabricates an implementation of an interface at runtime whose every method lands in one InvocationHandler. It is how a mocking library builds a mock, how a remote call looks like a local one, and how a transaction annotation wraps a method. It works only for interfaces; for classes you need a bytecode library (ByteBuddy, which is what Mockito and Hibernate use).
  • A MethodHandle is a typed, direct reference to a method, looked up once and then invoked at near-native speed: no boxing with invokeExact, access checked at lookup time rather than per call, and the JIT can inline through a constant handle. The cast (int) price.invokeExact(p) is not a normal cast — it tells the compiler the exact call-site type, which must match the handle's type to the letter.
  • A VarHandle is the same idea for a field, with atomic operations attached: compareAndSet, getAndAdd, volatile and acquire/release reads and writes. It is the official replacement for sun.misc.Unsafe and for AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater, and it is how the java.util.concurrent classes you met in §4 are implemented. The second CAS fails because the stock is no longer 10 — exactly the lost-update protection §1 wanted.

Annotations: metadata, not behaviour

An annotation does nothing by itself. @Audited on a method changes no bytecode in that method. It is a note attached to the class file that something else reads — the compiler (@Override, @FunctionalInterface), an annotation processor at build time (Lombok, MapStruct, records of configuration), or, most commonly, a framework using reflection at runtime. The retention policy decides how far the note travels.

javaAnnotations.java
import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Repeatable;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;
import java.lang.reflect.Field;
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
 
public class Annotations {
 
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    @Target({ ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD })
    @interface Audited {
        String by();
        int level() default 1;
    }
 
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE)             // discarded by javac
    @Target(ElementType.METHOD)
    @interface Draft { }
 
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    @Target({ ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.RECORD_COMPONENT })
    @interface NotBlank { }
 
    @Repeatable(Tags.class)
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    @interface Tag { String value(); }
 
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    @interface Tags { Tag[] value(); }
 
    @Audited(by = "ops", level = 3)
    @Tag("inventory") @Tag("critical")
    static class InventoryService {
        @Audited(by = "finance") void reprice() { }
        @Draft void experimental() { }
        void plain() { }
    }
 
    record Part(@NotBlank String sku, @NotBlank String name, int qty) { }
 
    /* A tiny validation framework: the metadata is on the type, the behaviour is here. */
    static List<String> validate(Object target) throws IllegalAccessException {
        List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
        Field[] fields = target.getClass().getDeclaredFields();
        Arrays.sort(fields, (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName()));
        for (Field f : fields) {
            if (!f.isAnnotationPresent(NotBlank.class)) continue;
            f.setAccessible(true);
            Object v = f.get(target);
            if (v == null || v.toString().isBlank()) problems.add(f.getName() + " must not be blank");
        }
        return problems;
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("-- reading annotation values --");
        Audited onType = InventoryService.class.getAnnotation(Audited.class);
        System.out.println("type: by=" + onType.by() + " level=" + onType.level());
 
        Method[] methods = InventoryService.class.getDeclaredMethods();
        Arrays.sort(methods, (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName()));
        for (Method m : methods) {
            Audited a = m.getAnnotation(Audited.class);
            System.out.println(m.getName() + "(): audited=" + (a != null ? "by " + a.by() + " level " + a.level() : "no")
                    + ", @Draft visible=" + m.isAnnotationPresent(Draft.class));
        }
 
        System.out.println("-- repeatable --");
        Tag[] tags = InventoryService.class.getAnnotationsByType(Tag.class);
        System.out.println("tags = " + Arrays.stream(tags).map(Tag::value).sorted().toList()
                + " (container present: " + InventoryService.class.isAnnotationPresent(Tags.class) + ")");
 
        System.out.println("-- annotations drive a validator --");
        System.out.println("valid   : " + validate(new Part("BOLT-7", "hex bolt", 3)));
        System.out.println("invalid : " + validate(new Part("BOLT-7", "   ", 3)));
    }
}
Expected output
-- reading annotation values --
type: by=ops level=3
experimental(): audited=no, @Draft visible=false
plain(): audited=no, @Draft visible=false
reprice(): audited=by finance level 1, @Draft visible=false
-- repeatable --
tags = [critical, inventory] (container present: true)
-- annotations drive a validator --
valid   : []
invalid : [name must not be blank]

@Draft is on experimental() in the source and invisible at runtime: RetentionPolicy.SOURCE means javac drops it after compilation (useful for annotation processors and lint tools). CLASS — the default if you write nothing — keeps it in the class file but does not load it, so it is equally invisible to reflection; RUNTIME is the one you want almost every time. The repeatable @Tag shows the mechanism behind the convenience: the compiler wraps the two tags in an implicit @Tags container, and getAnnotationsByType unwraps it. And @NotBlank on a record component was propagated by javac to the generated private field (its @Target includes FIELD), which is what lets the validator find it with getDeclaredFields.

Annotation meta-annotations and their effect
Meta-annotationControlsDefault
@RetentionHow long the annotation survives: SOURCE (javac only), CLASS (in the file, not loaded), RUNTIME (reflectable)CLASS — almost never what you want
@TargetWhere it may be written: TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, RECORD_COMPONENT, TYPE_USE…Any declaration
@InheritedWhether a class annotation is seen on subclasses via getAnnotation (classes only — never methods or interfaces)Not inherited
@RepeatableNames the container annotation that holds several copiesOne copy per element
@DocumentedWhether Javadoc shows it on annotated elementsHidden

Which tool for which job

Drag a tool onto the need it fits, or click one then click the other

Each need has one best answer; the others would work badly or not at all.

All four correct. Plain reflection is fine when it runs once and clarity matters more than speed. A hot path wants a MethodHandle held in a static final so the JIT can inline it. Atomic field updates are exactly what VarHandle exists for. And getRecordComponents returns components in declaration order — unlike getDeclaredFields, whose order is unspecified — which is why serializers use it.

What it costs, and what replaced it

A reflective call is slower than a direct one for four reasons, and knowing them tells you which alternative fixes which. Lookup: getMethod("sku") scans and copies the method table — cache the Method, never look it up per call. Access checks: each invoke re-verifies that the caller may call; setAccessible(true) skips that. Boxing: arguments travel as Object[] and primitives are boxed both ways. Opacity: the JIT sees a call into Method.invoke, not into your method, so nothing inlines. Method handles address the last two: invokeExact takes primitives as primitives, and a handle in a static final field is a constant the JIT can see through. That is also the machinery under lambdas — a lambda expression compiles to an invokedynamic instruction whose bootstrap method spins a class at first call and links a method handle to it, which is why a lambda is cheaper than the anonymous class it replaced (Intermediate §2).

Reflection gotchas
  • Method.invoke wraps every exception. Whatever the target throws arrives as InvocationTargetException; the real exception is getCause(). Frameworks that forget to unwrap it produce stack traces that blame the framework.
  • Reflection ignores generics (erasure, Intermediate §1). Field.getType() of a List<Product> is List; the type argument is only available through getGenericType() and only because javac kept a Signature attribute for it.
  • Strong encapsulation is on by default since JDK 17. A library that worked on 11 by opening java.base fails on 21 with InaccessibleObjectException. --add-opens is a stop-gap; the right fix is a library version that does not need it.
  • Reflection defeats the tools that make Java safe. Renaming a field breaks a string-based lookup silently; dead-code analysis cannot see reflective uses; ahead-of-time compilation (GraalVM native image) needs an explicit list of everything reflected on. Keep reflection at the edges — serializers, DI, tests — never in domain code.
  • A Proxy cannot wrap a class, only interfaces, and final classes cannot be subclassed by bytecode libraries either. Records are final: a framework that proxies entities cannot proxy a record.

Check yourself

1.You declare @interface Timed { } with no meta-annotations, put it on a method, and at runtime method.isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class) returns false. Why?

C. Without @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) an annotation defaults to CLASS retention — recorded in the .class file for tools, invisible to reflection. It is the single most common annotation mistake.

A is backwards: no @Target means it is allowed anywhere. B is invented — marker annotations are common and fully supported. D describes @Inherited, which widens what is found; it never narrows it.

2.A serialization library worked on JDK 11 and on JDK 21 fails with InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field private final byte[] java.lang.String.value accessible. What changed, and what is the correct long-term response?

B. JEP 403 (JDK 17) stopped the JDK from opening its packages to the class path by default. The library was relying on a hole that has now closed. The honest fix is a version of the library that uses supported APIs; --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED keeps you running meanwhile.

A is wrong on the facts — the field exists, which is exactly why the message names it. C is wrong twice: reflection was not removed, and method handles go through the same access checks. D is backwards — code on the class path (the unnamed module) can reflect on itself freely; modules make encapsulation stronger, not weaker.

3.A hot loop calls a method selected from configuration at start-up. Profiling shows Method.invoke at the top. Which changes actually help? Select all that apply.

A and C. Lookup per call is the first thing to remove — it copies the method table every time. Then a constant MethodHandle with invokeExact removes boxing and lets the JIT inline through the call, which a Method.invoke never allows.

B adds a layer: the proxy's handler still has to call Method.invoke underneath, so it is strictly slower. D confuses two unrelated things — retention is about annotations on the method, and nothing about annotations affects inlining.

Section 12

The module system

Everything before this section ran on the class path: a flat list of directories and JARs in which every public class is visible to every other class, duplicate packages silently shadow each other, and a missing dependency is discovered the first time a class is touched, as a NoClassDefFoundError in production. The Java Platform Module System (JPMS, Java 9) exists because the JDK itself suffered from exactly those problems. It adds a second mechanism, the module path, in which each JAR declares what it needs and what it exposes, and the JVM checks both at startup.

Two guarantees follow. Reliable configuration: if a module you require is missing, the JVM refuses to start, with a message naming the module, rather than failing later at an arbitrary call site. Strong encapsulation: a package that a module does not export is invisible to other modules at compile time and at run time, even to reflection. That second guarantee is why, since Java 16, code that pokes at sun.misc or java.lang internals fails with InaccessibleObjectException unless the JVM was started with an explicit --add-opens.

Worked example: what the running JVM knows

This program is not itself a module — it is compiled and run on the class path, like every other program in this course — yet it still runs inside a module graph. Every class belongs to some module, and the facts below are the ones worth knowing by heart.

javaModuleFacts.java
import java.lang.module.ModuleDescriptor;
 
public class ModuleFacts {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Module base = Object.class.getModule();
        Module mine = ModuleFacts.class.getModule();
 
        System.out.println("java.lang.Object lives in     = " + base.getName());
        System.out.println("this class's module is named  = " + mine.isNamed());
        System.out.println("java.sql.Driver lives in      = " + Class.forName("java.sql.Driver").getModule().getName());
        System.out.println("boot layer has java.base      = " + ModuleLayer.boot().findModule("java.base").isPresent());
        System.out.println("java.base exports java.lang   = " + base.isExported("java.lang"));
        System.out.println("java.base exports jdk.internal.misc = " + base.isExported("jdk.internal.misc"));
        System.out.println("unnamed module reads java.base = " + mine.canRead(base));
 
        ModuleDescriptor d = base.getDescriptor();
        System.out.println("java.base requires anything   = " + !d.requires().isEmpty());
        System.out.println("java.base is open             = " + d.isOpen());
    }
}
Expected output
java.lang.Object lives in     = java.base
this class's module is named  = false
java.sql.Driver lives in      = java.sql
boot layer has java.base      = true
java.base exports java.lang   = true
java.base exports jdk.internal.misc = false
unnamed module reads java.base = true
java.base requires anything   = false
java.base is open             = false
  • Code on the class path lives in the unnamed module, which is why isNamed() is false. The unnamed module reads every other module and exports everything, so class-path code keeps working exactly as before Java 9.
  • java.base is the one module every other module implicitly requires, and the only one that requires nothing. jdk.internal.misc is in it but not exported: that is strong encapsulation, observable from your own code.
  • The JDK is itself about seventy modules (java.sql, java.net.http, java.desktop…). jlink, below, builds a runtime containing only the ones you need.

A two-module application

A module is a JAR, or a directory, with a module-info.java at its root. Here the warehouse is split into an API module that other teams compile against and an application module that depends on it. The example is complete; it is not compiled during the build of this page because a module-info.java would turn every other program on this page into part of the same module.

inventory/
├── com.acme.inventory.api/
│   ├── module-info.java
│   └── com/acme/inventory/api/
│       ├── Product.java
│       └── StockSource.java          # a service interface
└── com.acme.inventory.app/
    ├── module-info.java
    └── com/acme/inventory/app/
        ├── Main.java
        └── internal/MemoryStock.java # implements StockSource; NOT exported
module com.acme.inventory.api {
    exports com.acme.inventory.api;          // the public surface: Product, StockSource
    // nothing else — no "internal" package is visible outside this module
}
module com.acme.inventory.app {
    requires com.acme.inventory.api;         // compile error if missing; JVM refuses to start if absent
    requires java.net.http;                  // a JDK module beyond java.base must be named
    requires static java.compiler;           // needed at compile time only, optional at run time
 
    provides com.acme.inventory.api.StockSource
        with com.acme.inventory.app.internal.MemoryStock;   // a service implementation, found via ServiceLoader
 
    opens com.acme.inventory.app.config to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind;  // reflection for ONE consumer
}
# compile both modules in one go; --module-source-path maps module names to directories
javac -d out --module-source-path . $(find . -name "*.java")
 
# run: -m names the module and its main class
java --module-path out -m com.acme.inventory.app/com.acme.inventory.app.Main
 
# package each module as a modular JAR (the module-info.class goes in the root)
jar --create --file mods/api.jar -C out/com.acme.inventory.api .
jar --create --file mods/app.jar --main-class com.acme.inventory.app.Main -C out/com.acme.inventory.app .
 
# what does this JAR actually depend on?
jdeps --module-path mods -s mods/app.jar
 
# a trimmed runtime image: only the modules reachable from the app, ~40 MB instead of ~300 MB
jlink --module-path mods:$JAVA_HOME/jmods --add-modules com.acme.inventory.app \
      --launcher inventory=com.acme.inventory.app --output inventory-runtime
./inventory-runtime/bin/inventory

The directives

Module declaration directives and their meaning
DirectiveMeaningReach for it when
requires MThis module reads M: its exported packages are accessible here.Always, for every dependency; the compiler will not let you forget.
requires transitive MAnyone who requires this module also reads M.M's types appear in your public API (a method returns an M type).
requires static MNeeded to compile, optional at run time.Annotation processors, compile-time-only annotations, optional integrations.
exports PPublic types in package P are accessible to every module that reads this one.Your API packages, and nothing else.
exports P to M1, M2Qualified export: only M1 and M2 may access P.A "friend" API shared between your own modules.
opens PP is accessible to deep reflection (setAccessible) at run time, but not at compile time.Frameworks that need to reflect into your entities (ORMs, JSON binders, DI).
opens P to MQualified open.The same, limited to the one framework that needs it.
uses SThis module looks up implementations of service interface S with ServiceLoader.Plug-in points.
provides S with CC is an implementation of S that ServiceLoader may hand out.Plug-in implementations; C may live in a non-exported package.
open module M { … }Every package is opened for reflection, none is exported unless stated.A module of plain data classes consumed by reflective frameworks.

Readability, accessibility, and what breaks

Two separate checks gate every cross-module reference. Readability is a relation between modules: A reads B if A requires B (or B is required transitively, or A is the unnamed module). Accessibility is a relation between a class and a package: a type in B is accessible to A only if A reads B, B exports the package, and the type is public. Reflection adds a third level: deep reflection into non-public members needs the package to be open to A as well. Try the combinations:

Can app use what is in api?
Declarations
What app tries to do

The class path did not go away

Everything on the class path is lumped into one unnamed module. It reads every named module, exports all its packages, and opens them all. That is why a 2015 application runs on Java 21 unchanged. The price: a named module cannot requires the unnamed module, so modular code cannot depend on class-path code. Migration therefore proceeds bottom-up, from the leaves of the dependency graph.

Most applications still run this way, deliberately. A module graph pays off for libraries (a clear API surface, no accidental dependency on internals), for the JDK itself, and for anything shipped with jlink. For a service deployed in a container with a fixed dependency list, the gains are smaller and the migration cost of every reflective framework is real.

A plain JAR placed on the module path becomes an automatic module: its name is derived from the file name (jackson-databind-2.17.0.jar → jackson.databind) unless the manifest sets Automatic-Module-Name, it exports every package, and it reads every other module including the unnamed one. That last point is the bridge that lets a modular application use a not-yet-modular library.

Split packages are the migration bug you will hit: two JARs containing classes in the same package (common with javax.* and old API-plus-implementation pairs) are legal on the class path and forbidden on the module path, because a package must belong to exactly one module. jdeps reports them before the JVM does.

# make an unexported package accessible at compile/run time
--add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.misc=ALL-UNNAMED
 
# allow deep reflection into a package (what most framework warnings ask for)
--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED
 
# resolve a module that nothing requires (e.g. a JDK tool module, or jdk.incubator.vector)
--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector
 
# resolve a module and pretend module M reads it
--add-reads com.acme.inventory.app=ALL-UNNAMED

These flags go on the java command line or into a JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS environment variable; they cannot be set from inside the program, by design. Treat each one as technical debt with a name: it records precisely which encapsulation boundary you are crossing and for whom.

// in the api module
public interface StockSource { int onHand(String sku); }
 
// in the app module's module-info: provides StockSource with MemoryStock;
// in any consumer's module-info:   uses StockSource;
 
ServiceLoader<StockSource> sources = ServiceLoader.load(StockSource.class);
StockSource first = sources.findFirst()
        .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalStateException("no StockSource on the module path"));

Services are how a module uses an implementation it cannot see: MemoryStock sits in a non-exported package, the consumer names only the interface, and the module system wires them together. It predates JPMS (the file META-INF/services/… does the same on the class path) but provides … with makes it checked and explicit. JDBC drivers, charsets and HttpClient implementations are all found this way.

Module gotchas
  • exports is not opens. An exported package lets other modules call public members. It does not let a JSON library set a private field. Frameworks need opens; give them a qualified one.
  • requires is not transitive by default. If your API returns a type from module M, callers cannot even name that type unless you write requires transitive M. The symptom is a baffling "cannot access class" error in their build.
  • The module name is not the package name. They usually coincide by convention (com.acme.inventory.api contains package com.acme.inventory.api), but the module declaration lists packages explicitly; a new package added to the API module is private until you export it. That is the point.
  • Reflection across modules fails late. setAccessible(true) on a member in a non-open package throws InaccessibleObjectException at run time, not at compile time, typically the first time a framework touches the class. Test the modular build, not just the class-path one.
  • Class.forName still works, access does not. You can load any class by name; you cannot instantiate or call it unless its package is exported to you. Loading and accessing are different checks.

Check yourself

1.Module app requires api, and api exports com.acme.inventory.api. Jackson, running in its own module, tries to set the private field sku of Product via reflection. What happens?

C. exports grants access to public members at compile and run time. Deep reflection into a private member additionally requires the package to be open to the caller, and the failure is a run-time exception at the setAccessible call.

A confuses exporting with opening. B is wrong because nothing in app references the private field; the compiler has no reason to complain. D gets the direction wrong: an automatic module reads everything, but reading api does not make api's private members accessible; accessibility is decided by the target module's declaration.

2.api has a public method JsonNode toJson() where JsonNode comes from module json, and api declares requires json;. Module app declares only requires api; and calls product.toJson().size(). Result?

B. Readability is not transitive unless declared so. app does not read json, so it cannot use JsonNode even though a method it can call returns one. The API module should say requires transitive json, which is the rule of thumb: anything in your public signatures must be transitive.

A describes what transitive would give you. C is impossible here because javac catches it first. D is wrong because json is resolved (api requires it); resolution and readability are different things.

3.Which statements about the unnamed module are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. Class-path code is one unnamed module that reads all resolved modules and exports and opens all of its packages, which is what keeps old applications working.

B is the migration constraint: named modules cannot depend on the unnamed module, so you modularise from the bottom of the dependency graph up (automatic modules are the bridge). C is false for java.sql, which is in the default root set for the class path; --add-modules is needed only for modules outside that set, such as incubator modules.

Section 13

Measuring: JIT tiers, JMH, JFR and profilers

Java performance intuitions imported from C are mostly wrong, and intuitions from Python are wrong in the other direction, because the code that runs is not the code you wrote. The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode, watches what is hot, compiles that with a fast compiler, keeps watching, then recompiles the hottest parts with an aggressive optimiser that inlines calls, removes allocations and deletes branches the profile says never happen. A method's speed therefore depends on how long it has been running, what types it has seen, and what the code around it looks like. Measuring it well means respecting all three.

This section has no verified program. Every number here is machine-dependent by definition, and the build of this page would prove nothing by printing one. Instead it shows you the tools that produce trustworthy numbers and the mistakes that produce confident wrong ones.

Tiered compilation

HotSpot's compilation tiers
TierWhoWhatEntered when
0InterpreterExecutes bytecode directly; counts invocations and loop back-edgesEvery method starts here
1C1, no profilingFinal tier for trivial methods (getters) that C2 could not improveC1 decides the method is trivial
2C1, light profilingUsed when C2's queue is long, so the method is not stuck at tier 3Compiler back-pressure
3C1, full profilingFast compile; instruments branches, receiver types, counters for C2~200 invocations or ~2,000 back-edges (defaults)
4C2The optimising compiler: inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling, vectorisation, profile-guided layout~5,000 invocations or ~15,000 back-edges, with a profile

A loop that is hot inside a method called once (a main that loops a million times) is handled by on-stack replacement (OSR): the compiled version is entered mid-loop, at a back-edge. Compiled code can also be thrown away. If a branch the profile called "never taken" is taken, C2's uncommon trap deoptimises the method back to the interpreter, re-profiles, and recompiles. Loading a new subclass can do the same thing to every compiled call site that assumed the old hierarchy. Steady state is a moving target, which is the first reason benchmarks need warm-up.

Watch a call chain get compiled

From interpreter to C2 Simulated ← → to step
Source
long total(List<OrderLine> lines) {
    long sum = 0;
    for (OrderLine line : lines)
        sum += line.subtotal();
    return sum;
}
 
long subtotal() {                 // OrderLine
    return product.price() * qty;
}
 
long price() {                    // Product
    return priceInCents;
}
Compiler state
-XX:+PrintCompilation

Which tier is my method in?

Tier and inlining for product.price() called from subtotal() Simulated

Modelled on HotSpot's default Tier3InvocationThreshold=200, Tier4InvocationThreshold=5000, MaxInlineSize=35, FreqInlineSize=325. The real policy also counts back-edges and compiler queue length; the numbers are illustrative, the tiers and rules are not.

Why microbenchmarks lie, and how JMH tells the truth

A loop with System.nanoTime() around it measures, in roughly this order: the interpreter, C1, a C2 compile, JIT compiler threads competing for the CPU, a GC pause, and then, if you are unlucky, nothing at all because C2 noticed the result was never used and deleted the code. The Java Microbenchmark Harness exists to remove each of those, one option at a time.

javaPricingBench.java
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.*;
import org.openjdk.jmh.infra.Blackhole;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
 
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)            // ns per operation, not ops per second
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)           // let tiered compilation finish BEFORE measuring
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Fork(2)                                    // fresh JVMs: run-to-run variance becomes visible
@State(Scope.Thread)
public class PricingBench {
 
    Product[] products;
 
    @Setup(Level.Trial)
    public void setUp() {
        products = new Product[1_000];
        for (int i = 0; i < products.length; i++)
            products[i] = new Product("SKU-" + i, 80 + (i % 7) * 25);   // data the JIT cannot fold
    }
 
    @Benchmark
    public void subtotal(Blackhole bh) {
        for (Product p : products) bh.consume(p.price() * 3);   // consumed: cannot be dead-code eliminated
    }
 
    @Benchmark
    public long subtotalReturned() {
        long sum = 0;
        for (Product p : products) sum += p.price() * 3;
        return sum;                                            // returning is the other way to keep it alive
    }
}
Sample JMH output — illustrative, from one laptop; yours will differ
Benchmark                        Mode  Cnt    Score    Error  Units
PricingBench.subtotal            avgt   10  512.431 ±  6.209  ns/op
PricingBench.subtotalReturned    avgt   10  341.877 ±  4.113  ns/op

Two benchmarks of "the same" loop and a 50% difference: Blackhole.consume per element costs a few nanoseconds itself, which the returned-sum version avoids. Neither number is wrong; they measure different things. Reading a benchmark means knowing exactly what the measured code was allowed to become.

@Benchmark
public void wrong() {
    long x = products[0].price() * 3;      // never read → C2 deletes the multiply AND the call
}
 
@Benchmark
public long right() {
    return products[0].price() * 3;        // the result escapes, so the work must be done
}

The wrong version reports an impossibly small number (often under 1 ns), which is the time of an empty method. C2 is not being clever; removing unobservable work is its job. Return the value or feed it to a Blackhole.

private static final int QTY = 3;          // a compile-time constant
 
@Benchmark
public long wrong() {
    return 80L * QTY;                      // folded to 240 at JIT time: you measure a constant load
}
 
@State(Scope.Thread)
public static class Input { int qty = 3; long price = 80; }   // non-final fields: real loads
 
@Benchmark
public long right(Input in) {
    return in.price * in.qty;
}

Anything derivable from final or literal values is computed once by the compiler. Benchmark inputs belong in non-final fields of a @State object so the JIT has to read them every time, the way production code would.

public static void main(String[] a) {
    long t0 = System.nanoTime();
    for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) work();
    System.out.println((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ns/op");
    // measures: interpreter + C1 + C2 compile time + JIT threads + first GC. Not work().
}

The first few hundred thousand iterations run at interpreter speed and include the compilers' own CPU time. JMH's @Warmup runs the method until the tiers settle, then measures; @Fork repeats in fresh JVMs because the order in which classes happened to load changes what gets inlined, and a single JVM's number is one sample of that distribution. Also: disable CPU frequency scaling, close the browser, and never benchmark on battery.

Measuring the real thing: JFR and profilers

Microbenchmarks answer "is A faster than B?" for code you have already decided to look at. The prior question, "what is slow?", is answered by looking at the running application, and the JDK ships the tool for that: JDK Flight Recorder. It is built into the JVM, costs about 1–2% overhead, and records allocation, GC, lock contention, I/O, exceptions and sampled stacks into a file you analyse offline with JDK Mission Control or the jfr command.

# record one minute, starting now, from a running process
jcmd 12345 JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/inventory.jfr settings=profile
 
# or from launch
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=inventory.jfr,settings=profile -jar inventory.jar
 
# what allocated the most?
jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationSample inventory.jfr | grep -A3 "objectClass" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
 
# summary of everything recorded
jfr summary inventory.jfr
 
# where are threads waiting on monitors longer than 10 ms?
jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter inventory.jfr
 
# a thread dump, when "it is slow right now" and you have thirty seconds
jcmd 12345 Thread.print

Sampling profilers (JFR's method sampler, async-profiler, YourKit) interrupt threads periodically and record the stack. JFR samples only at safepoints by default, points where the JVM can safely pause a thread, which biases the samples toward method exits and loop back-edges and away from the middle of tight compiled code. async-profiler uses the kernel's perf events and AsyncGetCallTrace to avoid that bias, which is why its flame graphs are the usual choice for CPU work, while JFR is unmatched for allocation, lock and I/O events. Use both; they disagree in instructive ways.

The first three things to look at when a service is slow
  1. GC log (-Xlog:gc*, §8–9). Long or frequent pauses explain latency spikes immediately, and a sawtooth that never returns to baseline is a leak.
  2. A thread dump under load (jcmd PID Thread.print, three of them ten seconds apart). Dozens of threads BLOCKED on one monitor, or WAITING in a connection pool, is a contention problem, not a CPU problem, and no profiler flame graph will show it.
  3. Hot methods (JFR or async-profiler). Only now. The hottest frame is usually a surprise — a toString in a log statement, a regex compiled per call, String.format in a loop.

Startup and the alternatives to JIT

JIT optimises for throughput after warm-up, which is the wrong trade for a CLI tool or a serverless function that lives for 200 ms. Class Data Sharing (CDS) maps a pre-parsed archive of classes instead of loading them from JARs; the JDK ships one for its own classes, and -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa then -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa extends it to yours, typically cutting startup by a third. GraalVM native image goes further: it compiles the whole program ahead of time into a native executable with no JIT, no bytecode and no class loading, starting in milliseconds and using a fraction of the memory, at the cost of a closed-world assumption (reflection, proxies and resources must be declared up front), a long build, and peak throughput that only recently caught up with C2 on some workloads. Project Leyden is bringing parts of that idea into the standard JDK.

Performance gotchas
  • A benchmark of a method measures the method in isolation, which production never runs. Inlining context changes the generated code. If the question is "which Map is faster in my service?", measure the service.
  • "Optimising" by making methods bigger can make them slower. Past FreqInlineSize a hot callee stops being inlined; past about 8,000 bytecodes (HugeMethodLimit) it is never compiled at all. The generated code for a giant switch or a 2,000-line method runs in the interpreter forever.
  • Interface calls on one implementation are free; on three they are not. A monomorphic List site inlines ArrayList.get. Mix in LinkedList and Arrays.asList at the same site and it becomes a megamorphic itable dispatch. This is also why Stream pipelines in hot paths can be slower than a loop: the lambda call sites inside the stream implementation are shared by every stream in the process.
  • Median, not mean. GC pauses and deoptimisations give latency a long tail. Report p50/p99/p999; a mean hides the pauses that pages your on-call.
  • The profiler changes the program. Instrumenting profilers (the kind that rewrite bytecode) disable inlining in instrumented methods and can slow code 10×, attributing time to the wrong place. Prefer sampling for CPU; use instrumentation only for counting.

Check yourself

1.A JMH benchmark of products[0].price() * 3 reports 0.3 ns/op, faster than a single CPU cycle on the machine. The most likely cause?

B. Sub-cycle times mean no work happened. A value that is neither returned nor passed to a Blackhole has no observable effect, and C2 removes it along with the call that produced it.

A cannot make one multiply take less than a cycle. C is backwards: JMH measures many operations per timer read precisely so granularity does not matter. D describes something that does happen but still leaves a field load and a multiply, which take time; inlining removes the call, not the work.

2.A service's p99 latency jumps from 20 ms to 400 ms a few times an hour, while CPU is at 30%. Where do you look first?

C. Intermittent tail latency with idle CPU is the signature of waiting: GC pauses or lock/pool contention. The GC log shows the former in seconds; thread dumps during a spike show the latter as many threads BLOCKED or WAITING on one thing.

A finds where CPU time goes, and CPU is not the problem. B measures the handler alone in a warm JVM, which is exactly the condition under which it is fine. D can explain a one-off spike after deployment (recompilation), but not a recurring one at steady state.

3.Which changes could make a hot method slower after C2 compiles it? Select all that apply.

A and C. A megamorphic site loses inlining and becomes a real dispatch, and a method past FreqInlineSize is no longer inlined into its callers; both remove optimisations the small, monomorphic version enjoyed.

B usually helps or is neutral: small methods inline back together. D changes nothing for the JIT; final on locals and parameters is a compile-time check with no bytecode footprint.

Section 14

Serialization, records and the HTTP client

Objects leave the JVM two ways: as bytes handed to something you control (a file, a cache, another JVM) or as a request to a service. Java has a built-in answer for the first, Java serialization, which is thirty years old, still everywhere (RMI, HTTP sessions, caches, message queues), and the source of more critical security advisories than any other feature of the platform. You need to know how it works in order to know why you should rarely use it and how to make it safe where you must. For the second, the JDK's java.net.http.HttpClient replaced the 1997-era HttpURLConnection, and you should know its shape well enough to never reach for the old one.

Worked example: what a round trip does and does not preserve

javaSerializeRecord.java
import java.io.*;
 
public class SerializeRecord {
 
    record Product(String sku, long priceInCents) implements Serializable {
        Product {
            if (sku == null || sku.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("sku required");
            if (priceInCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative price");
            VALIDATIONS++;
        }
        static int VALIDATIONS = 0;
    }
 
    static final class Session implements Serializable {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        private final String user;
        private transient String cachedToken;          // never written to the stream
 
        Session(String user, String token) { this.user = user; this.cachedToken = token; }
        String user() { return user; }
        String cachedToken() { return cachedToken; }
    }
 
    static final class Registry implements Serializable {
        private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
        static final Registry INSTANCE = new Registry();
        private Registry() {}
        // the stream carries a copy; readResolve swaps it for the real singleton
        private Object readResolve() throws ObjectStreamException { return INSTANCE; }
    }
 
    static byte[] write(Object o) throws IOException {
        ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
        try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(bytes)) { out.writeObject(o); }
        return bytes.toByteArray();
    }
 
    static Object read(byte[] data, ObjectInputFilter filter) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        try (ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(data))) {
            if (filter != null) in.setObjectInputFilter(filter);
            return in.readObject();
        }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", 80);
        int before = Product.VALIDATIONS;
        Product copy = (Product) read(write(bolt), null);
        System.out.println("record equal after round trip   = " + bolt.equals(copy));
        System.out.println("record is a different instance  = " + (bolt != copy));
        System.out.println("canonical constructor ran again = " + (Product.VALIDATIONS == before + 1));
 
        Session s = (Session) read(write(new Session("vasim", "tok-123")), null);
        System.out.println("session user survived           = " + s.user());
        System.out.println("transient token after read      = " + s.cachedToken());
 
        Registry r = (Registry) read(write(Registry.INSTANCE), null);
        System.out.println("readResolve kept the singleton  = " + (r == Registry.INSTANCE));
 
        // an allow-list filter: only our own classes and the JDK types they need
        ObjectInputFilter allow = ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter(
                "SerializeRecord$Product;java.lang.*;java.util.*;!*");
        System.out.println("filtered read of Product        = " + ((Product) read(write(bolt), allow)).sku());
        try {
            read(write(new Session("x", "y")), allow);
            System.out.println("filtered read of Session        = allowed");
        } catch (InvalidClassException e) {
            System.out.println("filtered read of Session        = rejected (" + e.getMessage().replaceAll("\\s+", " ").trim() + ")");
        }
    }
}
Expected output
record equal after round trip   = true
record is a different instance  = true
canonical constructor ran again = true
session user survived           = vasim
transient token after read      = null
readResolve kept the singleton  = true
filtered read of Product        = BOLT-7
filtered read of Session        = rejected (filter status: REJECTED)
  • Ordinary classes are deserialized without running any constructor. Session's fields are set directly from the stream by the JVM; the final keyword and every invariant you check in the constructor are bypassed. transient fields are simply left at their default, which is why the token comes back null.
  • Records are different, and better. A record is deserialized by calling its canonical constructor with the stream's component values, so the compact constructor's validation runs again. A stream with a negative price throws IllegalArgumentException at read time instead of producing an impossible object. This is the single strongest reason to make serializable value types records.
  • readResolve lets you substitute the object that comes out — here, to preserve a singleton — and writeReplace does the same on the way in. Together they are how you serialize an object as something simpler (an enum, an id) and rebuild it on read.
  • The filter is the security control. Without one, readObject will instantiate any class on the class path that the bytes name. The allow-list refuses Session before a single byte of it is used.

Why "deserialization of untrusted data" has its own CVE category

The bytes of a serialized stream are not data; they are instructions to the JVM: "create an instance of this class, set these fields, then call its readObject." Thousands of classes on a typical class path have readObject methods or readResolve hooks that do something — call a method on a field, look up a JNDI name, invoke a Comparator — and an attacker who controls the bytes chooses which classes, with which field values. Chaining a handful of such classes from common libraries into a sequence that ends in Runtime.exec is called a gadget chain, and public tools generate them. The 2015 Apache Commons Collections chain compromised application servers worldwide; the 2021 Log4Shell exploit used JNDI deserialization as its payload stage. None of that requires a bug in your code, only that you call readObject on bytes someone else produced.

Controls on Java serialization
ControlWhat it doesUse it
ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290, Java 9)A predicate run on every class, array length, depth and reference count before it is instantiated. Pattern syntax: com.acme.**;java.base/*;!*; ! rejects, last match wins, the trailing !* makes it an allow-list.Always, on every ObjectInputStream that reads anything you did not just write yourself in the same process.
-Djdk.serialFilter=… / ObjectInputFilter.Config.setSerialFilterA process-wide filter applied to every stream that does not set its own.Defence in depth; set it in production to an allow-list even if every stream also sets one.
Filter factory (JEP 415, Java 17)Config.setSerialFilterFactory composes a per-stream filter with the global one, so library code cannot weaken the global policy.When third-party code creates streams you cannot touch.
serialVersionUIDA declared version stamp. If the stream's value differs from the class's, readObject throws InvalidClassException. Left undeclared, it is computed from the class shape and changes whenever you add a method.Declare it on every Serializable class, and bump it only when the serialized form really changes.
Not implementing SerializableThe JVM refuses to instantiate the class from a stream, gadget or not.The default. Mark a class serializable only because something actually needs to serialize it.
 
private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream out) throws IOException {
    out.defaultWriteObject();                // the non-transient fields
    out.writeInt(cache.size());              // then a hand-written form of the transient part
    for (var e : cache.entrySet()) { out.writeUTF(e.getKey()); out.writeInt(e.getValue()); }
}
 
private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
    in.defaultReadObject();
    int n = in.readInt();
    if (n < 0 || n > 10_000) throw new InvalidObjectException("absurd cache size " + n);   // validate!
    cache = new HashMap<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) cache.put(in.readUTF(), in.readInt());
}

The private, oddly-signed writeObject/readObject pair is found by reflection. readObject is effectively a public constructor that takes a byte array, so it must validate as strictly as one. Externalizable is the all-manual variant: you write every field yourself and the class must have a public no-arg constructor.

public final class StockLevel implements Serializable {
    private final String sku; private final int onHand;
    // ... constructor validates ...
 
    private Object writeReplace() { return new Proxy(sku, onHand); }     // what actually gets written
    private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) throws InvalidObjectException {
        throw new InvalidObjectException("use the proxy");               // nobody can bypass the proxy
    }
    private record Proxy(String sku, int onHand) implements Serializable {
        private Object readResolve() { return new StockLevel(sku, onHand); }   // the real constructor runs
    }
}

Effective Java item 90. The stream contains only a dumb record; reading it goes through the real constructor, so invariants hold and the class's private representation can change freely. Records made this pattern mostly unnecessary for value types, because a record is its own proxy.

Serialization alternatives
FormatStrengthsCosts
JSON (Jackson, Gson, JSON-B)Human-readable, language-neutral, schema optional, the web's lingua franca; the deserializer calls your constructorsVerbose on the wire, numbers are doubles unless configured, polymorphism needs explicit type hints — and default typing in Jackson reintroduces gadget chains, so never enable it
Protocol Buffers / AvroCompact binary, versioned schema, generated code, cross-languageA build step and a schema to maintain; fields are optional by design, so absence is a state you must handle
Java serializationZero setup, handles arbitrary object graphs with cyclesJava-only, brittle across versions, slow, and the security liability described above

The rule: Java serialization is acceptable between two JVMs you both control, running the same code, with an allow-list filter. For anything that crosses a trust boundary or a version boundary, use a format with a schema.

The HTTP client

java.net.http.HttpClient (Java 11) speaks HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, follows redirects if told to, has a synchronous and an asynchronous API over the same request object, and pairs naturally with virtual threads because a blocked send parks the virtual thread rather than a carrier. The shape to memorise is: one long-lived client, one immutable request per call, a body handler that says what to turn the response into.

// ONE client for the application: it owns the connection pool and the executor
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))               // establishing the connection
        .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NORMAL)        // not from https to http
        .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)                 // falls back to 1.1 per server
        .build();
 
HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://stock.acme.example/stock/BOLT-7"))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))                     // the whole exchange — always set one
        .header("Accept", "application/json")
        .GET()                                              // or .POST(BodyPublishers.ofString(json))
        .build();
 
// synchronous: blocks this thread (fine on a virtual thread)
HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
if (res.statusCode() != 200) throw new IOException("stock service returned " + res.statusCode());
StockLevel level = parse(res.body());
 
// asynchronous: composes with everything in §6
CompletableFuture<StockLevel> future = client
        .sendAsync(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
        .thenApply(SerializationDemo::parse)
        .orTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

The following program is the same API against a server it starts itself, so it runs and verifies during the build of this page with no network access. The port is chosen by the OS and never printed.

javaHttpLocal.java
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
 
public class HttpLocal {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // port 0 = any free port; the real port is never printed, so the output is stable
        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 0), 0);
        server.createContext("/stock/BOLT-7", exchange -> {
            byte[] body = "{\"sku\":\"BOLT-7\",\"onHand\":42}".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            exchange.getResponseHeaders().add("Content-Type", "application/json");
            exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.length);
            try (var out = exchange.getResponseBody()) { out.write(body); }
        });
        server.start();
        int port = server.getAddress().getPort();
 
        try {
            HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
                    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                    .build();
 
            HttpRequest ok = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/stock/BOLT-7"))
                    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                    .header("Accept", "application/json")
                    .GET()
                    .build();
 
            HttpResponse<String> sync = client.send(ok, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
            System.out.println("sync  status = " + sync.statusCode());
            System.out.println("sync  body   = " + sync.body());
            System.out.println("sync  type   = " + sync.headers().firstValue("Content-Type").orElse("?"));
 
            CompletableFuture<String> async = client.sendAsync(ok, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
                    .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
                    .thenApply(body -> body.contains("\"onHand\":42") ? "42 on hand" : "unexpected");
            System.out.println("async result = " + async.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
 
            HttpRequest missing = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/stock/NOPE"))
                    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build();
            System.out.println("miss  status = " + client.send(missing, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding()).statusCode());
        } finally {
            server.stop(0);
        }
        System.out.println("server stopped");
    }
}
Expected output
sync  status = 200
sync  body   = {"sku":"BOLT-7","onHand":42}
sync  type   = application/json
async result = 42 on hand
miss  status = 404
server stopped
Body handlers and publishers
You wantUse
The body as textBodyHandlers.ofString() (charset from the response, UTF-8 if absent)
To ignore the body (health checks, HEAD-like GETs)BodyHandlers.discarding()
A large download without holding it in memoryBodyHandlers.ofFile(path) or ofInputStream()
Streaming lines (server-sent events, NDJSON)BodyHandlers.ofLines() → a Stream<String> you must close
To send JSONBodyPublishers.ofString(json) plus a Content-Type header
To upload a fileBodyPublishers.ofFile(path)
Gotchas
  • A 404 is not an exception. send throws only for transport failures (connect refused, timeout). Every HTTP status is a normal return; check statusCode() yourself.
  • No timeout means forever. The request builder's timeout defaults to none. A hung server then pins a platform thread for as long as the socket survives. Set it on every request, and connectTimeout on the client.
  • One client, not one per request. Each HttpClient owns a connection pool and threads. Creating one per call leaks both; it is the HttpClient equivalent of opening a new database connection per query.
  • serialVersionUID defaults are a time bomb. Add a method to a serializable class without a declared UID and every cached or persisted instance becomes unreadable with InvalidClassException: local class incompatible.
  • Serializable is inherited and permanent. If a superclass implements it, every subclass is serializable whether it wants to be or not, and once instances exist in storage, the serialized form is part of your API forever.
  • Jackson's default typing is Java serialization with a JSON syntax. @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.CLASS) or enableDefaultTyping lets the document name the class to instantiate: the same gadget-chain attack, and the same mitigation (an allow-list of subtypes).

Check yourself

1.A record Price(long cents) with a compact constructor rejecting negatives is deserialized from a stream an attacker edited to contain -1. What happens?

C. Records are reconstructed through their canonical constructor, so validation in a compact constructor protects deserialization exactly as it protects new. This is one of the design goals of records.

A is true of ordinary classes, not records; that difference is the point. B invents a rule; the stream is structurally valid. D is not something any part of serialization does.

2.Your service reads a serialized Order from a message queue that other teams also publish to. Which single change most reduces the risk of remote code execution?

B. The attack works by naming gadget classes in the stream; a filter that admits only Order and the JDK types it contains refuses every gadget before it is instantiated. The better fix is to stop using Java serialization on that queue, but among these options the filter is the one that closes the hole.

A helps versioning, not security; a UID mismatch only matters for classes the attacker is not choosing. C does nothing: the JVM sets fields directly, final or not. D catches the wrong thing; gadget classes are, by construction, present on the class path.

3.Which statements about java.net.http.HttpClient are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. Status codes are data; only transport problems throw. The async API hands you an ordinary CompletableFuture.

B is the trap: there is no default request timeout at all. C is backwards: the client is the pool, and one per request leaks threads and sockets; it is designed to be shared across the whole application.

Put it together

Hands-on lab: a concurrent reservation service

Six steps that turn the single-threaded InventoryService from Fundamentals into one that many pickers can hit at once without ever selling stock it does not have. Each step uses one tool from this module, and each has a trap that the single-threaded version never had to think about. Write every step before opening its solution, and run yours several times: a concurrency bug that shows up one run in twenty is still a bug.

Starter
mkdir reservation-lab && cd reservation-lab
# one file, ReservationLab.java, grown step by step
javac ReservationLab.java && for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do java ReservationLab | md5sum; done
# five identical hashes = the output does not depend on scheduling

JDK 21 is required for virtual threads (step 5) and for ExecutorService being AutoCloseable, which every try (ExecutorService …) below relies on. Print only facts and sorted data; if your output ever differs between runs, that difference is the bug to find.

Step 1 — stock that can never go negative §1, §4

Store stock levels in a ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger>. Write reserve(sku, qty) so that it returns false when there is not enough, and so that two threads reserving the last unit can never both succeed. No synchronized, no locks: a compare-and-swap loop. Count successes and refusals in two more atomics, and keep an AtomicBoolean that would record a negative level if one ever happened.

Solution — step 1
boolean reserve(String sku, int qty) {
    AtomicInteger level = stock.get(sku);
    if (level == null) { refused.incrementAndGet(); return false; }
    while (true) {
        int current = level.get();                               // read
        if (current < qty) { refused.incrementAndGet(); return false; }
        if (level.compareAndSet(current, current - qty)) {       // write only if nobody moved it
            reserved.incrementAndGet();
            return true;
        }
        // another thread won the race: loop, re-read, decide again
    }
}

level.get() >= qty followed by level.addAndGet(-qty) is the check-then-act race: both threads pass the check, both subtract, stock goes negative. CAS makes the subtraction conditional on the value still being what was checked. getOrDefault(sku, new AtomicInteger()) would be a subtler bug: it hands out a fresh counter not in the map, so reservations against it vanish.

Step 2 — moving stock between two SKUs without deadlock §3

Add transfer(from, to, qty) that must see a consistent pair: nobody may observe the stock after it left from and before it arrived at to. Use one ReentrantLock per SKU. Then call transfer("BOLT-7", "NUT-3", 1) and transfer("NUT-3", "BOLT-7", 1) from two threads at the same time, forever. Make it impossible for that to hang.

Solution — step 2
boolean transfer(String from, String to, int qty) throws InterruptedException {
    String lo = from.compareTo(to) < 0 ? from : to;         // a global order: always lock the
    String hi = lo.equals(from) ? to : from;                 // alphabetically smaller SKU first
    ReentrantLock first  = locks.computeIfAbsent(lo, k -> new ReentrantLock());
    ReentrantLock second = locks.computeIfAbsent(hi, k -> new ReentrantLock());
    if (!first.tryLock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) return false;   // bounded: a bug degrades, never hangs
    try {
        if (!second.tryLock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) return false;
        try {
            AtomicInteger src = stock.get(from);
            if (src == null || src.get() < qty) return false;
            src.addAndGet(-qty);
            stock.computeIfAbsent(to, k -> new AtomicInteger()).addAndGet(qty);
            return true;
        } finally { second.unlock(); }
    } finally { first.unlock(); }
}

Deadlock needs a cycle: thread A holds BOLT and wants NUT while B holds NUT and wants BOLT. Taking locks in a fixed global order makes a cycle impossible, because every thread that wants both takes BOLT first. tryLock with a timeout is the belt to that pair of braces: if someone adds a third lock in the wrong order one day, the symptom is a refused transfer rather than a frozen service. Note the two finally blocks: a lock acquired must be released on every path, including the early return false.

Step 3 — producers, a bounded queue, and a pool of consumers §4, §5
