Four producer threads each generate 100 orders into an ArrayBlockingQueue<Order> of capacity 32. Four consumer tasks on a fixed pool drain it, calling reserve for each. The hard part: how do the consumers know they are finished, and how does main know they all stopped? Count the processed orders and prove the total is 400.

Solution — step 3
static final Order POISON = new Order(-1, "", 0);
 
for (int c = 0; c < consumerCount; c++) {
    handled.add(consumers.submit(() -> {
        int n = 0;
        while (true) {
            Order o = queue.poll(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);      // bounded wait, not take()
            if (o == null || o == POISON) break;
            inv.reserve(o.sku(), o.qty());
            n++;
        }
        return n;
    }));
}
try (ExecutorService producerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(producers)) {
    /* submit the producers, each counting down a CountDownLatch when done */
    produced.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    for (int c = 0; c < consumerCount; c++) queue.put(POISON);   // one pill per consumer
}
int total = 0;
for (Future<Integer> f : handled) total += f.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

A bounded queue is back-pressure: when consumers fall behind, put blocks the producers instead of growing the heap. The poison pill is the classic shutdown protocol: one sentinel per consumer, enqueued only after every producer has finished, so no real order can follow it. Each consumer returns its count through a Future, and main blocks on get with a timeout: if a consumer is stuck, the lab fails loudly in ten seconds instead of hanging.

Step 4 — a quote that combines two lookups and degrades gracefully §6

A quote needs the price (from a pricing service that is down for GIRD-1) and the current stock. Fetch both asynchronously, combine them into one string, and make the failure case produce "GIRD-1: quote unavailable" rather than an exception. Request all four SKUs, wait for all of them with a timeout, and print the quotes sorted.

Solution — step 4
static CompletableFuture<String> quote(InventoryService inv, String sku, Executor pool) {
    CompletableFuture<Long> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        if (sku.equals("GIRD-1")) throw new IllegalStateException("pricing service down");
        return switch (sku) { case "BOLT-7" -> 80L; case "NUT-3" -> 25L; default -> 2_300L; };
    }, pool);
    CompletableFuture<Integer> onHand = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inv.onHand(sku), pool);
    return price.thenCombine(onHand, (p, h) -> sku + ": " + p + "c, " + h + " on hand")
                .exceptionally(ex -> sku + ": quote unavailable")
                .orTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
}
 
CompletableFuture.allOf(quotes.toArray(new CompletableFuture<?>[0])).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

thenCombine waits for both inputs; exceptionally turns a failed stage into a value, placed after the combine so a failure in either lookup is caught. The quotes complete in whatever order the pool runs them, so printing them as they complete would make the output depend on scheduling; collect, sort, then print. allOf plus get(timeout) is the bounded wait.

Step 5 — the same workload on virtual threads §7

Run step 3 again against a fresh service, but with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() as the consumer pool. Nothing else changes. Prove that the final stock levels and the reservation count are identical to the platform-thread run.

Solution — step 5
InventoryService inv2 = new InventoryService();
for (String s : SKUS) inv2.stock(s, 300);
try (ExecutorService vpool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    runPickers(inv2, vpool, 4);
}
System.out.println("platform == virtual totals  = " + (inv.reserved.get() == inv2.reserved.get()
        && inv2.snapshot().equals(afterPlatform)));

The code that was correct on platform threads is correct on virtual threads, because correctness came from the CAS loop and the queue protocol, not from the thread type. What changes is cost: the consumer that blocks in queue.poll parks a virtual thread, which costs a few hundred bytes of heap, rather than parking a carrier. With four consumers it does not matter; with four thousand it is the difference between a working service and one that cannot start.

Step 6 — a consistent report while writers keep going §3, §4

Add snapshot() returning an unmodifiable, sorted map of stock levels. Reads should not block each other, and the report must never contain a level that is mid-transfer. Decide what lock, if any, you need, and what snapshot must return to be safe to hand to another thread.

Solution — step 6
private final ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
 
Map<String, Integer> snapshot() {
    rw.readLock().lock();                       // many readers at once; writers wait
    try {
        TreeMap<String, Integer> copy = new TreeMap<>();
        stock.forEach((k, v) -> copy.put(k, v.get()));
        return Collections.unmodifiableMap(copy);   // a snapshot: later changes do not leak in
    } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
}

Returning the live ConcurrentHashMap would be safe to read but would not be a snapshot: the report would change while being printed. The copy is the consistency mechanism; the read lock only matters if writers take the write lock for multi-SKU operations, which is the extension to attempt below. TreeMap makes the output order deterministic, which is what lets five runs produce the same bytes.

The finished thing

All six steps assembled. This program is compiled and run during the build of this page, on real threads, and the output below is what it printed, byte for byte, which is only possible because every line is a fact that scheduling cannot change.

javaReservationLab.java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.*;
 
public class ReservationLab {
 
    record Order(int id, String sku, int qty) {}
    static final Order POISON = new Order(-1, "", 0);
 
    /* Step 1 — lock-free stock with a CAS loop that can never go negative */
    static final class InventoryService {
        private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger> stock = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        final AtomicInteger reserved = new AtomicInteger();
        final AtomicInteger refused = new AtomicInteger();
        final AtomicBoolean wentNegative = new AtomicBoolean(false);
 
        void stock(String sku, int qty) { stock.computeIfAbsent(sku, k -> new AtomicInteger()).addAndGet(qty); }
        int onHand(String sku) { AtomicInteger a = stock.get(sku); return a == null ? 0 : a.get(); }
 
        boolean reserve(String sku, int qty) {
            AtomicInteger level = stock.get(sku);
            if (level == null) { refused.incrementAndGet(); return false; }
            while (true) {
                int current = level.get();
                if (current < qty) { refused.incrementAndGet(); return false; }
                if (level.compareAndSet(current, current - qty)) {
                    if (current - qty < 0) wentNegative.set(true);
                    reserved.incrementAndGet();
                    return true;
                }
                // another thread won the race: re-read and try again
            }
        }
 
        /* Step 2 — two locks, always taken in SKU order, with a bounded wait */
        boolean transfer(String from, String to, int qty) throws InterruptedException {
            String lo = from.compareTo(to) < 0 ? from : to;
            String hi = lo.equals(from) ? to : from;
            ReentrantLock first = locks.computeIfAbsent(lo, k -> new ReentrantLock());
            ReentrantLock second = locks.computeIfAbsent(hi, k -> new ReentrantLock());
            if (!first.tryLock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) return false;
            try {
                if (!second.tryLock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) return false;
                try {
                    AtomicInteger src = stock.get(from);
                    if (src == null || src.get() < qty) return false;
                    src.addAndGet(-qty);
                    stock.computeIfAbsent(to, k -> new AtomicInteger()).addAndGet(qty);
                    return true;
                } finally { second.unlock(); }
            } finally { first.unlock(); }
        }
 
        /* Step 6 — a consistent snapshot while writers keep going */
        private final ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
        Map<String, Integer> snapshot() {
            rw.readLock().lock();
            try {
                TreeMap<String, Integer> copy = new TreeMap<>();
                stock.forEach((k, v) -> copy.put(k, v.get()));
                return Collections.unmodifiableMap(copy);
            } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
        }
    }
 
    static final String[] SKUS = { "BOLT-7", "NUT-3", "CAM-9", "GIRD-1" };
 
    /* Step 3 — producers feed a bounded queue, a fixed pool of consumers drains it */
    static void runPickers(InventoryService inv, ExecutorService consumers, int consumerCount) throws Exception {
        BlockingQueue<Order> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(32);
        int producers = 4, ordersPerProducer = 100;
        CountDownLatch produced = new CountDownLatch(producers);
        List<Future<Integer>> handled = new ArrayList<>();
 
        for (int c = 0; c < consumerCount; c++) {
            handled.add(consumers.submit(() -> {
                int n = 0;
                while (true) {
                    Order o = queue.poll(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
                    if (o == null || o == POISON) break;
                    inv.reserve(o.sku(), o.qty());
                    n++;
                }
                return n;
            }));
        }
        try (ExecutorService producerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(producers)) {
            for (int p = 0; p < producers; p++) {
                final int base = p * ordersPerProducer;
                producerPool.submit(() -> {
                    try {
                        for (int i = 0; i < ordersPerProducer; i++) {
                            queue.put(new Order(base + i, SKUS[i % SKUS.length], 1 + (i % 3)));
                        }
                    } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
                    finally { produced.countDown(); }
                });
            }
            produced.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            for (int c = 0; c < consumerCount; c++) queue.put(POISON);   // one pill per consumer
        }
        int total = 0;
        for (Future<Integer> f : handled) total += f.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        System.out.println("orders processed            = " + total);
    }
 
    /* Step 4 — a quote that combines two async lookups and degrades gracefully */
    static CompletableFuture<String> quote(InventoryService inv, String sku, Executor pool) {
        CompletableFuture<Long> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
            if (sku.equals("GIRD-1")) throw new IllegalStateException("pricing service down");
            return switch (sku) { case "BOLT-7" -> 80L; case "NUT-3" -> 25L; default -> 2_300L; };
        }, pool);
        CompletableFuture<Integer> onHand = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inv.onHand(sku), pool);
        return price.thenCombine(onHand, (p, h) -> sku + ": " + p + "c, " + h + " on hand")
                    .exceptionally(ex -> sku + ": quote unavailable")
                    .orTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        InventoryService inv = new InventoryService();
        for (String s : SKUS) inv.stock(s, 300);   // demand is 199 per SKU, so nothing is refused
 
        // Step 3 on a platform-thread pool
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { runPickers(inv, pool, 4); }
        Map<String, Integer> afterPlatform = inv.snapshot();
        int stockAfterPicking = afterPlatform.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
 
        // Step 2 — move stock between SKUs under ordered locks, from several threads at once
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
            List<Future<Boolean>> moves = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
                String a = SKUS[i % 4], b = SKUS[(i + 1) % 4];
                moves.add(pool.submit(() -> inv.transfer(a, b, 1)));
            }
            int done = 0;
            for (Future<Boolean> m : moves) if (m.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) done++;
            System.out.println("transfers completed         = " + done + " of 40");
        }
 
        // Step 5 — the same workload on virtual threads, fresh stock, identical totals expected
        InventoryService inv2 = new InventoryService();
        for (String s : SKUS) inv2.stock(s, 300);
        try (ExecutorService vpool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { runPickers(inv2, vpool, 4); }
 
        // Step 4
        try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
            List<CompletableFuture<String>> quotes = new ArrayList<>();
            for (String s : SKUS) quotes.add(quote(inv2, s, pool));
            CompletableFuture.allOf(quotes.toArray(new CompletableFuture<?>[0])).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
            for (CompletableFuture<String> q : quotes) lines.add(q.join());
            Collections.sort(lines);
            lines.forEach(l -> System.out.println("quote                       = " + l));
        }
 
        boolean refusedBig = !inv.reserve("BOLT-7", 1_000);          // more than exists: must refuse, never go negative
        System.out.println("oversized order refused     = " + refusedBig);
 
        // Step 6 — facts only
        int stockAfterTransfers = inv.snapshot().values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
        System.out.println("stock never negative        = " + !inv.wentNegative.get());
        System.out.println("reserved + refused == 401   = " + (inv.reserved.get() + inv.refused.get() == 401));
        System.out.println("stock conserved by transfer = " + (stockAfterTransfers == stockAfterPicking));
        System.out.println("platform == virtual totals  = " + (inv.reserved.get() == inv2.reserved.get()
                && inv2.snapshot().equals(afterPlatform)));
        System.out.println("final stock (virtual run)   = " + inv2.snapshot());
    }
}
Expected output
orders processed            = 400
transfers completed         = 40 of 40
orders processed            = 400
quote                       = BOLT-7: 80c, 104 on hand
quote                       = CAM-9: 2300c, 96 on hand
quote                       = GIRD-1: quote unavailable
quote                       = NUT-3: 25c, 100 on hand
oversized order refused     = true
stock never negative        = true
reserved + refused == 401   = true
stock conserved by transfer = true
platform == virtual totals  = true
final stock (virtual run)   = {BOLT-7=104, CAM-9=96, GIRD-1=104, NUT-3=100}

Why the numbers are what they are: each producer's 100 orders cycle through the four SKUs with quantities 1, 2, 3, so every SKU is asked for about 199 units per run, out of 300. Nothing is refused until the deliberate 1,000-unit order at the end, which is why reserved + refused is 401, and the forty one-unit transfers move ten units around each edge of a cycle and net to zero per SKU, which is why the stock is conserved and the platform and virtual runs agree.

Extensions worth attempting
  • Make transfer and snapshot truly consistent. Right now a snapshot can observe the moment between the subtract and the add. Take the write lock in transfer and the read lock in snapshot, then prove with a counter that the sum of all levels in every snapshot taken during 10,000 concurrent transfers is always 1,200. Then measure what the write lock costs the pickers.
  • Reduce stock to 100 per SKU so that refusals happen during the concurrent run. The reservation count now varies between runs. Which facts can you still print deterministically, and how would you test that the service is correct when its output is not?
  • Replace the poison pills with structured concurrency. Run the producers and consumers under a StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure (preview in 21, so --enable-preview) and make a producer throw. What happens to the consumers, and how does that compare to what happens today if a producer dies?

Reference

Cheat sheet

Everything worth having in front of you while a service is misbehaving. This section is laid out to print cleanly — controls and navigation are hidden, and tables are kept whole across page breaks. Each block names the section it condenses.

Thread states §1

Thread states and what puts a thread in each
StateMeansGets there byIn a thread dump
NEWcreated, not startednew Thread(r)not shown
RUNNABLErunning or eligible to run (includes blocking I/O)start()runnable
BLOCKEDwaiting to enter a monitorsynchronized held by another threadwaiting for monitor entry
WAITINGparked indefinitelywait(), join(), LockSupport.park(), lock()waiting on condition / in Object.wait()
TIMED_WAITINGparked with a deadlinesleep(ms), wait(ms), tryLock(t), join(ms)waiting on condition with a timeout
TERMINATEDrun() returned or threw—not shown

count++ is load, add, store — three operations with a gap another thread can fall into. Interruption is a request: interrupt() sets a flag, blocking calls throw InterruptedException and clear it, so restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() when you cannot propagate. The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread ends.

Happens-before edges §2

The happens-before rules of the Java memory model
RuleEdge
Program ordereach action in a thread → every later action in that thread
Monitor lockunlock of M → every later lock of the same M
Volatilewrite to v → every later read of v (and everything before the write becomes visible: piggybacking)
Thread startt.start() → every action in t
Thread terminationevery action in t → t.join() returning / isAlive() false
Interruptiont.interrupt() → t detecting it
Final fieldsconstructor end → any thread that sees the reference sees the final fields
TransitivityA → B and B → C gives A → C
java.util.concurrentevery submit → the task; task completion → Future.get; countDown → await returning; put → the matching take

A data race is a write and a conflicting access with no happens-before edge between them. volatile gives visibility and ordering, not atomicity: volatile int i; i++ still loses updates. Immutable objects published through any edge are safe; the holder idiom and volatile double-checked locking are the two correct lazy-init shapes.

Which lock §3

Lock types compared
ToolReach for it whenHasLacks
synchronizedthe default; short critical sections, one conditionreentrancy, wait/notifyAll, auto-release on exception, JIT lock elisiontimeouts, interruptible acquire, fairness, multiple conditions
ReentrantLockyou need tryLock(timeout), lockInterruptibly, several Conditions, or fairnessall of the aboveauto-release — unlock() must be in finally
ReentrantReadWriteLockmany readers, rare writers, long readsshared read lock, exclusive write lockupgrade read → write (deadlocks); cheapness for short reads
StampedLockread-mostly with very short readsoptimistic read (tryOptimisticRead + validate)reentrancy, conditions

Deadlock needs all four: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break the last one with a global lock order, or the second with tryLock and back-off:

void transfer(Account a, Account b, int qty) {
    Account first  = a.id().compareTo(b.id()) < 0 ? a : b;   // global order, never identityHashCode
    Account second = first == a ? b : a;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { move(a, b, qty); } }
}
 
boolean transferWithTimeout(Account a, Account b, int qty) throws InterruptedException {
    while (true) {
        if (a.lock().tryLock(10, MILLISECONDS)) {
            try {
                if (b.lock().tryLock(10, MILLISECONDS)) {
                    try { move(a, b, qty); return true; } finally { b.lock().unlock(); }
                }
            } finally { a.lock().unlock(); }
        }
        Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(5));   // back off, or livelock
    }
}

Lock on a private final Object lock, never on this, a String, or a boxed value. Always loop on the condition around wait(); prefer notifyAll.

Atomics and concurrent collections by need §4

Which concurrent type for which need
You needUseNot
a counter read as often as writtenAtomicInteger / AtomicLongvolatile int with ++
a hot counter read rarely (metrics)LongAdderAtomicLong under heavy contention
bounded decrement / any read-modify-writecompareAndSet loop, or updateAndGetcheck-then-act in two calls
swap an immutable snapshotAtomicReference + recordlocks around a mutable object
keyed counters / caches / multimapsConcurrentHashMap with merge, compute, computeIfAbsentcontainsKey then put; Collections.synchronizedMap
sorted concurrent map/setConcurrentSkipListMap / SetTreeMap under a lock
read-mostly listener listCopyOnWriteArrayListsame type for frequent writes
producer → consumer, boundedArrayBlockingQueue / LinkedBlockingQueue(cap)an unbounded queue (memory)

by priority / by delayPriorityBlockingQueue / DelayQueue—

ConcurrentHashMap: no null keys or values; per-bin locking on writes, lock-free reads; compute* is atomic per key only; iterators are weakly consistent; size() is an estimate under concurrent writes. CAS is one CPU instruction that succeeds only if the slot still holds the expected value — a retry loop, not a block. The ABA problem: the value went A → B → A and the CAS cannot tell; use AtomicStampedReference when identity matters.

Thread pools §5

ThreadPoolExecutor parameters and the factory methods
Factorycore / maxQueueHides
newFixedThreadPool(n)n / nunbounded LinkedBlockingQueueunbounded memory when producers outrun consumers
newCachedThreadPool()0 / Integer.MAX_VALUESynchronousQueueunbounded threads under a burst

ThreadPoolExecutor growth rule: below core → new thread; at core → queue first; only when the queue is full → grow to max; then the RejectedExecutionHandler (AbortPolicy default, CallerRunsPolicy for back-pressure). Size: CPU-bound ≈ cores; I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute). Always shutdown() then awaitTermination, or use the Java 19+ close() in try-with-resources; non-daemon pool threads keep the JVM alive. A task's exception goes into its Future — if nobody calls get(), nobody sees it.

Collectors compared §8

Garbage collectors compared
CollectorOptimisesPausesPick for
Serialfootprintstop-the-world, single threadtiny heaps, one core, containers under 2 cores
Parallelthroughputstop-the-world, all coresbatch jobs where pauses do not matter
G1 (default)balance; pause goal (MaxGCPauseMillis)short young pauses; concurrent marking; mixed collections; a Full GC only when it falls behindmost services, heaps up to tens of GB
ZGC (-XX:+ZGenerational in 21)latencysub-millisecond; concurrent compaction via coloured pointers and load barrierslarge heaps, strict latency
Shenandoahlatencyconcurrent compaction via Brooks pointerssame niche as ZGC; not in all JDK builds

Generational hypothesis: most objects die young, so eden is collected by copying survivors — cost is proportional to live objects, not garbage. Reference strength: strong → soft (cleared under memory pressure) → weak (cleared at the next GC) → phantom (post-mortem, via a ReferenceQueue). finalize() is gone; use Cleaner, and never capture this in the cleaning action. Four OOMs: Java heap space, Metaspace, GC overhead limit exceeded, unable to create native thread.

Old gen climbing after every Full GC is a leak; frequent Full GCs that do reclaim is an undersized heap; exit code 137 with a healthy heap is the kernel OOM-killing the container.

Class loading §10

Class initialization triggers and the loader hierarchy
Initializes the classDoes not
new; a static method call; a non-constant static field read or write; Class.forName(name); initializing a subclass; a reflective call; the main class at start-upreading a compile-time constant (static final primitive/String literal — it is inlined); loadClass; Class.forName(name, false, loader); an array type Prices[]; a .class literal; a subclass's static member that is inherited from a superclass (initializes only the declaring class)

Phases: loading (bytes → Class) → linking (verify, prepare defaults, resolve lazily) → initialization (<clinit>: superclass first, then textual order, once, under a lock). Loaders: bootstrap (null, java.base) ← platform ← app; parent delegation asks the parent first, so java.lang.String cannot be replaced. Identity is (loader, name): the same bytes in two loaders are two classes. ClassNotFoundException is "never found" (checked, from forName/loadClass); NoClassDefFoundError is "found at compile time, missing or broken now" — Could not initialize class means an earlier ExceptionInInitializerError.

Module directives §12

module-info.java directives
DirectiveEffect

Readability (requires) is necessary but not sufficient; accessibility also needs the package exported and the member public. Class-path code lives in the unnamed module, reads every module, and can reflect into any opens but not into java.base internals: the fix is --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED, the cure is to stop needing it. A jar on the module path without module-info becomes an automatic module named from Automatic-Module-Name or its file name. Split packages are forbidden. jdeps finds your dependencies; jlink builds a runtime with only the modules you use.

JIT tiers and JMH pitfalls §13

HotSpot compilation tiers
TierCodeEntered after
0interpreter, collecting countsfirst call
1–3C1 (3 = full profiling)~200 invocations or hot loops (OSR)
4C2, with inlining, escape analysis, scalar replacement~5,000 invocations / ~15,000 back-edges
deoptback to the interpreteran uncommon trap: a new subclass broke a monomorphic inline, a null appeared, a branch never taken was taken

Inlining limits (defaults): MaxInlineSize 35 bytecodes for cold calls, FreqInlineSize 325 for hot ones; megamorphic call sites (three or more receiver types) are not inlined. JMH pitfalls: dead-code elimination (return the value or sink it into a Blackhole), constant folding (read inputs from @State fields, not literals), no warm-up / no forks (@Warmup, @Fork(1+)), GC noise and CPU frequency. A result faster than a cycle is a bug in the benchmark, not a miracle. First three things to check for a slow service: the GC log, a thread dump under load, the hot methods from JFR.

Deserializing untrusted bytes runs other people's readObject methods — a gadget chain turns that into remote code execution. Prefer JSON/Protobuf at trust boundaries; if you must use Java serialization, filter. HttpClient: build once, set connectTimeout on the client and timeout on each request, BodyHandlers.ofString(), sendAsync returns a CompletableFuture.

Rehearsal

Interview questions

Twelve questions that actually get asked about this material, with the answer a strong candidate gives. Say your answer out loud before opening the reveal — recognising an answer and being able to produce one are different skills.

Easy  1. Why does count++ from two threads lose updates, and what are the two fixes?

Because it is three operations, not one: load the field into a register, add one, store it back. If two threads both load 41, both add, both store 42, one increment has vanished — and nothing throws, so the bug surfaces as a slightly wrong total weeks later. The two fixes are mutual exclusion or an atomic. synchronized (or a ReentrantLock) makes the three steps one critical section that only one thread enters at a time. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() uses a compare-and-swap instruction that succeeds only if the value is still what was read, and retries otherwise — no blocking, no lock. The one thing that is not a fix is volatile: it makes every read see the latest store, but the gap between load and store is still there.

Easy  2. What does volatile guarantee, and what does it not?

It guarantees visibility and ordering: a write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field, so a reader cannot see a stale cached value, and everything the writer did before the volatile write is visible to the reader after the volatile read — which is why a volatile flag can safely publish a whole object built before the flag was set. It does not guarantee atomicity of compound actions: volatile int i; i++ still races, and a check-then-act on a volatile field is still a race. The rule of thumb: volatile is right for a status flag written by one thread and read by others, and for the double-checked-locking instance field. For a counter use an atomic; for an invariant across several fields use a lock.

Easy  3. When would you use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized?

Only when I need something synchronized cannot give me. Four things: a timed or interruptible acquire (tryLock(10, MILLISECONDS), lockInterruptibly()) so a thread can give up rather than block forever; more than one condition queue on the same lock (notFull and notEmpty in a bounded buffer, instead of notifyAll waking everyone); fairness, rarely; or a lock whose acquire and release are in different methods, which a block cannot express. Otherwise synchronized wins: it cannot be forgotten in a finally, the JIT can elide it, thread dumps show the monitor, and both are reentrant with equivalent performance on modern JVMs. Mention that a read-mostly structure wants a ReadWriteLock or StampedLock, and that a counter wants no lock at all.

Easy  4. How do you prevent deadlock?

Deadlock needs four conditions at once — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a circular wait — so I remove one. The practical cure is to break the cycle with a global lock order: every thread that needs two locks acquires them in the same order, by a stable key such as an account id, never by identity hash code. The second cure breaks hold-and-wait: tryLock with a timeout, releasing everything and backing off randomly on failure, which also needs a bound so it does not livelock. The third is to not need two locks: one coarser lock, or a lock-free structure. Then I detect what is left: jstack prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the cycle, and a ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() health check catches it in production.

Medium  5. How do you size a thread pool, and why can Executors.newFixedThreadPool run out of memory?

By what the threads wait for. CPU-bound work wants about one thread per core — more just adds context switches. I/O-bound work wants cores × (1 + wait time ÷ compute time): if a request spends 9 ms waiting on a database for every 1 ms of CPU, eight cores can keep eighty threads busy. Past a few hundred threads the right answer is virtual threads, not a bigger pool. newFixedThreadPool bounds the threads but not the queue — it uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so when producers outrun the pool, tasks accumulate until the heap is gone, and the OOM surfaces in a thread that had nothing to do with it. A real pool is a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy, usually CallerRunsPolicy for back-pressure, and a named ThreadFactory so dumps are readable.

Medium  6. thenApply versus thenCompose, and which thread runs a stage?

thenApply is map: the function returns a plain value. thenCompose is flatMap: the function returns another CompletableFuture, and compose unwraps it so the chain continues with its value rather than with a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>. Which thread runs a stage depends on the method variant. A non-async stage such as thenApply runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage — the pool thread that finished the supplier, or, if the future was already complete when you attached the stage, the caller's own thread, which is how a "quick" callback ends up doing heavy work on a request thread. The thenApplyAsync variants always hand the stage to an executor: the common ForkJoinPool by default, which is shared with parallel streams and sized to cores, so I pass my own executor for anything that blocks.

Medium  7. What is a virtual thread, and when does it not help?

A thread whose stack lives on the heap and is scheduled by the JVM rather than the operating system. When it blocks — on a socket, a sleep, a j.u.c lock — the JVM unmounts it from its carrier platform thread and mounts another, so a handful of carriers can serve millions of virtual threads. That makes thread-per-request scale without async code. It does not help CPU-bound work: the carriers are still about one per core, so throughput is unchanged. It does not help in Java 21 when the blocking happens inside a synchronized block or a native frame, because the virtual thread is pinned to its carrier; JEP 491 fixes the monitor case in Java 24, and ReentrantLock avoids it today. And it is not a reason to pool: virtual threads are meant to be created per task and thrown away; bound the scarce resource with a Semaphore instead.

Medium  8. How does G1 differ from ZGC, and what is a GC pause actually doing?

Both are generational, region-based collectors; the difference is what they do while the application is stopped. A pause is the time when every mutator thread is at a safepoint so the collector can see a consistent graph: G1 uses that time to copy live objects out of the regions it is evacuating — young collections and mixed collections are all evacuation pauses, and the pause scales with the amount of live data, with marking done concurrently in between. ZGC moves objects concurrently: coloured pointers carry metadata bits, and a load barrier on every reference read fixes up a pointer to an object that has moved, so the pauses are only the tiny start and end of a phase, well under a millisecond, regardless of heap size. The cost is throughput — barriers on every load — and memory. G1 is the balanced default; ZGC is for large heaps with strict latency targets.

Medium  9. From a GC log, how do you tell a memory leak from an undersized heap?

Watch the after number of each Full GC. A Full collection reclaims everything unreachable, so what remains is the live set. If the post-GC occupancy climbs steadily across hours — 200M, then 260M, then 330M — something is holding references it should have dropped: a static cache, listeners never removed, a ThreadLocal in a pool, an unclosed resource. That is a leak and no heap size fixes it, only a heap dump and the dominator tree. If the post-GC occupancy is stable but close to the ceiling and Full GCs are frequent, the live set simply does not fit with room for allocation: that is an undersized heap, and -Xmx fixes it. A third pattern: the JVM reports nothing and the container is killed with exit code 137 — the heap fit, but heap plus metaspace, thread stacks and native memory exceeded the cgroup limit.

Hard  10. Walk through what happens when a class is first used, and why loaders delegate to their parent.

Three phases. Loading: the loader finds the bytes and defines a Class object. Linking: the verifier checks the bytecode, preparation allocates statics with default values, and resolution of symbolic references happens lazily. Initialization: the superclass initializes first, then <clinit> runs static initializers in textual order, exactly once, under a lock. Loading can happen early; initialization is deferred until the first active use — new, a static method call, a non-constant static field access, Class.forName — and reading a compile-time constant is not a use because the compiler inlined it. Delegation: before a loader looks for a class itself it asks its parent, up to bootstrap. That is how java.lang.String is always the JDK's, and why class identity is the pair (loader, name): the same bytes loaded by two loaders are two unrelated classes, which is the ClassCastException you get from plugin systems.

Hard  11. What is strong encapsulation, and what does --add-opens do?

Since Java 9 a package is accessible from another module only if its module exports it, and reflectively accessible to private members only if it opens it; setAccessible(true) on a member of a package that is not opened to you throws InaccessibleObjectException. Java 16 made this the default for the JDK's own internals, which is why a library that reached into java.lang.String's private value field worked on 11 and fails on 17. --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED is the escape hatch: it opens that one package of that one module to class-path code at run time. It is a workaround, not a fix — the fix is a library version that uses supported APIs — and I would make it explicit in the launch script rather than hidden in a manifest. The companion flags are --add-exports for compile-time access to non-exported public types and --add-modules to resolve a module that nothing requires.

Hard  12. Why is Java serialization dangerous, and what do records change?

Because deserialization instantiates whatever classes the byte stream names and runs their readObject methods, without calling a constructor and before your code sees the object. Attackers chain classes that are already on the class path — a gadget chain — so that the act of reading the stream ends in Runtime.exec. That is why "deserialization of untrusted data" is its own CVE category. The defences: do not accept serialized objects across a trust boundary at all (JSON or Protobuf); if you must, install an ObjectInputFilter allow-list, per stream or globally via jdk.serialFilter, with depth and size limits. Records change one thing substantially: a record is always reconstructed through its canonical constructor, so a compact constructor's validation runs on deserialization too, and the no-constructor path that makes classic classes unsafe does not exist for them. They are still subject to gadget chains in the rest of the stream, so the filter stays.

Assessment

Self-assessment quiz

Sixteen questions covering all fourteen learning objectives. Answer every one, then submit — nothing is marked until you do, and the explanations stay hidden until then. Your answers are saved locally, so you can leave and come back.

1.Two threads share one int count and each runs count++ once. Both start with count == 41. Which final values are possible?

C. count++ is load, add, store. If both threads load 41 before either stores, both store 42 and one increment is lost; if they run one after the other, 43. A is the intuition the bug relies on. B: memory writes never throw; a race is silent. D: each thread stores at least 42, so 41 cannot survive.

2.Thread t = new Thread(task); t.start(); t.start(); — what happens on the second line's second call?

B. A Thread object goes NEW → RUNNABLE → … → TERMINATED once; start() on anything but NEW throws, even after termination. A and C describe a reusable worker, which is what a thread pool is for. D is what calling run() directly does — the classic mistake, but not this one.

3.Thread W writes price = 80 (a plain field) and then does X. Thread R does Y and then reads price. Which (X, Y) pairs guarantee R reads 80? Select all that apply.

B, C and D. Each creates a happens-before edge: volatile write → volatile read (and everything before the write rides along), countDown → await returning, and thread termination → join. A is the one people reach for and it guarantees nothing: time is not synchronisation; without an edge the JIT may hoist R's read out of a loop and R can spin forever on a stale value.

4.A team "fixes" a lost-update bug by changing int hits to volatile int hits, leaving hits++ in place. What did they get?

C. volatile orders and publishes individual reads and writes; hits++ is still three of them. A is the single most common memory-model misconception. B: it compiles fine, which is the problem. D: the race is in the Java semantics, not the hardware; it loses updates everywhere. The fix is AtomicInteger or a lock.

5.Predict the output:

static synchronized void reserve() { audit(); System.out.println("reserved"); }
static synchronized void audit()   { System.out.println("audited"); }
public static void main(String[] a) { reserve(); }

A. Both methods lock the same monitor (the Class object), and a thread that already owns a monitor may enter it again; the JVM counts the depth. B would be true of a non-reentrant lock — Java has none in the standard library except StampedLock. C is thrown by wait/notify without owning the monitor, not by nested entry. D: nothing is ever skipped.

6.transfer(a, b) locks a then b; a concurrent transfer(b, a) locks b then a. Which change makes deadlock impossible?

B. A global order over a stable, unique key breaks the circular wait. A is almost right and is the textbook trap: identity hash codes can collide, and when they do the tie must be broken with a third lock, or the order is undefined. C locks only this — the other account is unprotected, so the invariant breaks instead of deadlocking. D changes the timing, which makes the deadlock rarer and therefore harder to reproduce; it removes nothing.

7.Eight threads count picks per SKU in a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> picks. Which line is correct?

C. merge performs the read-modify-write atomically for that key, inside the bin lock. A is a check-then-act in two calls; a concurrent map makes each call safe, not the pair. B locks on a String — two equal SKUs from different sources may be different objects, and interned literals are shared with the whole JVM; either way it is the wrong lock. D does not compile: get returns a value, not a variable, and the increment would be on an unboxed copy anyway.

8.Which statements about compare-and-swap are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. B is the opposite of the point: CAS never blocks; the caller reloads and retries. C: incrementAndGet is a retry loop around CAS, which is why LongAdder exists for hot counters — under heavy contention the retries pile up.

9.new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 8, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()) receives 1,000 quick tasks at once. How many threads does it run at peak?

B. The growth rule is core → queue → max → reject, and the queue step only passes when offer fails. An unbounded queue never refuses, so maximumPoolSize is dead configuration. A is what everyone assumes. C describes newCachedThreadPool, whose SynchronousQueue always "fails" to queue. D needs a full queue first.

10.pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); }); and nobody calls get(). Where does the exception go?

C. submit wraps the task in a FutureTask that catches everything; the worker thread survives and the exception is only observable through get(). A is what happens with execute() — the difference is a frequent interview follow-up. B: submit returns before the task runs. D: the worker is unharmed, which is precisely why nothing is logged.

11.Predict the output on a thread named main:

CompletableFuture<Integer> done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(1);
boolean onMain = done.thenApply(x -> Thread.currentThread().getName().equals("main")).join();
System.out.println(onMain);

A. A non-async stage runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage; when that stage is already complete at attach time, the attaching thread runs it inline. That is how a "callback" ends up doing heavy work on a request thread. B is the rule for thenApplyAsync with no executor. C: the rule is deterministic here. D: join is an ordinary method.

12.cf = supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("offline"); }, pool).thenApply(v -> v + 1).exceptionally(e -> -1); Which are true? Select all that apply.

B and C. A failed stage skips every dependent value-stage (A is false: the function is never invoked) and passes the failure, wrapped in a CompletionException, to the first recovery stage — which is why code in exceptionally should unwrap with getCause() before matching on type. D: get() throws ExecutionException with the original as its cause; join() throws CompletionException. Neither throws the original bare.

13.A JDK 21 service moves its JDBC-heavy request handling from a 200-thread pool to one virtual thread per request. The driver does its socket reads inside synchronized methods. What happens under load?

C. In 21 a virtual thread blocking inside a monitor cannot unmount, so each carrier is held for the duration of the read — -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads shows it. A driver using ReentrantLock would be fine; JEP 491 in Java 24 fixes synchronized. A is the promise, broken by pinning. B: virtual threads are not native threads; that error belongs to platform threads. D: socket reads are exactly the blocking the JVM detects.

14.A G1 log shows a Full GC every ten minutes; each one reclaims the heap from 3.9 GB back to a steadily rising 1.2, 1.5, 1.9, 2.4 GB. What is the most likely diagnosis and first action?

B. After a Full GC only reachable objects remain, so a post-GC floor that climbs is a live set that keeps growing — something is retaining references. A buys time and moves the crash later. C changes how the garbage is collected, not how much is not garbage. D: old gen filling is normal; its post-collection minimum rising is not.

15.Predict the output:

class Prices { static final int MAX = 8; static { System.out.println("init"); } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] a) { System.out.println(Prices.MAX); } }

A. static final int MAX = 8 is a constant variable (JLS §4.12.4); javac copies the literal into Main, and Prices is not an active use. Drop final, or make it Integer.valueOf(8), and B becomes correct. C: the JVM has no memory between runs. D: initialisation is synchronous and happens-before the first use.

16.Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

A, C and D. A is strong encapsulation of the JDK (default since 16). C was confirmed against JDK 21: the canonical constructor runs on every read and its IllegalArgumentException arrives wrapped in InvalidObjectException. D: the default retention is CLASS, kept in the bytecode but not loaded. B is false — forking isolates JVMs; it does nothing about dead-code elimination, which removes an unused result and the work that produced it. Return the value or sink it into a Blackhole.

Reference

Glossary

Thirty terms, each linked back to the section that introduces it. The same entries drive the flashcard deck below — one list, two ways to use it.

Flashcards

ABA problem
A compare-and-swap sees the expected value A and succeeds, not knowing the slot went A → B → A in between. Harmless for counters; dangerous when identity matters, which is what AtomicStampedReference is for. §4
Atomicity
An operation that other threads see either entirely done or not at all. count++ is not atomic: it is load, add, store, and another thread can fall into the gaps. §1
Automatic module
A jar without module-info.class placed on the module path. It gets a name from Automatic-Module-Name or its file name, exports every package and reads every module — the bridge for libraries that have not modularised. §12
Carrier thread
A platform thread in the virtual-thread scheduler's ForkJoinPool on which a virtual thread is mounted to run. When the virtual thread blocks it unmounts and the carrier picks up another. §7
Class loader delegation
Before defining a class itself, a loader asks its parent — app → platform → bootstrap. It is why java.lang.String cannot be replaced from the class path, and why class identity is the pair (loader, name). §10
Compare-and-swap
One CPU instruction: "if this location still holds X, store Y and report success". The primitive under every atomic and lock-free structure; a failure means retry, never block. §4
Completion stage
One step of a CompletableFuture pipeline: a function that runs when the previous stage completes, on the completing thread (non-async) or on an executor (*Async). A failed stage skips value stages until a recovery stage. §6
Data race
A write and a conflicting access to the same variable from two threads with no happens-before edge between them. The JMM then permits stale, reordered or torn values; the program is incorrect even if it appears to work. §2
Deadlock
Two or more threads each holding a lock the other needs, forever. Requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and a circular wait; cured by a global lock order or tryLock with a timeout. §3
Deoptimization
The JIT throwing away compiled code when an assumption it made stops holding — a new subclass breaks an inlined monomorphic call, an untaken branch is taken — and falling back to the interpreter until it recompiles. §13
Escape analysis
C2 proving that an object never leaves the compiled method, so it can be replaced by its fields in registers (scalar replacement) and never allocated at all — the reason short-lived objects are often free. §13
G1 region
G1 divides the heap into equal regions (1–32 MB) and assigns each a role — eden, survivor, old, humongous — dynamically. A collection evacuates the regions with the most garbage first, which is the "garbage first" in the name. §8
Gadget chain
A sequence of classes already on the class path whose readObject methods, invoked in order by deserializing a crafted stream, end in arbitrary code execution. Why untrusted Java serialization is treated as remote code execution. §14
Generational hypothesis
Most objects die young. Collectors exploit it by collecting the young generation often and by copying the few survivors, so the cost tracks live data rather than garbage. §8
Happens-before
The JMM's partial order. If A happens-before B, B sees A's effects. The edges: program order, monitor unlock → lock, volatile write → read, start, join, and transitivity; everything in java.util.concurrent is built to provide them. §2
Initialization trigger
The first active use that runs a class's static initializers: new, a static method call, a non-constant static field access, Class.forName, or initializing a subclass. Reading a compile-time constant is not one. §10
Inlining
The JIT copying a callee's body into the caller, removing the call and enabling every other optimisation. Limited by bytecode size (35 cold, 325 hot by default) and by megamorphic call sites. §13
Livelock
Threads that keep running but make no progress — two tryLock loops that both back off and retry in step. Cured with randomised back-off or a bound on retries. §3
Load barrier
A few instructions ZGC runs on every reference load that check the pointer's colour bits and, if the object has moved, fix the reference up. The mechanism that lets ZGC relocate objects while the application runs. §8
Metaspace
Native memory holding class metadata, unbounded by default. It grows with every class loader that cannot be collected, which is how hot-redeploy and plugin systems leak until OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. §9
Monitor
The lock every object carries for synchronized: one owner, an entry set of threads blocked trying to enter, and a wait set of threads parked in wait() that must re-acquire it after notify. Reentrant. §3
Pinning
A virtual thread that cannot unmount from its carrier while blocked — in JDK 21, inside a synchronized block or a native frame. Pinned carriers are the usual reason virtual threads fail to scale; JEP 491 fixes the monitor case in 24. §7
Poison pill
A sentinel object placed on a BlockingQueue to tell a consumer to stop — one per consumer — so shutdown needs no flag polling and no interrupt. §4
Reachability
An object is live if a chain of references leads to it from a GC root — a thread stack, a static field, a JNI handle. Collectors reclaim everything else; a "leak" in Java is an object that is reachable but no longer wanted. §8
Reentrancy
A thread that holds a lock may acquire it again without blocking; the lock counts the depth. Both synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant, which is what lets one synchronized method call another on the same object. §3
Rejection policy
What a ThreadPoolExecutor does with a task when its queue is full and it is at maximumPoolSize: throw (AbortPolicy, the default), run it on the submitting thread (CallerRunsPolicy, back-pressure), drop it, or drop the oldest. §5
Safe publication
Making an object visible to other threads through a happens-before edge — a volatile field, a lock, a concurrent collection, a thread start — so they see its fully constructed state rather than a half-built one. Immutable objects with final fields are safe through any route. §2
Stop-the-world
A GC phase during which every application thread is halted at a safepoint so the collector can see a consistent object graph. All of Serial and Parallel, the evacuation pauses of G1, and only the brief phase boundaries of ZGC. §8
Strong encapsulation
The module system's rule that a package is accessible only if exported, and open to deep reflection only if opened. Enforced for the JDK's own internals since Java 16; --add-opens is the per-package escape hatch. §12
Tiered compilation
HotSpot's pipeline from the interpreter (tier 0) through C1 with profiling (tiers 1–3) to C2's optimised code (tier 4), driven by invocation and loop counters, with deoptimization back down when a speculation fails. §13

Where to go next

Further reading

Primary sources only — the specification chapters that define the memory model and class loading, the JEPs behind each runtime feature, the HotSpot documentation, and the few books worth the shelf space. These are links, but nothing on this page loads them; the module remains fully offline.

Specifications

  • JLS SE 21, Chapter 17 — Threads and Locks — the Java memory model itself: happens-before, the definition of a data race, the rules for volatile and final fields, and wait/notify semantics. Dense, but §17.4 is the one chapter every concurrency claim in this module traces back to (§1, §2, §3).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html
  • JLS SE 21, §12.4 — Initialization of Classes and Interfaces — the exact list of what triggers initialization and the locking procedure that makes it happen once (§10).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-12.html#jls-12.4
  • JVMS SE 21, Chapter 5 — Loading, Linking, and Initializing — loading, verification, preparation, resolution, and the class-loader delegation contract, from the virtual machine's side (§10).
    https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se21/html/jvms-5.html
  • Java Object Serialization Specification — the stream format, writeReplace/readResolve, and the record serialization rules (§14).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/serialization/index.html

The JEPs

  • JEP 444: Virtual Threads — the design, the mounting model, what pins, and why pooling them is wrong (§7).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/444
  • JEP 453: Structured Concurrency (Preview) — StructuredTaskScope and the argument for treating a group of subtasks as one unit (§7).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/453
  • JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning — the Java 24 change that removes the synchronized pinning described in §7.
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/491
  • JEP 439: Generational ZGC — why a concurrent collector still wants generations, and the -XX:+ZGenerational flag (§8).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/439
  • JEP 290: Filter Incoming Serialization Data and JEP 415: Context-Specific Deserialization Filters — ObjectInputFilter, jdk.serialFilter, and the filter factory (§14).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/290 · https://openjdk.org/jeps/415
  • JEP 261: Module System — the module path, readability, the unnamed and automatic modules, and the --add-* flags (§12).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/261
  • JEP 403: Strongly Encapsulate JDK Internals — the Java 17 change behind every InaccessibleObjectException (§11, §12).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/403
  • JEP 328: Flight Recorder — what JFR records and why its overhead is low enough for production (§13).
    https://openjdk.org/jeps/328

HotSpot documentation

  • HotSpot Virtual Machine Garbage Collection Tuning Guide — the generations, each collector's knobs, and the ergonomics that pick defaults for you (§8, §9).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/gctuning/index.html
  • JDK Mission Control and jfr tool documentation — recording, the event catalogue, and reading a recording from the command line (§13).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/jfapi/ · https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/jfr.html
  • java.util.concurrent package summary — the "Memory Consistency Properties" section states, in one page, every happens-before edge the library provides (§2, §4, §5).
    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html
  • JMH — Java Microbenchmark Harness — the samples directory is the documentation; read them in order, they are numbered (§13).
    https://github.com/openjdk/jmh

Books

  • Java Concurrency in Practice, Brian Goetz et al. — still the reference for §1 to §6. It predates virtual threads and CompletableFuture, but the model it teaches — publication, confinement, invariants, the memory model — is exactly what those features are built on. Read it cover to cover.
  • Optimizing Java, Benjamin J. Evans, James Gough and Chris Newland — GC internals, the JIT, JMH, JFR and the measurement discipline of §8, §9 and §13, written for working engineers rather than JVM implementers.
  • The Java Module System, Nicolai Parlog — the long-form treatment of §12, including the migration strategy for a class-path application.
  • Inside the Java Virtual Machine, Bill Venners — dated in detail (it predates HotSpot's JIT) but the clearest conceptual account of class loading, linking and the execution model in §10.
  • Effective Java, Joshua Bloch, 3rd edition — items 78 to 84 are the concurrency chapter; items 85 to 90 are the case against serialization that §14 summarises.

Tools worth knowing now

Diagnostic tools for this module's material
ToolUse it to
jcmdEverything, by pid: Thread.print, GC.heap_dump, VM.flags, JFR.start. The one tool to learn if you learn one.
jstackA thread dump; take three ten seconds apart and diff them. Prints the deadlock cycle when there is one.
jfrStart, dump and print Flight Recorder recordings without Mission Control: jfr print --events jdk.GCPhasePause rec.jfr.
jdepsFind which modules and packages a jar really uses, and which JDK internals it reaches into, before you migrate it.
jlinkBuild a runtime image containing only the modules you need — smaller containers, faster start.
async-profilerSampling CPU and allocation profiler without the safepoint bias of the JDK's built-in sampler; produces flame graphs.
JDK Mission ControlOpen a .jfr file and see GC pauses, allocation, lock contention and hot methods on one timeline.
Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT)Open a heap dump; the dominator tree and "path to GC roots" answer "what is holding this" in minutes.
Where to go from here

This is the last module of the course. Everything from here is practice on real systems, and three things will teach you more than any further reading.

  • Finish the lab's extensions. Each one — a reservation timeout, a rate limiter on the quote service, an idempotent transfer log — forces a design decision this module only described.
  • Read Java Concurrency in Practice cover to cover, now that every chapter has a section here you can check it against. Then reread §2: the memory model is the part people get wrong years into their careers.
  • Profile a real service. Attach JFR to something you run, for an hour, under real load. Read the GC log, take a thread dump during a slow request, find the three hottest methods. Nothing in §8, §9 or §13 is really yours until you have done that once on a system whose behaviour you did not already know.
